en: Preface to the Collected Annotations on the *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment*, composed by the Tóngchuān śramaṇa Jūjiǎn.

There may well be those who are awakened yet not perfect; however, there has never been anyone who is perfect yet not awakened. To be perfect yet not awakened— (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the extant portion.)
There have been such persons, yet there has never been one who was awakened and not perfect. It is manifest within the midst of daily life, yet people do not know it.
That the single nature is perfectly complete, yet they do not know it, is why they do not awaken. What the nature possesses is called "perfection" (*yuan*).

This perfection is neither diminished by the ordinary fool nor augmented by the sage or spirit; it is self-originating and self-rooted, co-arising with birth, and its perfection is identical to the Great [Ultimate].

Empty yet without deficiency or excess, identical to the great void, it receives all and transforms together with them. This is truly because habitual practice has separated from innate nature and emotion has diverged from wisdom.
When the Great Illumination is present, one dwells in a room of great darkness; drifting through long slumber, one fails to realize this awakening.
Even if one were to realize it, the realization would not be perfect. Because it is not perfect, the realization is likewise so; thus, there arises the need for cultivation.
To testify to this, it is designated as three types of practice; the reason for this distinction lies therein. What is cultivated? It is that which cultivates this.
What is realized? It is that which realizes this. Although what is cultivated differs, what is realized is one. Although what is awakened to differs, what is perfected is one. Therefore it is said:
"All sentient beings realize perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*)," yet it is not that they do not awaken to it.
To stop at what is awakened through wondrous awakening is not yet perfect; only by reaching the ultimate perfection does one stop at what is truly perfected.
From the forty-first stage downward, all stop where they ought to stop, yet they do not know the reason for their stopping.
Without cultivation, how can one reach realization? Without realization, how can one clarify one’s cultivation? When both realization and cultivation are forgotten, [one attains true liberation].
To cultivate [the path] while vainly hoping for that which is called Perfect Enlightenment is like setting out for Yue today and arriving there yesterday.

If one must first cultivate before being able to realize, and only after realization can one forget, then the twelve great bodhisattvas would never have had occasion to ask, and the assembly of one hundred thousand would never have had occasion to hear it.
Thus, the six sense-objects would be pure without being washed, and the four ailments would be cured without medicine.
Healing is stillness; illusion and quiescence are neither one nor three. Whether single or manifold, they are perfect, without before or after.
Thus, even the perfect encompassing of the three periods of time—pure, equal, and all being the Treasury of Light—is like this.

Guifeng elucidated this sutra by composing a commentary of tens of thousands of words; yet, from within its vast and extensive abundance, he abridged it into a separate version for the sake of conciseness.
From the Tang dynasty to the present, the extensive and the abbreviated versions have been practiced side by side; students in the southwest possess these texts in their own homes. How magnificent!
While the regions of Jianghuai and Jingman were for a time somewhat lacking in competition [for these teachings], Tiantai was reborn during the period of fragmentation between the Five Dynasties.

As the teachings spread through Wu and Yue, masters emerged one after another, their towering presence like the horns of emerging bulls. Thus, the words of these two schools became as transparent to one another as liver and gall.
Though Chu and Yue are but a few inches apart, they are as distant as clouds and earth; what they venerate and honor, I seek to reject, and what I proclaim and expound, they seek to criticize.
When my eminent insights differ from theirs, they will surely surround me like a wall and join together to hiss at me, striving to ensure that my doctrine does not find favor.
When those who share my own stubborn ignorance are ten thousand miles away, they will surely draw them in and incite them, desiring only to have their beaks [speak out against me].
It is rare indeed that the teachings of these two schools can avoid being submerged by mouths of inevitable contention;
this is why our late master Guyun Cui, filled with indignation and fervent resolve, compiled commentaries on this scripture to demonstrate their commonality.

He used the principles of his own school to elucidate the words shown by others, and used the profound depths of other schools to reveal the mysteries of his own, all based upon the fundamental source.
The principle does not originate from its own sect, nor is it derived merely from one's own mind; it does not align with those of one's own faction, nor does it strike down those who differ.

It holds the balance impartially and establishes its discourse with elegance, so that those who are mired in a single perspective may come to know that the limbs of a lion are of one gold, and the Yangtze, the Yellow River, the Huai, and the Ji are one water—let there be no seeking of difference within the Gui Peak school.
Nor should one seek to find commonality by ignoring what is different; rather, let that which is different remain different while that which is the same remains the same.

That five hundred generations hence there may be those who attain Guifeng through Guzhenyun, or those who attain Guifeng through Guzhenyun, is the work of Heaven—it is not something that can be achieved through the private efforts of a single individual.
Collected Commentaries on the Mahāvaipulya Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment, Volume One (Including Preface), composed by the Śramaṇa Yuancui of Taishui.
How magnificent is the nature of enlightenment!
It perfectly encompasses the ten directions; demons and Buddhas travel therein together, and matter and mind penetrate one another. Wherever there is seeing, all becomes perfected.
Deluded thoughts are wordless yet remain halfway; when the single characteristic does not exist, ten thousand functions arrive simultaneously.

Therefore, our Bhagavān dwells at the fundamental limit of the holy and the ordinary, shaking the great framework of practice and realization. Mañjuśrī asks about the cause of the original arising, and Samantabhadra consults on conduct that is like an illusion.
Thus, perfect illumination is clearly manifested and all doubt is swept away. This is the "Chapter of the Universal Eye" concerning the Three Studies.

Through mutual support, although the contemplation is perfected, it gradually assists the Vajragarbha; sentient beings are fundamentally Buddhas, yet gold mixed with ore must be smelted. Maitreya exhausts the source of the flow of craving;
through pure wisdom, one strikes the proof and cultivates the stages and positions. Below this, the methods are not fixed, as the perfect inclusion has three aspects:
majestic power, hearing and practice, and the essence of thought and cultivation. Distinguished speech opens the wheel of concentration, and they mutually prove one another.
Awakening to the realization that grasping at marks is an obstruction, he rewarded his pure karma by eliminating the root diseases of "activity, cessation, spontaneity, and extinction.
He revealed the *Pujue* (Universal Awakening) to select true friends and established the *Yuanjue* (Perfect Awakening) as a model for the three periods of practice.

With Shan-shou upholding the five eyes to circulate the teachings, the golden threads were linked and the sounds of metal and jade resonated. Now, intending to provide benefit for the Dharma, one must expound the gates of meaning; following the Tiantai school...
This single school has explored the various commentaries of Guifeng, distilling their essential points and supplementing them with what was previously heard.

It is hoped that by means of these words, one may transcend words to attain the moon and forget the finger that pointed to it. Preface written on the ninth day of the ninth month in the seventh year of the Jiading era of the Song dynasty, the year of Jiaxu.
Commentary and Sub-commentary by Chan Master Zongmi of Guifeng;
Commentary by Dharma Master Shenhuang of Zhangnan;
Commentary by Dharma Master Jushi of Dongyang.
Master Ke-guan of Zhuan-an personally examined Master Mi-yun’s *Direct Explanation of the Compassionate Chamber* (*Cishi Miaoyun Zhi jie*); I,
the śramaṇa Yuan-cui of the Tiao River, have collected the essential subtleties of various commentaries and added my own private annotations.
*The Collected Commentaries on the Mahāvaipulya Samantabhadra-bodhi-citta Sūtra of Definitive Meaning*, Volume One.
Now, a sūtra possesses a general title established by synthesizing the essential purport of its specific passages.

Here, the Dharma King himself proclaimed five titles, all of which are fully evident in the chapter concerning the Venerable Śrībhadra. The compilers have extracted the essentials and presented these five; the first two, moreover, are abbreviated *dhāraṇīs*.
The three characters "Nirvāṇa" (Ni) and these eleven characters [of the title] consist of ten distinct names derived from various scriptural sources;

because the word "Sūtra" (Jing) is a general term for the holy teachings and a common designation, it follows the general category while being applied specifically to this section. Zhuan’an’s commentary states:

"Perfect Enlightenment" (*Yuanjue*) is the single nature. "Mahāvaipulya" (*Dafangguang*) refers to that single nature as possessing essence, characteristics, and function. "Perfect Enlightenment" is the one...
Because its essence is vast, it transcends all conceptual distinctions; there is nothing outside its magnitude. Vertically, it penetrates the three periods of time;
horizontally, it pervades the ten directions. Not a single dharma precedes this Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*); Perfect Enlightenment is prior to all dharmas.
It was born before heaven and earth, encompassing heaven and earth in its greatness. Even the great void of space is but a minute thing within this Perfect Enlightenment.
Because its characteristic is square [perfect], it maintains, encompasses, and sustains with mastery;
thus, although one may wander through birth and death and receive various bodies, this Perfect Enlightenment (Vajrasattva) is never lost. Therefore, the original sutra says:
"All sentient beings realize Perfect Enlightenment," and although they rely on virtuous friends for true faith and understanding, this Perfect Enlightenment has likewise never been absent.

The *Original Sutra* states that the Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*) gives rise to all bodhi, nirvāṇa, and pāramitās, and that both the gains and losses in the instruction of bodhisattvas are the manifestations of Perfect Enlightenment.

Because its function is so vast, this nature of Perfect Enlightenment arises secretly and responds mysteriously without ceasing and without limit; therefore, the *Original Sutra* states that the nature of enlightenment is all-pervasive.
Because it is perfectly boundless, the six sense faculties are all-pervasive; the eighty-four thousand *dhāraṇī* gates pervade the entire Dharma-realm.
By means of this meaning of the Great Vaipulya, one praises and elucidates that the single nature of Perfect Enlightenment is fully endowed with such essence, attributes, and functions.
Furthermore, there is not a single dharma outside of Perfect Enlightenment; it is free from all marks and equal to empty space.

The *dhātu* (element/realm) is precisely the Tathāgata’s pure *dharmakāya*; because this *dharmakāya* encompasses all things without exception, this *Amitāyur-jñāna-dharmakāya-samādhi-sūtra* is also called the *Tathāgatagarbha*.
This scripture elucidates such a teaching; its general title, *Sūtra*, signifies that it is spoken in accordance with the ultimate principle (*tattva*).
This scripture directly points to the root-source of all phenomena, transcending all [other teachings].

Because it is definitive and unsurpassed, this scripture is called the *Mahāvaipulya-bodhimaṇḍa-vajra-samādhi-sūtra-artha-nirdeśa* (The Mahāvaipulya Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra of Definitive Meaning).
[As cited by Guifeng: "Now, according to the Tiantai school’s doctrinal principles, one must set forth five chapters:
explaining the name (*nāman*), discerning the essence (*tattva*), clarifying the core tenet (*mūla-śāsana*), and discussing the function (*prayojana*)."
Regarding the classification of teachings (panjiao): generally, when a sutra has a name, that name must necessarily have a dharma as its referent to serve as its essence (ti);
it must be based on a specific practice to serve as its principle (zong); and it must result in a specific efficacy to serve as its function (yong).

Only then can one distinguish the time of its preaching, the category of teaching to which it belongs, and whether it is gradual or sudden, partial or complete—these constitute the characteristics of the teaching (jiaoxiang). Thus, these five meanings apply to all [sutras].

Explaining the title: it is incomplete if even one element is missing. Furthermore, by combining the three aspects of person (*pudgala*), dharma, and metaphor—either individually or in combination—one establishes seven types of titles.
This sutra is titled using a single dharma; its essence (*tattva*) is the awakened nature (*bodhi-svabhāva*); its thesis (*śāstra-artha*) is the aspect of perfect illumination;

its function (*karman*) is the severance of delusions and the attainment of Buddhahood; and its doctrinal characteristic (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) is the Vaipulya, Perfect, and Sudden teaching. First, regarding the title as a single dharma:
*Mahāvaipulya-samyak-saṃbodhi*: this invokes the principle that is expressed; *Sūtra-arthaviniścaya*: this indicates the teaching that expresses it.

Both principle and teaching are "Dharma," thereby distinguishing them from persons. "Great" (*mahā*) refers to the all-pervasive Dharmakāya; "square" (*vaipulya*) refers to the sustaining track of Prajñā;
"vast" (*vaipulya*) refers to the unimpeded liberation of the awakening that is free from conceptualization. These three names signify the ultimate perfection of the Sage.

Increasing the lower realms of ordinary beings and never diminishing the body and land of Vairocana—where even the form and mind of Avīci hell are exhausted within the Great Vaipulya—there is nothing that is not Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*).

To speak of "Perfect Enlightenment" is to point directly to the essence of the Dharma; by means of "Great Vaipulya," its vast capacity and measure are manifested, which is precisely the Perfect Enlightenment that possesses this Great Vaipulya.
In Sanskrit, *sūtra*; in Chinese, it is called *qijing* (契經). "Qie" (契) means to accord with the faculties [of sentient beings].

This teaching accords with principle and its meaning is pervasive across all doctrines; it is described as the most perfect and complete, specifically termed "definitive" (*nītārtha*). It is the definitive meaning within the *sūtras*. Regarding the term *sūtra*, it is explained as "constant" (*nitya*) and "dharma.

Being constant means it cannot be altered; being dharma means it is universally followed. It extensively demonstrates the three aspects of translation: existence and non-existence, as well as practice, doctrine, and principle.
As for the general and specific categories of the *sūtras*, they are as discussed in the great works of Tiantai. Question: [As asked in] the Great Works of Tiantai... [end of fragment]
Regarding the difference between the Indic *sūtra* and the Chinese *jing*, why is it not redundant to place both titles? We reply:

the former refers generally to all sections of the canon, while the latter specifically designates this particular scripture. Since the specific is praised in contrast to the general, there is no redundancy.

Furthermore, terms such as *sūtra* were personally proclaimed by the Buddha, whereas the single character *jing* is a collective convention established by later compilers; thus, its use is logically appropriate.
Regarding the second point—that the essence is the nature of *Anala* (Perfect Enlightenment)—the Sūtra states:

"The Unsurpassed Dharma King possesses a Great *Dhāraṇī* gate called Perfect Enlightenment (*Pariniṣpanna-bodhi*)," and it is further said that "the self-nature of Perfect Enlightenment" or "the pure nature of Perfect Enlightenment.

This serves as the fundamental substance upon which the primary principle and its functions depend. Although it is ultimately realized by the Dharma Kings, it is fundamentally established even within ordinary beings.
Transcending names and severing all traces, it extends horizontally and reaches vertically; taking one is to reach three, and reaching three is to return to one.
It is the source of the myriad practices and the ultimate destination of this single teaching. To avoid treading upon the various evils, one should contemplate this essence.

The third [section], which takes the "Perfectly Illuminating Aspect of Awakening" as its principle, is the essential core of practice; this is what is called the "Essence of the Sutra. As the Sutra says: "All Tathāgatas..."

The original arising of the ground of practice all relies upon the aspect of pure, perfect-illumination awareness (*jñāna*). Once one recognizes perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*), one should give rise to perfect illumination;
this "perfect illumination" is wisdom (*prajñā*), and the "aspect of awareness" is the object (*viṣaya*). Wisdom arises from the object, and through wisdom one illuminates the object;

when object and wisdom are in silent accord, the essence of awakening (*bodhi-tattva*) becomes perfect. The illusory cataracts of ignorance (*avidyā*) are extinguished in their very place. Through this single sutra, all practices are fulfilled.
It is not that all cases are thus; although it is not fixed, gradual cultivation does not deviate from perfect illumination.

The fourth stage takes the severing of delusions and the attainment of Buddhahood as its function, thereby manifesting the essence through the completion of the practice. As the *Sūtra* says: "Only by eternally severing ignorance does one attain the Buddha-way.

Because one contemplates the characteristics of awakening and realizes that delusion is fundamentally empty, there is no need to wait for a transformation or removal; this is called "severing emptiness," a severance in which nothing is severed.
The place where [delusions] are severed is precisely where the Buddha-way is realized; thus, the establishment of the teachings and the salvation of sentient beings are fully contained herein.

Fifth, regarding the Vaipulya (fangděng) as the Perfect and Sudden (yuántùn) teaching: this provides a general classification of all sutras by establishing four teachings. The Tripiṭaka (sānzàng) teaches only birth-and-death and is primarily for the sake of the Two Vehicles.

The Shared Teaching (tōngjiào) elucidates non-arising and is the initial stage of the Mahāyāna gate. The Distinct Teaching (biéjiào) specifically clarifies the process of destroying delusions and revealing reality. Finally, the Perfect Teaching (yuánjiào) is the ultimate realization.
To clarify, the capacity of sentient beings to progress or not is further distinguished by five periods: the *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra includes both distinct and perfect teachings;

at the Deer Park, only the Tripitaka was bestowed; in the Vaipulya period, there was censure and praise to accommodate all four teachings equally; in the Prajñā period, the common and distinct teachings were brought along while the perfect teaching was correctly expounded;
and finally, in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and *Mahāparinirvāṇa* Sūtras, the provisional was opened to reveal the real, upholding the Vinaya to discuss the eternal.

To synthesize and clarify the source of these transformations would be difficult to exhaustively enumerate; yet, upon reverently reading this scripture, one sees that it is subsumed within the Vaipulya section and the Perfect and Sudden Teaching (*yuantun jiao*).
The sutra states: "This sutra is named the Great Vehicle of the Sudden Teaching, and sentient beings with sudden faculties awaken through it.
It further states: "This sutra reveals only the realm of the Tathāgata. This is the meaning of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*). Furthermore, it says: "May I now..."

"One who dwells in the Buddha’s Perfect Enlightenment should seek a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) and must not encounter non-Buddhists (tīrthika) or those of the Two Vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha). It further states:
"One should seek those with all correct knowledge and vision whose minds do not dwell on signs and who do not cling to the realms of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

Since these passages disparage the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna), their meaning ultimately returns to the Vaipulya (Mahāyāna). Yet, the scriptural text also says: "It also encompasses the gradual [approach]."
If one asks whether the cultivation of all classes of beings involves anything other than this [complete] division—namely, a partial or Hinayana approach—the answer is:
it is solely the One Complete Teaching (*ekāyana-pūrṇa-śāsana*). What is called "gradual cultivation" is merely the gradual within the complete.

It is just as in Tiantai, where the three types of *śamatha-vipaśyanā*—the complete-sudden, the gradual, and the non-fixed—all take the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*) as their object and are entirely Mahayana; yet, in terms of practice, the gradual and the non-fixed are employed as aids.

When we reach the section below that explains the meaning of this scripture, the question will naturally arise: "Since this is exclusively sudden and perfect, how does it differ from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*?

We reply: "The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* reveals the provisional (*upāya*) in a manner not comparable to this. The five chapters are now arranged; the great significance of this single scripture can be raised and put into practice.
May those who read this understand them fully.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Buddhadeva of Kaśmīra.
"Kaśmīra" is the Sanskrit term for the frontier region of North India;

it is translated here as "Low-born," because its original inhabitants were people of low status who established their own rulers. "Śramaṇa" is translated as "Diligent and Quiescent. "Diligent" refers to...
The collective name for the practice of all virtues and the cessation of all evils through renunciation is the *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment*.
According to the *Kaiyuan Catalogue of the Tripiṭaka*, the śramaṇa Buddhatrāta—whose name means "Awakening Savior" in the language of Tang—was a native of Jibin (Kaśmīra) in North India.

He translated this one-fascicle *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* at the Baima Monastery in the Eastern Capital; the date of translation is not recorded, and it is included in the continuation of the *Catalogue of Ancient and Modern Translations of the Sūtras*.
The *Tujiji* and the *Zhenyuan Catalogue* are likewise identical. Furthermore, the commentary by Dharma Master Daoquan of Zanghai Temple in Beidu states:
"The Tripiṭaka Master Buddhatoṭa of Kaśmīra brought the Sanskrit manuscript to the Divine Capital in the second year of the Changshou era, the year of the Earth-Snake (*guisi*).
At Baima Temple, he translated it into two fascicles, totaling two [volumes]."

The eighteen scrolls consist of the translated words, the oral transmission, the certification of the meaning, and the literary refinement by various virtuous masters, as detailed in the separate record;
thus, the translation is easy, being merely the rendering of Sanskrit into Chinese. According to the Zhou system, there were terms for the languages of the four directions:
those of the East were called *ji*, those of the South *xiang*, those of the West *didi*, and those of the North *yi*. Now, we are translating Western speech.
Regarding the term "yì" (translator): because the Han period was frequently occupied with affairs in the north, the translation officials were also proficient in Western languages.

When Kāśyapa Mātanga first arrived, he translated the *Sūtra of Forty-two Sections*; for this reason, the title came to be used [for translators]. Furthermore, there are four distinct types, such as "jì" (to entrust) and so forth; "yì" signifies "to penetrate" or "to communicate.

Just as the Eastern Yi, Western Rong, Southern Man, and Northern Di are collectively termed the "Four Barbarians," so too does the *Rites of Zhou* state: [the various tribes] are all encompassed under the general designation.
They are collectively termed *xiàngxū* (interpreters).
The scriptural text is broadly divided into three sections: from "Thus have I heard" up to the "Assembly of the Equal Dharma" constitutes the introductory section (*nidāna*).
From "Thereupon Mañjuśrī... down to the end of the "Chapter on Perfect Enlightenment" constitutes the main body (*samyak-artha*). Thereupon, the Venerable... [text continues].

The section from "Śrīsaṃbhava" onwards constitutes the *pariṇāmanā* (concluding) section. △ Regarding the initial *nidāna* (introduction): according to the precedent of various sūtras, it must consist of both the general and specific introductions.

Dongyang states: "In the present case, there is only the general introduction; although there is no formal 'occasioning event' (*nidāna*), the entry into samādhi and the gathering of the assembly serve as its substitute.
Furthermore, since the assembly has gathered, it cannot be for nothing; there must be extraordinary teachings [to follow]. The *Lüshù* (Brief Commentary) refers to this as the "Introduction."

The "Internal Testimony of Faith" refers to the initiation [of the teaching]: it describes how the Buddha enters the Great Radiance Treasury (Mahāprabhāsa-garbha) and dwells together with all Buddhas on the ground of the pure awakening of sentient beings, manifesting all pure lands. Therein, the Bodhisattvas, as both leaders and their retinues, enter samādhi, sharing the same realm as the Buddha.
This serves to demonstrate that cause and effect are non-different and that ordinary beings and sages share the same source, thereby revealing the essential purport of this sutra.

In the Qiuchu (Chu-ju) tradition, it is said that "entering samādhi" and "hearing together" both belong to the specific introduction (*pratyeka-nidāna*), while the general introduction (*sāmānya-nidāna*) is abbreviated regarding the two matters of the dwelling place and the assembly of the multitude.
It should be stated in full as: "At one time, the Bhagavān was at such-and-such a place together with a great multitude.
While the Sanskrit original may be complete, the translators have abbreviated it; my private opinion is that the clarity of the sūtra text [is due to this].
When Kāśyapa enters meditative absorption, manifests the land, assembles the multitude, and dwells together with them, the narrative flow is continuous.

If one were to treat the intermediate sections as separate introductory sequences, they would be disjointed and beyond comparison. When the Buddha appears in a shared realm, his manifestation of a pure land must necessarily depend on locations such as Śrāvastī or the Vulture Peak;
that the Sūtra author does not explicitly mention these places indicates the extraordinary nature of this initial resolve, which will be further explained below.
Furthermore, following Guifeng Dongyang’s initial preface, this is divided into six sections. First is "The Dharma Heard.
Thus, combining the explanations of *evam* (thus) and *mayā śrutam* (heard by me), these are terms that point directly to the Dharma: "Such a Dharma as this, I have heard from the Buddha."
The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states: "At the time of the compilation, the assembly of bodhisattvas all together requested, saying, 'Just as you have heard it, so should you speak.
The Bodhisattva who transmits the Dharma then granted permission, saying, 'So shall I speak, just as I have heard it.
The phrase 'just as' (yathā) signifies the perfection of faith. Master Sengzhao says: "These are words of faithful compliance."
If one considers the causes and effects of ordinary beings and sages within this very sutra, they are no different from the Perfect Enlightenment (Yuanjue);

thus, it is called "Suchness" (*tathatā*). Only these causes and effects are free from faults and errors, and are therefore "correct. (Guifeng’s commentary states: "The phenomena are such, yet the principle is correct. The name "Suchness" implies non-differentiation; this is called being "without error.

This refers generally to everything transmitted and expounded throughout the entire sutra as the essence of what is heard. When distinguished according to the four teachings (*catasro yānāni*), the present context applies exclusively to the [Perfect Teaching].
[Private Note: "Yuan" (Complete/Perfect)]. Second, the person who hears:
"I have heard.
This refers to Ānanda as the person who hears. Since a sage has no [conceptual] mind, he follows worldly convention and uses the terms "I" and "self. This is merely a matter of terminology.
The Lord summarizes all conditions by means of four: first, the sense organ; second, the object; third, space; and fourth, mental attention (*manasikāra*). As the treatise states:
"Ear-consciousness arises from four conditions; because these four conditions harmonize, it is called 'hearing. (Private Note:

According to the purport of this sutra, the Dharma-transmitting Bodhisattva [takes] the True Self—the non-duality of self and non-self—as the sense organ, and the wondrous [reality] wherein object and subject are neither identical nor different.)
This is the dharma-gate of the unimpeded interpenetration of the ultimate and conventional truths, as heard by the ear (Guifeng). Regarding the "single time" when the Dharma was heard:

it refers to the moment when teacher and disciple were assembled together, and the teaching and listening reached their consummation; this is termed "a single time" to distinguish it from other times. Furthermore, in all directions...
Because time and its divisions differ in duration, one speaks merely of "one time.

According to our own school, this is the time when mind and object vanish, principle and wisdom merge, and ordinary beings and sages are as they were in the union of the phenomenal and the fundamental; it is the time when all these dual dharmas are one (Guifeng).
Fourth, the Lord of Dharma.

Regarding the term *Bhagavat*, the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states that the sound *bhagavat* functions according to six meanings: first, sovereignty (*vaśitā*); second, brilliance (*tejas*); third... [and so forth].

1. Majestic and dignified; 2. Renowned in the four directions; 3. Auspicious; 4. Noble; 5. The five "non-translations" (among which this belongs to the category of *anvaya-anuvāda*, i.e., containing multiple meanings).
[Private Note: *Nirvāṇa* states that "one who can destroy afflictions is called Bhagavat," which is an alternative name for the Tathāgata.

It is also called *Bhagavān*; these are merely differences in the pronunciation of the *Brahma*-language. Regarding the teacher of this sutra, he possesses the four teachings and the three bodies (*trikāya*). When [the title] should be...
Regarding this Buddha, Guifeng said that when the *dharmakāya* and *sambhogakāya* are not distinguished, it is not the *nirmāṇakāya*. If such a definitive body is what is meant, what is its standard?
Now, I maintain that it must be the *saṃbhogakāya* of the *dharmatā-kāya*, the sublime and distinctive form (*viśiṣṭa-rūpa*). Yet, there are two types of this sublime and distinctive form:
first, the manifestation described in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* as having marks numbering as many as the atoms in a hundred billion worlds; second, the manifested form, which is the *nirmāṇakāya*.
The thirty-two marks of the Sahā world pertain merely to the resonance between the middle way and karmic consciousness;
each mark accords with the nature (*dharmatā*), and these marks are boundless. The *Lotus Sūtra*’s Glorious and Extraordinary Body (*vairocana-viśeṣa-kāya*) is precisely this:

since this sūtra manifests in the Pure Land for those of the Perfect and Sudden capacity, if it were not a manifestation of the Glorious and Extraordinary Body, who would serve as the Teacher? (Cishì). Fifth, the places where he preached the Dharma.
Entering the Samādhi of the Great Luminous Treasury of Supernatural Powers, they are sustained by the radiant adornment of all Tathāgatas;
this is the ground of pure awakening for all sentient beings, wherein body and mind are extinguished in tranquility, equal to the primordial limit, perfect throughout the ten directions, non-dual,
and in accordance with the non-dual realm, manifesting all pure lands.
The "Treasury" (garbha) refers to the Dharma-realm as the nature of jewels; the arising of faith in suchness is the fundamental source of all Buddhas and sentient beings.
Its essence is the nature of spiritual powers and radiant light, wherein countless meritorious functions are all contained.
Since hundreds of thousands of penetrations and lights all arise from this, it is called a "Treasury. It is also termed the "Dharma-nature Land" and the "Land of Constant Quiescent Light."

The cessation of all discursive thought and the merging of wisdom with principle is called "entry. Abiding within the treasury [of the Tathāgata-garbha] without undergoing any sensations is called "right reception" (samyaksamādhi).
This scripture teaches that the locus of reality is suchness within phenomena themselves; it does not posit a separate, eternal quiescence apart from this Sahā world.
Because the enlightened nature discussed in the orthodox tradition is equal and impartial, entering the Great Samādhi is precisely this.
The *Śūraṅgama-samādhi* contains the treasury of the principle of the three virtues (*tri-guṇa*). This treasury is perfectly complete; ordinary beings and sages share the same source.

It extends horizontally and exhausts the vertical [of time], being inconceivable and singular. Yet, the principle does not manifest itself; rather, it descends through the teaching from that principle.

The Teacher’s body and land manifest their entire essence as function; therefore, it is said: "Within the non-dual realm, all pure lands appear. The pure lands thus manifested are precisely what is explained.

The general preface to the *Dharmapada* also encompasses its specific intent, which can be understood; the ancients all maintained that the "Great Luminous Treasury" (*Mahā-ābhāsvara-garbha*) is the locus where this sutra was preached.
Furthermore, in his response to King Shu, Wen Guanxi stated: "That which is expounded by the Sudden Vehicle directly reveals the daily activities of sentient beings as they manifest before them;
it does not belong to past or present, nor is it contingent upon time or place. Moreover, the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* and others also clarify the state of abiding.

Is this not the Sudden Vehicle? As for what was previously stated regarding "at one time," how could there be no time? Furthermore, the Treasury of Radiance (*Prabhāsa-kośa*) is the very basis for the manifestation of lands;
how can you rely on that basis to establish the location of the teaching while remaining ignorant of the lands that are manifested?

Since both [previous] explanations are untenable, my current interpretation shall be divided into two parts: first, entering the nature of profound awakening; second, realizing the manifestation within non-duality.

The first section of the "Earth" (Bhūmi) further has three parts: first, the heading on the wondrous samādhi of the three virtues; second, from "all" (*sarva*) onwards, the manifestation that the bodies of ordinary beings and sages are identical;

third, from "body and mind" (*kāyacitta*) onwards, the clarification of the functions of supernatural powers, radiance, concentration, and wisdom, which are pervasive and perfect in accordance with the essence.

The "Treasury" (*garbha*) is precisely the Dharma-body; the two "functions" are the three virtues fully present within that essence, termed the "Secret Treasury," wherein wisdom is in profound accord.

Because this is the objective realm, it is called "entry. "Samādhi-samyak-pratipatti" (入三昧正受) is a dual manifestation of both the Indic and the Chinese; because one does not fall into erroneous thought, it is called "samyak-pratipatti" (正受).

That which is "upheld by the light-adornment of all Tathāgatas" means that they are of one identical perfect luminosity, mutually interpenetrating and illuminating one another, abiding securely without loss.
That which is "the ground of pure awakening for all these sentient beings" refers to the single limit where the true and the delusive coincide.

The essence of defilement is originally empty; from the beginning, it shares the same basis. This "equal primordial limit" (benji) signifies vertical depth, while "perfectly filling the ten directions" signifies horizontal pervasiveness.

As for "non-dual compliance," it means being eternally one and unchanging, because body and mind, the environment and its inhabitants, birth and buddhahood, self and other, are all equally in a state of quiescence.
The manifestation of various pure lands is the substance of the Dharma-realm of tranquil light (jiguang), universally appearing according to the capacities of beings.
One should see that there are three lands. This sutra addresses [the assembly] entirely as the Dharma-body (dharmakāya) and is properly the Land of True Reward (vipākabhūmi).
Although at the end of the sutra there are eight classes of miscellaneous assemblies who pervade the other two lands, the land manifested here is not separate from the Sahā world;

its meaning is identical to the purification through the "three transformations" in the *Lotus Sutra*. Question: Since the land has already been manifested as pure, is the Buddha’s body not his constant body? Answer: It is manifested.
If there is no manifestation of the formless, how does this differ from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, which is likewise so? Do not harbor doubts regarding this.

While the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* may be said to "manifest" by opening up the provisional (*upāya*), how could the earlier sūtras possibly "distinguish the superior from the inferior"? This is because in the past, the two vehicles were subject to censure and refinement;

it was only when they were made to manifest [the truth] that they were called "Exalted and Distinct" (*viśiṣṭa*). Now, in contrast to the bodhisattvas, whether such a manifestation occurs or not makes no difference.

Fanghuazhiyi (Fanghua) and Guishan held that "non-dual" (*advaya*) is the essence and "conforming" (*anuloma*) is the function; the Translator [Kumārajīva] reversed the phrasing and did not fully capture this, so it should rather be read as "conforming to non-duality.
Huanshi held that "non-dual" is the substance and "conforming" is the function. Zhijie held that all the characters are merely glosses.
I fear none of these views are entirely correct; let the reader examine this carefully. (Private Note). Sixth, the assembly of those who heard together.
He was accompanied by one hundred thousand great Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, whose names were: Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva,
Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, Samantanetra Bodhisattva, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva, Maitreya Bodhisattva, Viśuddhamati Bodhisattva,
Vaśavartin-tejas Bodhisattva, Ghoṣadatta Bodhisattva, Sarvakarmāvaraṇaviśodhana Bodhisattva, and Samantabodhi Bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattva Perfect Enlightenment, the Bodhisattva Worthy and Virtuous Chief, and others as their leaders, together with their retinues,
all entered into samādhi and dwelt together in the Tathāgata’s assembly of the equal Dharma.

First, the enumeration of the number and listing of the names; second, their commonality with other [categories]. Regarding "the Buddhas entering meditative absorption and the Bodhisattvas," the full term is *bodhisattva-mahāsattva*.
*Bodhi* is translated as "awakening" (*jue*); *sattva* is translated as "sentient being" (*youqing*); *mahā* means "great.
These sentient beings believe in the Great Dharma, understand the Great Meaning, give rise to the Great Mind, and proceed toward the Great Fruit, practicing the Great [Vehicle].
Because he practices and realizes the Great Way, in the *Avataṃsaka*, those prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) are called *mahāsattvas*, whereas here [in the *Śūraṅgama*], they are on the stages.

(Guifeng) lists twelve names, respectfully following the commentaries of Tiantai and interpreting them through the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*). Contemplation is the root of the myriad practices (*sarvacaryā*) of a bodhisattva;
thus, Mañjuśrī is translated as "Wondrous Virtue" (*Miaode*), and the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states that he "clearly perceives."
The Buddha-nature is like Samantabhadra; because he contemplates the three virtues in union and is secretly and perfectly endowed with them, he is named "Wondrous Virtue" (Miaode).
He is also called "Wondrous Auspiciousness" (Miaojixiang) and "Samantabhadra" in the *Mahāśāstra* and the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*, respectively, both being titled "Pianji" (Universal Auspiciousness).

Now, abiding at the summit of the path of subduing [afflictions], his cause is all-pervasive, hence "Universal" (Pu); after severing the path [of afflictions], he is adjacent to the ultimate sage, hence "Virtuous" (Xian). If...
If one does not unify the mind through the three contemplations, how could one reach the pinnacle of universal subjugation?

One with the Universal Eye contemplates the mind through the three contemplations and universally perceives that all phenomena, from ordinary beings to Buddhas, are non-dual. This encompasses both compassion and wisdom: universally perceiving all phenomena as pure is called Great Wisdom, the Universal Eye;
universally perceiving all sentient beings attaining Buddhahood is called Great Compassion, the Universal Eye. This is the Vajragarbha.

The Vajra possesses three meanings: being "solid" (*kaṭhina*), it cannot be destroyed by anything; being "sharp" (*tīkṣṇa*), it can shatter all things; and being "luminous" (*prabhāsvara*), its essence is translucent.

When the contemplation of the mind (*cittāvalokana*) is endowed with these three virtues, it is called the *garbha* (womb/treasury) of Maitreya. This is translated here as "Maitreya" (the Compassionate One). There are three kinds of compassion: that directed toward sentient beings (*sattvālambana*), that directed toward phenomena (*dharmālambana*), and that which is objectless (*anālambana*).

These correspond respectively to the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*). Furthermore, "Maitreya" is derived from the name [of his father]. *Note: The final character "阿" (Ā) appears to be a transcription marker or an abbreviation for the Sanskrit vowel.*
*Eita* (Avalokiteśvara) means "Unsurpassed" (*anabhibhūta*). Because the three contemplations can purify the three delusions, he is named Pure Wisdom (*viśuddha-prajñā*).

Because the three contemplations can subdue the three obstructions and the four māras, he is named Sovereign in Majestic Virtue (*vibhu-tejas*). By virtue of the three contemplations, he attains the three *dhāraṇīs* and the four unhindered eloquences, hence he is named Sound of Eloquence (*ghoṣa-viśuddha*).
Because the three contemplations serve as the antidotes to the three paths, he is named Purifier of All Karmic Obstructions (*sarva-karma-āvaraṇa-viśodhana*).

The three contemplations universally observe that all phenomena return to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*); this is called Universal Enlightenment (*Prajñā*), which is also the Perfect Enlightenment (*Pariniṣpanna-bodhi*).

"Worthy and Good Leader" (*Bhadramukha*) means that "worthy" refers to one who is a near-sage, while "good" refers to one who accords with principle; thus, the three contemplations accord with principle and serve as the foremost of all virtues.
(Dongyang) Dwelling together in the Tathāgata’s assembly of equal Dharma, who is the host and who are the companions? Who is...?

The questioner and the respondent are none other than those who sport within the great ocean of Perfect Enlightenment (Zhuan-an). Regarding the entry into samādhi in this sutra compared to other sutras, there are three differences in its presence or absence:
first, while other sutras describe both entering and emerging from samādhi, this one only mentions the entry at the conclusion of the assembly, with no sign of emerging;
second, other sutras speak only of the substance of samādhi, as the *Lotus Sutra* says: "Without... [and so forth].
Regarding the meaning of the measure [of this sutra], the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* states: "The profound dharma-nature.

In this present sutra, it is fully explained that both its essence (*tǐ*) and function (*yòng*) enter the Great Radiant Treasury of Supernatural Powers (*abhijñā-mahāprabhāsa-garbha*). Its essence is to manifest all pure lands within the non-dual realm; its function is likewise so.

Thirdly, while the teaching masters of other sutras enter this state alone, the teaching master and his retinue (*parivāra*) of this sutra enter together. Why is this so? It is because of this sutra...

Since the meaning of the *Awakening of Perfect Enlightenment* (*Yuanjue*) regarding *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* is such that there is no wisdom without dhyāna, one must remain in meditative concentration from beginning to end;

this is especially true for the twelve Bodhisattvas who initiate this sutra, as they must first enter samādhi to discern the capacities of beings in the present and future before posing their questions.
Furthermore, because they possess the two kinds of adornment, they are able both to inquire and to respond. This teaching is exclusively for those of perfect capacity; behold the *nāga*.

If one is constantly in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), how could there be any emerging from it? When concentration and wisdom are integrated in essence, there must necessarily be the wondrous application of the Dharma.

Although the *Lotus Sūtra* is likewise pure and perfect, as it does not exclusively focus on cessation and contemplation (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*) but rather intends to reveal and clarify the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*), it requires emerging from concentration.

Since the capacities of those with inferior faculties have not yet been fully understood, how could this be the same as entering into *samādhi*? (Zhangnan) At the end of the sūtra, regarding the circulation [of the text], there is already...

How could it be appropriate for the entire assembly of principal and attendant figures to enter samādhi together? One might fear that this would make the discourse identical to the Buddha’s own entry [into samādhi].

Moreover, since there is no mention of emerging from samādhi at the end, and this differs from the *Prabhāsa* (Light) Sūtra, it would seem that the preaching and listening must have occurred entirely while remaining in samādhi from beginning to end.

Since the questioner already stated that he rose from his seat to pay homage to the Buddha, the Teacher praised each [of his questions] and encouraged him to expound upon them; one merely fears that this constitutes the introduction.
The final translator merely provided a brief introductory text. Since the Buddha’s realm is difficult to conceive, let later worthies examine it further.

Furthermore, although the *Lotus Sūtra* mentions the essence of concentration (*samādhi*) only in its description of the emission of light and the manifestation of auspicious signs, why would this be restricted solely to the essence?
Although this is not a primary concern, it is impossible not to know it (Private Note).

△ Second, the section on the correct teaching (*samyak-artha*) consists of eleven questions and answers. Guifeng [Zongmi] judges that the first clarifies understanding and faith (*adhimukti*), while the subsequent ten clarify practice and realization (*pratipatti*).
Furthermore, he distinguishes between superior, middling, and inferior faculties. Dongyang [Huihai] divides it into seven sections.

Master Xian (Xianshi) considers the first chapter to correspond to the "opening of understanding" (*kaijie*) in the *Mohe Zhiguan*, and the latter ten chapters to correspond to the "ten vehicles" (*shicheng*). A brief evaluation follows the *Shangnan Shu*.

To the south of Mount Zhang, [the author] himself composed two versions, an extensive and an abbreviated one. The first five sections briefly clarify Perfect Enlightenment (*yuanjue*), while the latter six sections extensively clarify Perfect Enlightenment;

the division of chapters and their sequential development are extremely detailed. Master Cishi [Zongmi] held that the first two chapters provide intellectual understanding (*kaixie*) and the latter nine chapters concern spiritual practice (*xiuxing*).
Now, I say that each of these masters excels in his own particular merit, so I have no leisure to offer a comprehensive critique; I shall simply follow the tradition of the North.
Feng follows the Tiantai tradition in treating the three types of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* as all belonging to the Mahāyāna, equally taking the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) as their object.

Categorizing them according to practice and the capacities of practitioners, they are divided into three sections: the gradual, the indeterminate, and the auxiliary to the Great [Vehicle]. The first two chapters clarify the realization of the perfect-enlightenment practice;

the next four chapters clarify the realization of the gradual practice; and the final five chapters clarify the realization of the indeterminate practice. Within the first section, there are further two parts. ○ [End of Section] ○
The first section, the Chapter on Mañjuśrī, correctly elucidates the practice and realization of the Perfect and Sudden [Vehicle]. It has three parts. First, the formal posture of the inquiry:
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī rose from his seat amidst the great assembly and prostrated at the Buddha’s feet.
[The text] says: "Having circumambulated three times, he knelt long with palms joined and addressed the Buddha.
This is the narration of the compilers. Regarding the two characters "yú shì" (於斯), Guishan calls them words that point toward the Dharma;

Cishi calls them words that follow upon what preceded. Furthermore, to seek the meaning of "yú shì" by conflating the general introduction (*sūtra-nidāna*) with the specific [introduction] is an error.
At the beginning of each subsequent chapter, it says, "Thereupon," which should be understood as follows: "Immediately rose from his seat" refers to the *Qu-lǐ* (Book of Ritual), which states:
"One rises when requesting to begin a lesson; one rises when requesting further instruction. "Circumambulating to the right" is the ritual practice of Western India.

Regarding "kneeling long" (*chángguì*), some say both knees touch the ground, which differs from "kneeling on the heels" (*qiáo guì*). To request something from a superior is called "to report" (*bái*). [Private Note: "Immediately from his seat."
Regarding "arising" and so forth: from the essence of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), the function of compassion and salvation arises.

To prostrate with one’s own most supreme [head] to the Buddha’s most lowly feet is the ultimate form of reverence. Reverence is a mental action (*manas-karma*); since mental action has no physical form, it is manifested through body and speech.
In the Sūtra, the statement "and spoke these words" marks the beginning, while the subsequent praise of Great Compassion constitutes vocal action (*vāk-karma*). Thus ends the right-hand section.

Circumambulating signifies following the meaning; the three circuits symbolize conforming to the nature of enlightenment. "Three" refers to revering the Three Jewels as one with the Buddha, while "extinguishing" refers to eliminating the evils of the three paths [of affliction, karma, and suffering] and so forth.
Kneeling on both knees signifies that safety and peril do not alter one's resolve. Joining the palms signifies faith and understanding;

body and mind merge, and the objective realm and the subjective consciousness intersect (Guifeng). In the commentaries of Tiantai, joining the palms is often used to represent the union of the provisional and the real (Dongyang). These two [meanings] are consistent.

The formal presentation of the questions consists of three parts: first, questioning the causal practices of the Tathāgata; second, questioning the bodhisattva’s production of the resolve for enlightenment (*cittotpāda*);

and third, questioning the separation from views in the final age. Regarding the question as to why Mañjuśrī’s rank is equal to that of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), and how he asks about the meaning of producing the resolve:

if this question is considered as being established through provisional means initiated in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings, then there is nothing that cannot be explained. However, if it is considered...

Although the vertical and deep practice still involves subsequent minds, the horizontal discussion of the ten vehicles and ten objects may also allow for a lack of realization, as this constitutes a question arising from a stage that remains shallow.

Therefore, the fact that Mañjuśrī could not rouse the woman from her concentration in the *Sarvabuddhasamāyoga-sūtra*, and that the great bodhisattvas subsequently raised questions, can be understood by analogy with this principle. (Zhuangnan)
The initial question concerns the causal practices of the Tathāgata:

"O Greatly Compassionate World-Honored One, we pray that for the sake of this assembly of gathered Dharma-practitioners, you will explain the Tathāgata’s original arising of pure causal-ground practices."

Although the fruition possesses ten thousand virtues, the Great Compassion is singled out for mention; the consultation on the essentials of the Dharma is fundamentally for the sake of sentient beings.
Possessing the Ten Epithets, he is honored as the World-Honored One; seeking to realize Perfect Enlightenment, he is thus called the Assembly of the Dharma.

In the past, when the Buddha first gave rise to the Bodhicitta, he perfectly illumined the source, whereby the defiled substance was entirely purified. Relying upon this, he entered into the Unsurpassed Awakening.
The city is thus called "The Original Arising of the Dharma-Practice of the Ground of Purity. Those who seek Buddhahood must rectify their cause;
if the cause is not true, the fruit will ultimately not be achieved. Below, the Tathāgata extensively expounds upon this question, while the other two [sections] are briefly concluded.
(Private Note: Past Bodhisattvas are the ground of the present Tathāgatas; present Bodhisattvas are truly...)
From the stage of the causal ground of future Tathāgatas until their eternal attainment of the fruit of Buddhahood by severing ignorance—who could do so without relying on this correct path?
Therefore, it is said below: "It enables sentient beings of the final age not to fall into false views" (Cishi).
Second, the question concerning the bodhisattva’s arousal of the mind,
and the explanation that when a bodhisattva arouses a pure mind within the Mahāyāna, they remain far removed from all afflictions;
the essence of the Mahāyāna is original and initial awakening, and within this awakening, one arouses the *bodhicitta* and maintains right mindfulness of reality.
As before, it is pure. In the verse, it is simply called the "bodhicitta. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:
"To cultivate various roots of goodness while forgetting the bodhicitta is to be possessed by Māra. Once one is possessed, there are many faults;

therefore, I request that you generate the causes and conditions for the awakening mind so that you may be forever freed from this. Furthermore, even if one forgets it in the interim, one is still possessed.
How much more so for those who have not yet resolved their minds—how could their various practices ever be free from such karma? Once the resolve has been made, it is never lost;

because it is not lost, the delusions of Māra cannot disturb them. When the Buddha answers that one is free from both existence and non-existence, when awakening-illumination is also extinguished, and when subject and object are severed, this is precisely being free from all ailments.
This is what is called "not giving rise to any mind," which is truly giving rise [to the resolve].
This is the pure mind (Guifeng). Now, regarding the arousal of the mind according to the Great Teaching, one should believe that all phenomena are the substance of Mind-only;

that the entire Mind is fully present and gives rise to all things; that they are mutually pervasive and mutually inclusive; that they simultaneously negate and illuminate; and that they are devoid of intrinsic nature and devoid of characteristics—being entirely true and entirely suchness.

In this state, the mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings are non-dual and without distinction. Thus, the delusions of worldly toil and false conceptualization are themselves the Great Perfect Enlightenment.
If it were not thus, it would not be the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* (private note).
[The Buddha] asked three times about being free from views in the final age,
so that sentient beings of future ages who seek the Mahāyāna would not fall into false views.

After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma (Saddharma) and the Semblance Dharma (Pratirūpakadharma) each lasted for one thousand years, followed by the Final Dharma (Paścimadharma) for ten thousand years. This "Final Dharma" constitutes the End Age;
as it is far removed from the Sage, there is deep cause for concern. Therefore, among the manifest benefits, [Guifeng] specifically provides this pointed instruction for the End Age:
those who resolve their minds [to practice] will mostly be hindered by partial expedients, various demons, and external paths. Without correct understanding, how can one avoid [such obstacles]?
Prostrating with utmost sincerity (Private Commentary:
three times), having spoken these words, one should cast down the five limbs upon the ground. Thus one should request three times, beginning again after each cycle ends.
To prostrate while speaking correctly is not the proper ritual; if the five limbs—the four members of the body plus the head—are not fully extended even once, it is incomplete.
If devotion exceeds three prostrations, it becomes cluttered and chaotic; therefore, the three circumambulations from beginning to end manifest the true mind.

Although the Buddha already knew this, he established this model as a standard for emulation (Guifeng). To reach the number three is the ultimate expression of reverence for the person and gravity toward the Dharma (Dongyang).
Second, the Buddha’s response in three parts: first, his praise and consent.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying: "Excellent, excellent, son of good family!

It is well that you are able to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding the dharmic practices of the causal stage for the sake of all bodhisattvas, and for the sake of all sentient beings in the final age who seek the Mahāyāna, so that they may abide in correct retention and not fall into false views. Listen attentively now, and I shall explain."
"I shall speak for you.
First he praises, then he grants permission, and again he says "Excellent! (*sādhu*). The *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* commentary states that this is the ultimate form of excellence.

Regarding the term "good son" (*kulaputra*), one who accords with principle is called a good son. As for the phrase "I urge you all," although it is the word of a single person, it is spoken [with such authority].
When the minds of the multitude attain right abiding, the holder of the Dharma rests in the ocean of awakening and sustains the myriad practices;
he should admonish them to be discerning and not allow themselves to be distracted by other conditions. (Guifeng) Vimalakīrti said:

"Do not use a mind of arising and ceasing to speak of the dharma of true reality. Since it cannot be spoken with a mind of arising and ceasing, it likewise cannot be heard with a mind of arising and ceasing. (Dongyang)
Second, the Receiving of the Mandate.
At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, having received the instruction with joy, along with the great assembly, listened in silence.

Having been granted permission to speak, they desired to hear it with longing; purifying themselves and emptying their minds, they withdrew their gaze and turned their hearing inward, remaining in profound stillness.

The eleven subsequent sections following the passage on "waiting to listen" are all explained in this same manner (Guifeng). III. The Direct Answer has two parts: A. The Extended Exposition; B. The Verse Summary. A. The Extended Exposition has two parts: 1. The Broad Response to the First Question;

2. [The Response to the Second Question]. 1. The Broad Response to the First Question has two parts: A. General Demonstration; B. Specific Explanation. Within the General Demonstration, there are three points:

"Perfectly Awakened" (*yuanjue*) is the essence (*ti*) of the sutra; "Perfectly Illuminating" (*yuanzhao*) is the school (*zong*) of the sutra; and "Permanently Severing Ignorance" (*yongduan wuming*) is the function (*yong*) of the sutra.
Furthermore, this refers to practicing based on the essence; once the primary principle is established, it becomes functional.

In the subsequent detailed explanation, first ignorance is shown, next enlightened wisdom is clarified, and finally the essence of enlightenment is revealed. This constitutes the realization of cultivation through the penetration of delusion; such cultivation must necessarily rely upon the essence.
Those who examine these interrelated general and specific aspects should understand that there are two initial headings. First, establishing the teaching based on the essence.
"Good son, the Unsurpassed Dharma King possesses a great gateway of dhāraṇī called Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*),
from which flow forth all pure *tathatā*, bodhi, nirvāṇa, and the pāramitās, thereby instructing bodhisattvas."

The Tathāgata possesses supreme mastery over all dharmas through the *dhāraṇī*—translated as "total retention" (*saṃgraha*)—which signifies that within the essence of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*), there are sands-of-the-Ganges virtues and functions that have been maintained without loss from the very beginning. "Great" refers to the boundless nature of the essence itself;
"gate" has the meaning of entering and exiting. Heze (Heshang Moheyan) said: "The single word 'knowledge' is the source of all wonders."
The gates named "Perfect Enlightenment" (Yuanjue) refer to the aforementioned characteristics of meaning; now they point to the essence of the Dharma.

It is not that there is some separate dharma flowing out from within to the exterior; rather, it is based upon the nature of enlightenment (*bodhi*) that the merits of these various gates are manifested without end, and their application is without weariness—this is what is meant by "flowing forth. *Bodhi* translates as "enlightenment," while *nirvāṇa* translates as "extinction."
It is called "perfect quiescence" (*parinirvāṇa*) because the enlightened nature is already perfect and there is no phenomenon that is not quiescent.

As for *pāramitā*, this is translated as "reaching the other shore. In brief, there are six types corresponding to the six obscurations; collectively, they counteract all defilements, numbering eighty-four thousand.
They do not merely flow forth from the fruit of the principle, but also pertain to the cause. By practicing in reliance upon them, one can produce [the result].
"Understanding" (jie) is termed "instruction" (jiaoshou); because it is like taking a treasure from within one's robe to show it to others, it is said to "flow forth.

Because it reaches the ultimate ten realms, it is called "all-encompassing. Because it distinguishes itself from [the state of] being entangled in afflictions, it is called "pure True Suchness" (*viśuddha-tathatā*).
Here, "bodhi" is the ultimate (paramārtha), and "nirvāṇa" is the conventional (saṃvṛti). Furthermore, regarding the *pāramitās*, they are based upon the objects of these three truths.
This gives rise to eighty thousand gates of practice. "The one who instructs Bodhisattvas" refers to the capacity of the recipient of the teaching (Zhāngnán).
The Unsurpassed Dharma King is the Buddha of ultimate fruition. Now, the Middle Way Dhāraṇī is also called Perfect Enlightenment (*yuanjue*); who does not possess it? What dharma is not so?
It is spoken of as "the Buddha possesses it" because it is realized through direct knowledge; this very Perfect Enlightenment is the essence itself.
To speak of the gate as the complete nature arising through cultivation, establishing teachings based on principle, and expressing this in words—this is merely what is said.
That which is meant is: "From the root of non-abiding, all dharmas are established. Even the worldly teaching says: "Who can exit without passing through a door? Who does not follow this path?
[The author] considers it improper that the *Cishi* (Compassionate Chamber) takes the *Yuanjue* (Perfect Enlightenment) as the gate of penetration. (Private Note).
Second, illuminating the nature to sever delusions:
"The original ground of practice for all Tathāgatas relies upon the aspect of perfect illumination and pure awakening; only by forever severing ignorance do they achieve the Buddha-way."
Awakening is the nature (*prakṛti*); perfect illumination is cultivation (*bhāvanā*). When the nature fully gives rise to cultivation, one accords with the nature through cultivation.
Because the nature is not defiled, it is called "pure. Because the substance of ignorance is empty, evil in cultivation is immediately the nature;

because it is ultimately quiescent, it is called "permanently severed. One who achieves the Way is one whose awakened wisdom is all-pervasive; once achieved, everything is achieved, for all phenomena share the same essence.
When one person awakens to the truth and the void is dissolved, this is precisely the meaning of the Perfect Buddha’s realization of the Way.
Since it is so for one Buddha, it is likewise for all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time (Private Note). Second, the explanation of the subject matter has three parts:

first, a detailed clarification that the characteristics of delusion are empty in essence; second, [the following]; first, clarifying the characteristics of delusion has three parts: first, the inquiry.
What is ignorance (*avidyā*)?

It is called ignorance because one does not comprehend the single dharma-realm (*ekadharmadhātu*). There are both general and specific branches, as well as fundamental afflictions (*mūlakleśa*), residual tendencies (*vāsanā*), and outflows (*anuśaya*).

Now, by means of perfect illumination, the fundamental primary delusions, the general [delusions], and the two types of residual tendencies are all fully encompassed and severed without exception. (Private Note)
The second section has two parts. First, the formal definition:
"Good son, all sentient beings, from time immemorial, have undergone various inversions, just like a person who has lost their way and confuses the four directions."
The three teachings and nine realms have not yet realized the nature; they are entirely subsumed within the "all-encompassing" (sarva-dharmāḥ).

Because their arising has no initial characteristic, it is called "beginningless. Because awakening is taken as delusion, it is called "inversion. Once the aperture of emotion is pierced, the wild waves flow unrestrained;
errors and confusions abound in many paths, and conceptual attachments are manifold. Therefore, it is said to be "various" (*nānāvidha*). [Cishì] now proceeds to definitively establish its falsity.
It merely speaks of "inversion" (*viparyāsa*) without yet revealing its specific characteristics. When there is inversion, there is grasping; when one is inverted, one becomes deranged.
It is like a person who, suddenly arriving at a riverbank or entering a village, is abruptly deluded in mind such that they take east for west.

Since one direction is mistaken, the other three follow suit; thus it is said that the directions have shifted. Yet, while one is in the midst of this confusion, the directions themselves do not actually change. Suddenly, one awakens.

Upon awakening, one returns to the original state; yet when one investigates this delusion, it leaves no trace—having no place of origin in the past and no place of departure in the present (Guifeng).
Second, the explanation of characteristics has two parts. First, the illustration of characteristics through both principle and metaphor.

To falsely recognize the four elements as the characteristics of one's own body and the reflected shadows of the six sense objects as the characteristics of one's own mind is like a person with diseased eyes seeing flowers in the sky or a second moon.
When the four elements combine, they are conventionally designated as a "body"; the mind that perceives and deliberates exists because of sense objects, like a shadow following a form.

Because form arises, it is called a "conditioned shadow. Sentient beings do not know that the eternally abiding true mind—the essence of pure luminosity—pervades the three periods of time and extends throughout the atoms of all lands.
They falsely cling to body and mind, giving rise to various fetters and delusions, like discarding a hundred thousand clear, vast oceans to recognize only a single floating bubble.
The above has clarified the nature of inversion; now, by way of analogy, we shall address the current state of being lost in one's direction.
Because of the body and mind, they are likened to flowers seen by one with cataracts; what is illustrated here is the aforementioned inversion. Because of inversion, attachment arises.

Just as one with cataracts sees flowers where there are none, so too do the principles of the mind, objects, and phenomena all conform to this analogy. (Private Note: When a person with cataracts looks into empty space, there are no flowers, yet they falsely see flowers.
When pressing the eyes while gazing at the lunar disk, one sees a separate moon beside it. Empty flowers and illusory moons are all metaphors.)
False views may also be separately correlated with two metaphors: the flower represents the misapprehension of the body, and the moon represents the misapprehension of the mind (Guifeng).
These two serve as metaphors for manifesting delusion.
Good son, in emptiness there are truly no flowers; it is only the sick person who falsely clings to them. Because of this false clinging, they are not only deluded regarding this void.
The nature of space itself is also deluded regarding the place where those real flowers arise; because of this, there is the false existence of saṃsāra.
Since space originally has no flowers, yet one clings to them as existing, it is called "delusion" (*moha*).

Because one does not reflect upon oneself when flowers arise from an eye-disease (*timira*), it is called "confusion" (*bhrānti*). Because one clings to that place where real flowers arise as being truly existent, it is called "name" (*nāman*).

In the analogy of the "real flower" (the *citsi* or "compassion-chamber") and the moon, the flower should likewise be called the "moon. In reality, there are no two; those who "pinch" [their eyes] are merely deluded attachments.

Because the scriptural text is abbreviated, it does not state this explicitly. Having clung to the idea that the flower arises from empty space, they fail to realize it arises from a visual impairment (*timira*).
This impairment is actually the place where the flower arises; it is not a real flower. They merely marvel at how flowers appear within empty space, failing to see their true origin.
One perceives a film before the eyes and externally laments the suffering of body and mind, unaware that deluded sentiments are harbored within (Guifeng).
Because of delusion one creates karma; because of karma one receives retribution, wandering through the six realms of existence in a cycle of birth and death.
Failing to recognize the source of delusion, how can one attain liberation? (Private Note): The Three Bonds.
Therefore, it is called ignorance.
Second, revealing that its substance is empty. First, indicating that its substance is empty:
"Good son, this ignorance has no real substantiality."
Cultivating evil is itself the substance of the obstruction of nature, which is fundamentally void (private note). Second, it is revealed through analogy: it is like a person in a dream;
while dreaming, it is not non-existent, yet upon waking, nothing is to be found. It is like various empty flowers vanishing into space;
one cannot say there is a specific place where they are extinguished. Why? Because there is no place of their arising.

First, by means of the analogy of the dream-incident, it was shown that ignorance is fundamentally empty; next, by citing the "flowers in the sky," it was revealed that the dream has no arising or ceasing, because there is no place where such non-arising occurs.
Previously, this was based on the "clouded eye" as the perceiver, which is called the actual place where the flowers arise;

now, it refers to the empty space confronted [by the eye], wherein arising and ceasing cannot be found. Guifeng used this to distinguish between delusion and enlightenment; Master Huan did not accept this distinction, yet Guifeng did not reject Huan’s view.
To take these illusory flowers for real flowers is likewise not yet the case (Private Note). The three fetters cause cyclic existence;
all sentient beings falsely perceive arising and ceasing within that which is non-arising, and for this reason it is called "revolving in birth and death."
Although it is said that there is no birth, because of deluded vision, it is called "revolving in saṃsāra" (Private Note).
Second, explaining the accomplishment of the perfectly illuminating awakened wisdom. First, realizing that the source of delusion is fundamentally empty.

Good son, when a Tathāgata cultivates Perfect Enlightenment while on the causal ground, he knows that these are like flowers in the sky; thus there is no cyclic wandering, nor is there a body or mind that undergoes birth and death.
Because they are not created, they have no inherent nature; because they have no inherent nature, they do not exist.

Regarding "one who cultivates Perfect Enlightenment," this refers to the aforementioned realization and penetration of knowledge (Private Note: that is, the dharma of neither cyclic existence nor birth-and-death;
likewise, there is neither body nor mind, nor is there a person subject to birth-and-death). Since one already knows them to be like flowers in the sky, how could there be cyclic existence?
A single grain of elixir transforms iron into gold; a single word of True Principle transforms the ordinary into the sage.
Illuminating the emptiness of the five aggregates, one transcends all calamities; externally, one leaves the world behind, and internally, one liberates body and mind.

One does not reckon with the body, for the body is identical to empty space; one does not reckon with the mind, for the mind is identical to the Dharma-realm (Guifeng). Ignorance is fundamentally empty and quiescent by its own nature;

it is not something that becomes non-existent only through being extinguished or destroyed today. The wise say that the aggregates and sense-bases are all suchness, and thus there is no suffering to be found.
Abandoning the root of worldly toil, it is fundamentally pure and has no accumulation to be severed; because its nature supersedes cultivation, all practices are without action (*āvaraṇa*).
These three knots form wondrous contemplation.
That which perceives is like empty space; that which knows empty space is itself a mark of a flower in the sky, which cannot even be described.
When both existence and non-existence of the nature of cognition are dispelled, this is called "conformity with pure awakening.
One who knows that cognition is empty eliminates that which performs the observation; since the observer is empty, even that emptiness is like the appearance of flowers in the sky.
As previously described, once the fire has consumed all the wood, it naturally subsides of its own accord—this is the contemplation of emptiness, which likewise cannot be said to be non-existent.

The nature of cognition is the provisional contemplation (*prajñapti-vipaśyanā*); the simultaneous elimination of both existence and non-existence is the Middle Way (*madhyamaka*). Although these expressions appear sequentially, their function resides in a single mind;
because verbal deliberations are suddenly forgotten, it is called "pure awakening" (*viśuddha-bodhi*). Because this awakened wisdom accords with the principle, it is called "conformity.

Furthermore, what is termed "the conformity of pure awakening" is precisely the illumination of the object itself. Based on such passages, this constitutes the practice of the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna-caryā*).
Regarding the characteristics, Guishan classified them as "faith-and-understanding" (private note). Third, the inquiry reveals the essence of the awakening upon which it relies:
Why? Because its nature is like space; because it is eternally unmoving; because within the Tathāgatagarbha there is no arising or ceasing; because it is devoid of cognition or vision;
and because, like the nature of the Dharma-realm, it is ultimately perfect and pervasive throughout the ten directions.
The previous section clarified that wondrous contemplation must arise fully from the object; if the object were not manifest, contemplation would have nothing upon which to rely.

Therefore, it is now investigated and manifested so that one may contemplate it with truth. Furthermore, this contemplation is a perfect illumination of the object, for the object is the characteristic of awakening.

If the contemplation were not awakening and illumination, it would not be called a "perfect" object; and if it were not perfect, this characteristic would not be awakening, because its nature is like empty space—eternally unmoving.
This is the True Truth (*paramārtha-satya*); its true nature is like space, fundamentally unmoving. Within the *tathāgatagarbha*, it is the Equal Conventional Truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
