Its essence possesses all phenomena, being pure and original; since birth and death have perished, how could knowledge and vision reach it?

It is equal to the Dharma-realm, the Middle Way, thoroughly penetrating the three periods of time, perfectly pervading the ten directions, beyond all dependence, and inconceivable. It is mutually... [interpenetrating].

Fusion and mutual inclusion mean that three are one and raising one is raising three; thus demons and Buddhas share the same path, and what distinction can there be between the environment and its inhabitants?

What was previously called "the simultaneous negation of existence and non-existence" and "the dual negation of the Middle Way" is here termed "ultimate perfection," wherein the two truths mutually illuminate one another.
The Buddha’s words are truly wondrous! Guishan spoke of the nature of the Dharma-realm and the Tathāgata-garbha.
Their substance is identical while their meanings differ: among sentient beings it is called the *tathāgatagarbha*, and among insentient things it is called the nature of the *dharmadhātu*.
This involves the essential eye of our school, which scholars all know (private note). Second, the conclusion responds to the three points of intent.

This is what is called the practice of the Dharma on the causal ground; by means of this, Bodhisattvas give rise to a pure mind within the Mahāyāna, and sentient beings of the末代 (final age) who rely on this for practice will not fall into false views.
The Master asked three questions, and [the disciple] answered them extensively by restating the causal practices; thus, there is no further remainder.

(Private Note) The second part, the verses in meter, is not a set of isolated stanzas. They are either spoken again for those of dull faculties, or for the sake of future followers, or to further clarify what was previously stated.
Generally speaking, when prose and verse are compared, there are five pairs of correspondences. Namely, there is...
Regarding the expansion and contraction, separation and combination, sequence and priority, and concealment and manifestation, the headings of the questions in this sutra are all extensive;

where there are verses but no prose commentary, they are all extensive. Verses that are expanded are contrasted with the concise versions as appropriate within the text; (Guifeng) notes that the prose is complete while the verses are abbreviated therein.

This is done because [the verses] respond to the capacities and inclinations of sentient beings, and because the concise can encompass the extensive, making it easier to remember and uphold; thus, they are divided into two.
First, the brief introduction.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse.
Second, the formal verses, which consist of three parts: first, the verses on the wisdom of perfect illumination and awakening.
Mañjuśrī, you should know that all Tathāgatas, from their original stage of practice,
have awakened through wisdom to the fact that the two kinds of delusions have a real substance yet are empty in essence.
Thoroughly comprehending ignorance, one knows it to be like flowers in the sky; thus one can escape the cycle of transmigration.
Furthermore, it is like a person in a dream who cannot be found upon waking.
First, to explain the verse on ignorance, the verse first praises awakened wisdom; because one illuminates delusion with wisdom, it says "thoroughly comprehends."
[Private Note]: The three verses concern the essence of awakening as the basis.
Awakening is like space: Equal, unmoving, and unchanging; Awakening pervades the realms of the ten directions, And one thereby attains the Way of Buddhahood.
When all illusions have ceased and left no trace, Even the attainment of the Way is non-existent.

Because its fundamental nature is perfect, one immediately attains [the realization of] the latter two lines; this extends the preceding verse and completes the path, yet there is no attainment—thus the verse is extended (Guifeng).
Furthermore, "like a person in a dream," the following four lines eulogize emptiness (*śūnyatā*); "awakening is pervasive," the latter two lines eulogize the conventional (*saṃvṛti*).

When a single Buddha attains enlightenment, there is nothing in the Dharma-realm that is not the Buddha’s reliance (the environment) or his realization (the body); thus it is said he pervades the ten directions.
Regarding the "various illusions" in the three lines of the verse below: they are "complete," which refers to the cessation of illusions—this is the negation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

"Attaining enlightenment" is also "without attainment"—this is the negation of the provisional (*prajñapti*). Because the fundamental nature is perfect and complete, one simultaneously illuminates both sides [of existence and non-existence] without any [obstruction].

Question: Since the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*) are only established in the subsequent "Chapter on Majestic Power and Sovereignty" (*Vaibhutvādhipatya-paṭala*), why are they presented here in their entirety?
Answer: The subsequent text specifically establishes these manifest names for those who have not yet understood; thus, while the names appear later, their meaning permeates from beginning to end.
(End of Southern Section) The two verses conclude the response.
If a Bodhisattva within this context is able to give rise to the Bodhicitta, then all sentient beings of the final age who practice this will be freed from false views.
[Section Two: The Chapter on Samantabhadra Resolving Doubts] Having already shown the grand outline of the sudden, perfect, and immediate Dharma-practice, next—
This chapter, which resolves doubts and inspires joy, is divided into two parts. First, the inquiry, which has three sections. First, the manner of approaching the question:

At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, from within the great assembly, rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
Second, the actual presentation of the inquiry, which has three parts. First, the general inquiry:

"O Greatly Compassionate World-Honored One, we pray that for the sake of the assembly of bodhisattvas here and for all sentient beings of the future age who practice the Mahāyāna, you will explain how they should cultivate this pure realm of Perfect Enlightenment upon hearing it."

The preceding section clarified that the mark of perfect illumination-awareness eternally severs ignorance, and that the principle of cultivation and realization is sufficient through the contemplation of the essence-as-such;

now, the question is asked again: "How does one practice? This merely resolves remaining doubts and further elaborates upon the previous meaning. (Private Note: Part Two, specifically the third sub-section, consists of three parts.
First, the objection that one uses illusion to return to and cultivate within illusion.)

"World-Honored One, if those sentient beings know that [the world] is like an illusion, then since their own bodies and minds are also illusions, how can they use an illusion to further cultivate within an illusion?
This question follows from the preceding passage, "If one knows these are flowers in the sky, there is no more cyclic existence," etc.; its meaning concerns the body.
Since the mind is like an illusion, one can know that it too is an illusion; by using illusion to eliminate illusion, where does illusion end?

What is called "illusion" refers to the illusory phenomena in the world that rely upon grass, wood, and so forth to conjure humans and animals, appearing with lifelike movements and gestures of coming and going.
In an instant, when these phenomena cease, they return to being mere grass and wood. Thus, among all the scriptural teachings, the metaphor of illusion is used most frequently.
It is largely because this artifice is quite prevalent in the Five Indies that its principles are easy to understand once one has heard and seen it extensively;

however, when transmitted here to this land, it becomes difficult to comprehend. Now, following the ancient masters’ interpretation of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*’s passage on "the illusion-like," I shall explain the five dharmas for both the principle and the metaphor.
Within the metaphor, there are five elements: first, like a single cloth being knotted and illusorily transformed into a horse, which serves as the basis.
1. The two illusionists; 2. the magical arts and methods; 3. the illusory horse; 4. that which exists as a horse is immediately non-existent; 5. the deluded attachment to it as a horse.
Regarding these five factors within the [illusory] phenomena: 1. true nature; 2. mind-consciousness; 3. the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*);
4. the emptiness of self and phenomena; 5. the deluded attachment to self and phenomena. One should understand that all subsequent metaphors of illusion follow this pattern (Guifeng).

Second, if illusion is extinguished and the illusory person has no cultivation, then if all illusory natures were completely extinguished, there would be no mind; who then would perform cultivation? Why, then, do you further say that cultivation is like an illusion?
If all things are empty because they are like illusions, such that both subject and object are entirely non-existent, who is there to perform cultivation? (Guifeng) [asks:
If one does not cultivate, how can one attain liberation? This is the third objection.
If sentient beings have fundamentally not practiced cultivation, constantly dwelling within birth and death amidst illusion and transformation,
and have never understood the illusory nature of their realm, how can they liberate their mind of false conceptualization?

Sentient beings possess the principle of perfect enlightenment, yet their emotions are deluded; if they do not fully give rise to cultivation based on their inherent nature, there is no way to attain liberation.

Thus, although there are three meanings to the question, its ultimate intent lies in the practice of cultivation. (Private Note) Question: Previously, the meaning of the three contemplations and the three truths was established;
why is it that here the question concerns only the single meaning of "true emptiness"? Answer: Since all three contemplations are illusory, why would "true emptiness" alone be the case?
Just as the twenty-five royal samādhis all possess the three truths (Zhāngnán), [the text] reiterates the intent of the inquiry three times:
"I pray that you will provide for all sentient beings of the末法 (mòfǎ) age some skillful means for gradual cultivation,
so that all these beings may forever be free from all illusions."

The Treatise says: "If a person merely contemplates True Suchness (*tathatā*) without practicing various forms of cultivation through skillful means (*upāya*), they will ultimately never attain purity.

This is contrasted with 'temporary detachment'; here, it is called 'eternal detachment. Although one may realize the entirety of reality upon first contemplating the single essence, later, when encountering the eight winds [of worldly fortune], delusions arise in profusion.
One's practice is like that of a destitute son who understands [his true identity] for only a moment, like a flash of lightning. By what dharma is this cultivated and purified?"

"Forever free from all illnesses" (Guifeng): Although this question concerns the gradual sequence of skillful means (*upāya*), its intent is primarily to clarify the practice and realization of the Perfect and Sudden (*yuan-dun*).
Therefore, below, the World-Honored One answers by setting aside the question, saying: "To know that illusions are such is itself liberation;

no skillful means are required. To be free from illusions is itself awakening; there is likewise no gradual sequence. To forever leave behind all illusions, to realize that the cultivated evil is itself the nature, reaches the ultimate in the Wondrous."
[Private Note: *Jue* (Awakening/Realization)].

Having thus spoken these words with threefold prostrations of utmost sincerity, they cast their bodies to the ground in five parts; having thus made this request three times, beginning again from the end, the two Buddhas answered them thrice, first praising and granting their request.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, saying: "Excellent, excellent, son of good family!

You are indeed able to provide for all bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age the skillful means and gradual stages for practicing the illusion-like samādhi of a bodhisattva, so as to enable all sentient beings to become free from all illusions. Listen attentively now; I shall explain it for you."
[Private Note: These are the words of sentient beings of inferior capacity in the final age asking the Tathāgata. Second, receiving the mandate:
At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, having received the instruction with joy, along with the great assembly, listened in silence.
The third section is the direct answer, which has two parts; the first is the prose exposition, which has three sub-sections. First, a brief indication of the basis:
"Good son, all the various illusory transformations of sentient beings are born from the Tathāgata’s wondrous mind of perfect enlightenment."
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states that one knows the Dharma is eternally without self-nature, and that the seeds of Buddhahood arise from conditions.

The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says that all dharmas are established based on the root of non-abiding. Therefore, we know that the nine realms are truly created while the Buddha-realm is provisionally bestowed;

both are manifestations of the nature of perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-jñāna*). All the teachings of the Mahāyāna convey this same essential meaning. Thus, it is by means of the illusory mind that one contemplates the illusory.

All objects depend upon the nature of awakening; being in accordance with this nature, they are without effort and are termed "illusory practice. This practice fully encompasses all dharmas, wherein the three truths are perfectly interfused.

When illusion is exhausted, awakening is perfected, for there is ultimately no increase or decrease. Therefore, it is said that both the phenomenal function and the underlying principle are simultaneously established through the power of what is inherently endowed by principle.
If one does not first clarify that the nature of awakening is the basis of practice, then even if one speaks of "cultivating illusion," it remains partial.

"In the teachings, there is only emptiness of essence" (Private Note). The present text, for the time being, distinguishes and correlates according to the capacity of the recipient and the response of the teacher;

thus, sentient beings are taken as the illusion and the Tathāgata as awakening. "Various illusory transformations" refers to the nine realms and the three paths, including both the environment and its inhabitants, the provisional and the real.

"The wondrous mind of perfect enlightenment" refers to the three hundred dharma-gates of the Buddha-realm (Huǎn explains their correspondence, stating that the three hundred being perfectly complete is precisely the three thousand).
Second, the detailed explanation of the previous objections, divided into two parts: first, clarifying that while illusion ceases, awakening remains, thereby resolving the two previous objections;
third, the initial illustration by means of a metaphor:
just as illusory flowers arise from space, although the illusory flowers perish, the nature of space is not destroyed.
The preceding passage stated that space is fundamentally without flowers and that it is the sick person who falsely clings to them;

the present statement that "flowers arise from space" is intended to reveal that when the flowers cease, space appears. Thus, it speaks briefly of the flowers in relation to space, bypassing the cataracts in the eye.

One should know that because the eye actually possesses cataracts, one perceives flowers arising within space; when a diseased eye sees these flowers in space, those flowers— [Note: The provided source text ends abruptly. The translation above reflects the full context of the preceding argument.]
The whole is empty; when the cataract is removed and the flowers vanish, the essence of space itself has never increased or diminished (Cishi).

Although the illusory flowers are extinguished—referring to the icchantikas severing their cultivation of good and the Buddhas severing their cultivation of evil—the nature of emptiness is not destroyed;
the inherent goodness or evil of this nature cannot be diminished by even a hair’s breadth, whether in the icchantika or the Buddha (Zhangnan). This is the teaching of the two dharmas.
The illusory minds of sentient beings are extinguished by relying on illusion; when all illusions are extinguished, the awakened mind remains unmoving.

(Guifeng) The first two lines explain the initial difficulty mentioned above—that one uses illusion to cultivate illusion—while the latter two lines explain the subsequent [point]. This clarifies that while the former describes the defiled dependent origination arising from awakening, this describes the pure dependent origination where illusion is exhausted and awakening is fulfilled.

Regarding the illusory extinction of the mind: once one knows that illusion arises from awakening and that delusion originates from the True, one recognizes the way to turn back from confusion and return to enlightenment.
When cultivation is initiated entirely from within the Nature, one uses illusion to cultivate illusion; there is no reason for doubt here.

Furthermore, since the nature of awakening is perfect and constant, embodying both essence and function, even though all illusions may be exhausted, they do not enter into annihilation. Thus, in the illusory extinction of the mind, who [could doubt it]?

Regarding the difficulty of practice, he further explains himself: furthermore, that "all illusions are extinguished" refers to the extinction of the nature [of delusion], not its annihilation (*pralaya*).

(Private Note: When the illusory mind of sentient beings returns to be extinguished by means of illusion, there is no beginning the cultivation of contemplation without taking the *kleśas* and mental factors (*caitta*) as the starting point for developing contemplation.
Arising from the True to produce the false is fundamentally the mind of ignorance; one must return from the false to the True.)
Returning to the truth is also like using sound to stop sound or using a wedge to extract a wedge; it is the unmoving mind of awakening.
Although the mind perfumed by the three delusions undergoes arising and ceasing, one is able to contemplate the three kinds of wondrous contemplations without ever altering them;
therefore, it is called "unmoving" (Zhuangnan). This is the third: clearing away traces.
To speak of awakening based on illusion is also called illusion; to say that there is awakening is still not free from illusion, and to say that there is no awakening is likewise so.
Therefore, the extinction of illusion is called immovability.

The nature of awakening is equal and transcends all verbal designations. When one speaks of awakening as being either existent or non-existent, it is merely a conventional expression regarding an illusion.

If the illusory perception of awakening is suddenly forgotten and both existence and non-existence are simultaneously extinguished, then the unmoving essence of awakening will manifest right where it is. (Private Note)

The first two lines directly demonstrate [the point]; the next two lines cite the preceding discussion of awakening in contrast to illusion; the final two lines show that even the absence of awakening is itself an illusion.
This also serves as the foundation for what follows: "cultivating illusion with illusion. The phrase "when illusion ceases, there is no movement" reiterates the essence of awakening (Cishì).
The statement "to speak of awakening based on illusion is also called illusion" means that speaking of awakening in contrast to illusion is, in fact, still an illusion.
Since the meaning of "belonging," "following," "delusion," and "mutual dependence" involves speech, thought, and cognition, they constitute non-awakening; scholars should know this.

When first turning the mind toward the Way and establishing contemplation in relation to objects, one must distinguish between illusory awakening and its application; when using contemplation to observe objects, truth and falsehood merge.
If one speaks of having awakening yet remains still not free from illusion, it is because one has not yet abandoned views and thoughts.
The statement that "those who speak of the absence of awakening are likewise so" means they have not yet departed from the sands of dust.

Therefore, when illusion ceases, the dualistic mind is extinguished; thus, ignorance is severed and the Middle Way is established. Since all three contemplations are centered within this, it is called "immovable.
(Zhuangnan) Second, explaining the third difficulty by exhorting the practice of illusory conduct. Part one: the Dharma.
Good son, all Bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age should distance themselves from all illusory and false realms.
Because they maintain a mind that is free from attachment, they distance themselves even from that which is like an illusion.

They distance themselves from the very act of distancing itself as being illusory, and they distance themselves even from that distancing of the illusory distancing. Thus, they attain a state where there is nothing further to be distanced.
This means immediately eliminating all illusions.
"All Bodhisattvas" refers to those who point toward and guide the appropriate recipients; "should" serves as an exhortation and admonition. There are four ways to depart from illusion:

first, departing from the objects of illusion, where the objects are that which is to be departed from and wisdom is that which departs from them; second, departing from the act of departing from illusion.
The mind that arises from firm attachment possesses the wisdom capable of detachment; since this wisdom is also illusory, it is said:

"That which is like an illusion is also further detached" (3). This is the detachment from the detachment from illusion, for one detaches from the preceding wisdom capable of detachment, and this detachment is also illusory;
thus it is called "further detached. (4) This is the detachment from the detachment from detachment, detaching from the preceding [wisdom].
Third, because this mind is also illusory, it is said: "Depart from the illusory, and further depart from that departure.
These four stages all constitute using illusion to cultivate illusion; although they are arranged in sequence, their cultivation occurs within a single mind.

When a single thought does not arise, the past and future limits are severed, and one attains a state where there is nothing to depart from—this is the "removal of all illusions," which concludes the demonstration of attaining the essence and eliminating [delusion].

If a student of illusion can, before the signs of illusory awakening have emerged and before the Tathāgata has yet taught it, embody and contemplate that which is the natural state of the awakened nature (bodhicitta), such that nothing is separated from it, then what virtue will not be manifested and what illusion will not be eliminated?
Tiantai calls this "originally empty of both [self and phenomena]" and "perfectly free from the four positions. As the text below states: "If one attains suchness..."
"Coming to quiescence and conforming to original non-existence" refers to both the state of stillness and that which undergoes quiescence (Cishi).

First, it demonstrates that the realms of the aggregates (*skandha*) are entirely illusory and false; though these objects are manifold, they do not transcend the internal realms of the nine destinies and the three categories of aggregates.
Internally, they are the mind; externally, they are form (*rūpa*). Thus, these false objects give rise to false subjectivity.
"Cutting down the tree, one finds its root; all illusions cease. Next, it is shown that the wondrous realm arises from the mind's detachment through firm upholding.
"The mind, being like an illusion, is likewise detached" means that firm attachment is the deluded view and thought, and detachment is the realization of the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
"Detachment, being an illusion, is likewise detached" means that realizing the [countless] dharmas as they are is the Conventional Truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
To distance oneself from distancing and further distance oneself from illusion means to realize that ignorance is the two extremes; this is the Middle Way that simultaneously negates both.

To attain that which is beyond distancing is to eliminate all illusions. This concludes the formation of the wondrous realm: "diminishing it again and again until one reaches the unconditioned" (Zhuangzi).
The essence of Great Perfect Enlightenment is such that the slightest movement of thought deviates from it; only when conceptual discrimination does not arise can one truly abide in it.
Because it accords with [the principle], the conclusion states: "Attaining that which is free from separation is precisely the elimination of all illusions. This is the same as above;
therefore, the extinction of illusion is termed "immovability"—it is merely a change in phrasing (Dongyang). Second, the analogies.
It is like drilling for fire: when two pieces of wood are used as the cause, fire emerges; once the wood is exhausted, the ashes fly and the smoke vanishes.
Suppose there is a piece of dry wood that is drilled with a wooden fire-drill; when fire emerges, it in turn burns up both pieces of wood.
Once the wood and the fire are spent, the smoke naturally ceases, and the piece of wood, having become ash, disperses spontaneously by its own nature.

The wood and fire-drill represent the delusive cultivation that serves as the object; the smoke represents the illusory wisdom that serves as the subject; and the absence of fire represents the elimination [of delusion].

The scriptural passage previously mentioned "the ash flies away," which was translated in reverse order (Guifeng). The metaphor of drilling for fire illustrates the aforementioned contemplative object;

the two pieces of wood represent the object and the contemplation; the emergence of fire represents the realization of the principle; the exhaustion of the wood represents the simultaneous forgetting of both subject and object; and the flying of the ash represents...
The metaphor of "delusion falling and smoke extinguishing" illustrates the extinction of emotion. Guifeng said: "The scripture first says 'ashes fly,' which is a reversal in translation;
it should rather be that the smoke first extinguishes and the remaining ashes fly away. Master Shi said: "The ashes still have substance, whereas the smoke is most ethereal.
There is no need to fault the reversal in the translation; however, since this is currently used as a metaphor to illustrate a principle, why must one insist on such literal accuracy?"
"Difficult to illustrate" (Zhuānnán). The third [point] is combined.
Using illusion to cultivate illusion is likewise; although all illusions are exhausted, they do not enter into annihilation.
The first two lines directly combine with the current exhortation to cultivate illusory practice. This explains the third difficulty by citing the wording of the initial difficulty.
Regarding the phrase "for the sake of those who conform to the Dharma," although the question contains three points, they ultimately converge upon the practice of cultivation.
The final two lines reiterate the basis of reliance—that the awakened nature is eternally abiding—so that the practitioner may forever be free from the net of doubt (private note).
The three stages of delusion are bound together as a single retribution.
Good son, if you know that illusion is itself detachment, no expedient means need be employed; if you detach from illusion, it is awakening, and there is no gradual progression.
All Bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age should practice according to this; in this way, they will be able to forever leave behind all illusions.

For one who cultivates the perfect contemplation (*yuan-guan*), the very creation of an object is itself the Middle Way; there is no need for the expedient means of phenomenal meditation (*shi-chan*) or the three contemplations as a single mind, nor is there any gradual progression.
"Knowing that illusions are themselves detachment" concludes the section on the wondrous object; "detaching from illusions is itself awakening" concludes the section on the wondrous contemplation.

The passage beginning with "All... concludes the response to the request (Zhangnan). This refers back to the previous question: "By what expedient means and in what gradual sequence should one practice?"
The Buddha’s response concludes that there is no need for expedient means nor any gradual stages of reconciliation regarding the questions posed in the text.

Once one knows this is an illusion, it is called "detachment. Yet, the very attainment of detachment from illusion is fundamentally awakening itself; there are no further grades or gradual transformations required to become awakened.
It is like a person who dreams of a wound on their body and seeks a physician for medicine, only to realize upon waking that it was a dream.
If one asks what skillful means (*upāya*) should be employed: if one waits for skillful means to cultivate [the path] and gradually becomes detached from it, this is itself the true dharma;

how then can it be called an illusion? If one clings to it as truly existent, this is still a false conceptualization; how then can it be called cultivation? (Guifeng) Part Two: Verses in Pairs. First, the General Introduction.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses.
[The first two verses praise the four aspects; the first verse praises the essence of the awakening which is the basis.
"Samantabhadra, you should know: All sentient beings Have, since beginningless time, been deluded by illusory ignorance."
All arise from the Tathāgatas; they are established within the mind of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*).
The phrase "ignorance" (*avidyā*) is long; there is no verse concerning its existence (Guifeng). The two stanzas describe the extinction of illusion and the persistence of awakening.
Just as flowers in the sky appear with forms depending upon space, yet when those sky-flowers vanish,
space itself remains unmoved; so too, illusions arise from various perceptions, yet when the illusions cease, awareness is perfected—
for the mind of awareness is fundamentally unmoving.
In the successive clearing away of traces, there are verses (Guifeng). Three stanzas exhort the practice of illusory conduct:
If those bodhisattvas And sentient beings of the final age Constantly distance themselves from illusions, Then all illusions will be left behind.
It is like fire produced within wood: When the wood is exhausted, the fire is extinguished.
In the legitimate version, there is no verse; rather, there are four stanzas that conclude the characteristics of sudden cultivation.
"Awakening is without gradual stages; skillful means are also thus.
The phrase "also thus" means not employing skillful means. This stanza briefly concludes the response [to the question] (Private Note).

○ Second, regarding gradual practice and realization, the *Tiantai Zhiguan* states: "The gradual approach first involves knowing the true aspect (*dharmatā*). Since the true aspect is difficult to comprehend, the gradual path is easier to practice.
First, one cultivates the return to the precepts, turning away from heterodoxy toward the correct [Dharma], thereby stopping the fires, blood, and swords and reaching the three good realms.
Next, one cultivates meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), stopping the net of desire and distraction, thereby reaching the concentrations of the realm of form and the formless realm. And so forth.

"Subsequently, one cultivates the true mark (*dharmatā*), ceasing the two extremes and exclusively attaining the path of eternal abiding; this is the characteristic of the gradual progression of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, being shallow at first and deep later.

(Text) Now, in response to the request of Universal Eye (*Samantacakṣus*) to "expound the gradual stages of a bodhisattva’s cultivation," the answer fully clarifies morality (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), and wisdom (*prajñā*) as a collective reply. It further states: "Cultivating in this manner, following such a gradual sequence."

This is largely identical to the *Zhiguan* (Calming and Contemplation), which is what is meant by "perfect understanding followed by gradual practice" (*jieyuan xingci*). (Private Note) This section is divided into four parts:
first, the "Chapter on the Universal Eye," which correctly elucidates the gradual stages of practice and realization; second, the initial inquiry; third... [and so forth].
First, regarding the etiquette for approaching to inquire [of the Buddha]:
thereupon, the Bodhisattva Universal Eye rose from his seat amidst the great assembly, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet,

Second, the formal presentation of the request has two parts. First, the actual request:

"O Greatly Compassionate World-Honored One, we pray that for the sake of the assembly of bodhisattvas here and for all sentient beings of the future age, you will expound the gradual stages of a bodhisattva’s practice:
how they should contemplate and how they should maintain themselves, for sentient beings have not yet awakened."
"What skillful means should be employed to cause all to attain universal awakening?
Previously, upon hearing [the teaching], one might practice it all at once without employing skillful means;

fearing that those of gradual capacity might think that knowing [the truth] is sufficient and that cultivation is entirely unnecessary, he again requested the gradual practice of cultivating precepts, concentration, and wisdom to awaken to Perfect Enlightenment. "Contemplation" refers to mental engagement.

By taking the dharma-realm as the condition, one realizes that the aggregates are fundamentally empty; the "upholder" (zhuchi) settles the mind in the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*) so that deluded thoughts do not arise.

Because observing the precepts and practicing meditative concentration assist in the accomplishment of contemplative wisdom, it is called "expedient means" (*upāya*). Guifeng stated that "contemplation" refers to the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*), while "upholding" refers to the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*);

the subsequent waiting to listen constitutes the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*). Huanshu stated that "contemplation" refers to the wisdom of inquiry (*paryeṣaṇā-prajñā*) and "upholding" refers to...

Regarding the ritual for requesting the preceptor for the formal reception of the precepts (*śīla-ācārya*), it is said that "contemplation" (*manasikāra*) is the skillful means of insight (*vipaśyanā*) and "abiding" (*sthiti*) is the skillful means of calm abiding (*śamatha*).

This refers to the twenty-five dharmas prior to the actual cultivation. Now, the subsequent section concludes [the preceding discussion] and responds to the middle [section], citing these six [points].

While various commentaries may divide and correspond [the text] in this manner, it is not necessarily exhaustive; moreover, there is no textual basis or logical justification within the response for the twenty-five dharmas.

The explanation of the "Becoming Proficient" (Chengqu) section is for the reader to examine in detail. (Private Note: *Sīwéi* [Contemplation] refers to requesting instruction on that which is practiced;
*Zhùzhí* [Abiding] refers to requesting instruction on that which is realized. However, contemplation must rely upon skillful means (*upāya*), while abiding must arise from awakening;

therefore, one requests again. Furthermore, the gradual stages of cultivation should also be subsumed within what is practiced. Although there are six types of requests, they are all simply cultivation.)
[The Section on] Realization (Maitreya’s Chamber). Second, the statement of intent:

"World-Honored One, if those sentient beings lack correct skillful means and correct reflection, and upon hearing this samādhi spoken by the Buddha, the Tathāgata, their minds become confused and distressed such that they cannot awaken to and enter into Perfect Enlightenment (Vimalakīrti), I pray that you will arouse compassion for me and [explain it]."
These are provisional teachings for the sake of those of equal standing and sentient beings of the final age.

Because those who are bewildered and distressed repeatedly inquire about what they should practice, I have briefly provided awakening and sustenance by speaking only of skillful means (*upāya*) and contemplation (*manasikāra*).
Furthermore, regarding these provisional teachings, the six matters previously requested were all derived from skillful means.
Therefore, the present summary and invocation employ skillful means by provisionally speaking of cultivation and realization within that which is beyond cultivation and realization;
thus it is called a "provisional teaching" (Cishi). With threefold prostrations, I extend my sincere devotion.
Having spoken these words, they prostrated themselves with their five limbs touching the ground; thus they made this request three times, beginning again and again.
The two Buddhas answered three times, first praising and granting permission.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Universal Eye, saying: "Excellent, excellent, son of good family! You all..."

"You have been able to ask the Tathāgata on behalf of all bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age concerning the gradual stages of cultivation, contemplation, and maintenance, as well as various provisional skillful means; listen attentively now, and I shall explain them for you."
Second, receiving the mandate.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Universal Eye, having received the instruction with joy, along with the great assembly, listened in silence.
Third, the formal response, which has two parts; first, the prose section, which has three sub-sections. First, stating the intent.

Good son, those newly initiated bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age who wish to seek the Tathāgata’s pure and perfect awakened mind should maintain right mindfulness and remain far removed from all illusions.
Now, the pure, perfect, awakened mind is originally possessed by all sentient beings; while the Buddhas have thoroughly revealed it, we have now turned back from delusion toward awakening.

Therefore, the Tathāgata (Private Note: one should maintain right mindfulness and remain far removed from all illusions)—as Guifeng said—points to the aforementioned inquiry and explanation regarding the mind that is free from illusion as the foundation for initiating practice.
If one clings to [phenomena] as fixed and real, contemplative practice will not be accomplished; therefore, one must...
To tread upon what precedes is the skillful means. "Right mindfulness" (*samyak-smṛti*) is non-mindfulness. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:

"Mindfulness is the work of Māra; non-mindfulness is the Dharma-seal. This forms a reciprocal relationship with the subsequent section on "leaving illusion behind": because one leaves illusion behind, there is right mindfulness; because there is right mindfulness, one leaves illusion behind. Master Shi said:
"Right mindfulness is precisely the reviling of the five desires, the abandoning of the five hindrances, and the practicing of the five [precepts]."
The Dharma also disciplines and regulates five matters; if it were otherwise, one would not abide in right mindfulness.

The Master says that because both extremes are the middle, it is called "right mindfulness. "Remaining far removed from all illusions" refers to what precedes indicating what follows. Now, I say this is merely a general heading:
"right mindfulness" indicates the precepts, concentration, and wisdom, while "all illusions" refers to the defilements to be abandoned through these three trainings.

The flaws and blemishes of the precepts are obstacles to meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and the delusions regarding the nature of reality are obstacles to the principle. (Nan-zhang) II. Extensive Explanation.
Part One: Precepts and Concentration.
First, following the Tathāgata’s practice of *śamatha*, one firmly maintains the prohibitive precepts and settles the assembly in quiet chambers for seated meditation.

*Śamatha* is translated as "stopping" (*zhi*), meaning the stabilization of stillness. As the subsequent text states: "To reach ultimate stillness is the practice; this is the practice of the Tathāgata.

Since this already reveals Perfect Enlightenment (*yuanjue*), one is instructed to rely upon it. Furthermore, by designating "the Tathāgata," it distinguishes this from the precepts and concentrations of heterodox or Hinayana paths. While one studies both precepts and concentration, one becomes capable of entering the gate of contemplation;
yet even when dwelling among a community of disciples and mutually exhorting one another toward diligence, one must completely cease all攀缘 (*pānyuan*, mental clinging or discursive distraction).
"Seated in tranquility" (*yanju*) refers to quietude and composure. One who wishes to cultivate concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) must restrain both body and mind;

thus, the term "seated in tranquility" (*yansuo*) establishes the preceding practice of *śamatha* (calm abiding) and establishes the subsequent wisdom of *vipaśyanā* (insight). Therefore, the text below immediately states, "Constantly maintain this thought," and so forth.
If one were to interpret the present passage by means of the Twenty-five Expedient Means (*pañcaviṃśati-upāya*) of the Tiantai school, it would seem to correspond to the first [expedient means].
The five conditions lack only the single condition of food and clothing; "firmly maintaining the prohibitive precepts" means keeping the precepts pure;
"settling among the assembly" means drawing near to virtuous friends; and "sitting in quietude in a still chamber" refers to dwelling in a secluded place and ceasing all worldly affairs.
Although the text is extensive, it stops at the practitioner because it intends to clarify the gradual stages of practice and realization, speaking directly only of precept and concentration.
The expedient means that assist and perfect contemplative wisdom and the mutual dependence of the three trainings directly answer the question regarding their gradual sequence;
however, as the Buddhas and Patriarchs established their precedents according to what was appropriate—whether extensive or concise—one should not adhere to a single standard.

Dongyang Cishi remarked that this text contains twenty-five dharmas, yet he sought them through forced interpretation, which is why they are not adopted here. (Private Note) It is called "first" because it is the beginning of entering the Path.
Taking the precepts as the basis for reliance and *śamatha* (calm abiding) as the support, the three trainings of the Perfect Teaching are collectively termed "unconditioned" (*anabhisaṃskāra*).
This is because one acts in accordance with the Middle Way; specifically, the term "Tathāgata" refers to the three Tathāgatas of inherent virtue.

As for the "assembly," these are those who share the same practice and the same view, refining one another as conditions for the long path to enlightenment. Guifeng cites the *Jing*... [text fragment].
It is said that sitting is not necessarily what constitutes "sitting in meditation" (*yàn-zuò*).

Now, it is claimed that because Vimalakīrti used the Perfect [Vehicle] to critique the Lesser [Vehicle], he rebuked Śāriputra, saying, "Not arising from the meditative concentration of cessation while manifesting all majestic deportments is true sitting in meditation.
However, the present text specifically instructs one to sit in a quiet room; how can one instead explain it by means of "not sitting"? Nevertheless, this section merely sets forth the heading.

The physical demeanor does not explicitly state the characteristics of the meditative absorption (*samādhi*), yet it is capable of manifesting that which one should enter—the fundamental four dhyānas.

Regarding the question of why the *Sūtra on the Samādhi of Constant Sitting* does not mention this, the answer is: the fundamental four dhyānas are the Buddha’s constant discourse; however, by citing the physical demeanor alone, one knows this samādhi.

(Zhuangnan) Regarding the two types of contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā-prajñā*), all commentaries explain them by classifying them under the two kinds of emptiness: the emptiness of arising (*utpatti-śūnyatā*) and the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).

Now, examining that this is not so, it is divided into two parts: first, entrusting oneself to the aggregates (*skandha*) to clarify contemplation; second, inferring through the phenomena. Regarding the first, there are two sections: first, thoroughly investigating the objects of the aggregates;
second, contemplating the body as an illusion by means of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). First, [the section on] contemplating the body as an illusion by means of the four great elements.

He constantly reflects: "This body of mine is a composite of the four great elements. That which is called hair, body hair, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, tendons, bones, marrow, brain, and impurities—all these colors and forms return to earth.
Saliva, mucus, pus, blood, lymph, fluids, spittle, phlegm, tears, semen, vital energy, and the excretions of feces and urine—all these return to water.
The warmth returns to fire; and movement returns to wind. These are the four great elements."

Each person should reflect: "Where will this present deluded body go when it perishes? One should then know that this body ultimately has no substance; its appearance arises from a combination of elements and is truly like an illusion or a magical transformation.

One who constantly maintains this reflection must not for a moment abandon the practice of *smṛtyupasthāna* (mindfulness) and *vipaśyanā* (insight). As for the term "four great elements" (*mahābhūta*), [it was spoken by] Vimalakīrti.
The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā* states: "The four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are the 'created' (*bhautika*), while the four subtle particles (*paramāṇu*) are the 'creators' (*bhūta*).

Because the four subtle particles combine and create the four great elements, these are called 'derived matter from the four great elements' (*catvāri mahābhūtāny upādāya rūpam*). Question: The meaning of "subtle" (*sūkṣma*) may be understood;

what is the meaning of "great" (*mahat*)? Answer: Earth, water, fire, and wind are all pervasive; therefore, they are called "great. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "As the Buddha taught, the four great elements have no..."

Because they do not exist as distinct entities, they are called "great" (*mahābhūta*). As for "each being separate," this refers to the ancient false conceptualization that clings to the four great elements as a self;

this is spoken of in terms of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) regarding their combination. Now, in terms of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), they are refuted, hence it is said they are "each separate.

Herein, one should apply the four propositions—neither self nor other, and so forth—to investigate them, until ultimately no essence is found and the deluded attachment of the grasping mind is exhausted.
(Southern Zang) "Harmony" refers to the provisional combination of solidity, moisture, warmth, and motion. The *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* states:
"When this body is born, it is of the same category as the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) of its parents;
at the stage of the *kalala*, if there were only the earth element and no water element, it would be like a person grasping dry flour or ash—it would never cohere. If there were only water..."
Regarding the absence of the earth element: it is like water or oil, which, lacking solidity, immediately flow away and disperse.

If there were only the elements of earth and water and no fire element, it would be like a mass of flesh in the shade during the summer months; without the illumination of the sun, it would quickly rot and decay.
If there were only the elements of earth, water, and fire and no wind element, then the vital essence and warmth would not increase.
Regarding "qi" (vital energy): qi is the fundamental substance of the four great elements; it is not merely wind, for it is also spoken of as "qi" within water and fire.
As for "moving and turning, it returns to wind": the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states that this body is without agency and is turned by the power of wind.

All say it "returns" because, having combined the great elements to form a body, one now investigates the body and finds it has no master; hence it is said to "return. As for "each [element] separating": [it refers to the dissolution of the body].

Observing by way of names is called "detachment," but this does not mean the end of life. Therefore, one knows that when the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are in conflict, it remains uncertain to which element one's body belongs.
If it belonged to all four collectively, there would be four selves; if it belonged to none collectively, there would be no self apart from the four.

Thus, seeing reality as it is, one knows that the four great elements are a provisional combination and ultimately lack any intrinsic substance. (Guifeng) This scriptural passage concerns the four great elements.

The *Brief Commentary on the Essential Dharma of the Pushen-gai* states that regarding the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), the self is non-existent and "self" belongs to conventional designation (*prajñapti*).

However, in the perfect contemplation of the Mahayana, since both body and mind are empty, the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*) is also exhausted. Although [this text] speaks of only one aspect, it is not possible not to distinguish the complete [teaching].
(Private Note) Second, contemplating the mind as quiescent by means of the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*). First, the sense organs arise in response to the mind.

The four conditions combine in a provisional manner to give rise to the delusive existence of the six sense organs. These six organs and the four great elements combine internally and externally to produce a delusive "conditioned breath" which accumulates therein;
appearing as if there were a sign of conditioning, it is provisionally named "mind."
The body is fundamentally without a body; because it arises in dependence upon the four great elements, it is called the "four conditions.

The six sense organs depend upon the body to exist, and for the time being are called the "internal four great elements. Because they are gathered from the outside, they are for the time being called the "external-internal.

The exterior is empty, yet the mind is situated within this intermediate emptiness, firmly bound therein; therefore, it is said that "they accumulate therein. This condition is precisely the subjective cognizer.
The mind is also not real; like the breath rising above, it perceives shadows that all manifest as empty in essence.
Since there is no essence, there are no marks; how, then, could there be names? For now, because we perceive them through arising and ceasing, we say they are "similar" (or "semblances");

because we designate them through deliberation and cognition, we say they are "provisional. The fact that various texts speak only of "name-and-form" (nāmarūpa) also carries this same meaning. (From the *Cishi Zhongwai*)
Regarding "the composite," Guifeng said that the four great elements constitute the internal and the six perceptions constitute the external.
I, however, say that the faculty of mind (*manas*) is also internal, while hair, fur, nails, and teeth are also external; how can these be categorized by such an analogy?
Regarding "delusory conditioning-energies" (*wang you yuan qi*), Guifeng said: "This delusory mind, though produced through conditions, does not depart from the energy of the true mind."
Because it is divided, it is called "conditioned breath" (*yuanqi*). Now, I maintain that this conditioned breath is precisely the deluded sentiment of the grasping subject;

since it is termed "deluded," what can be called the "True Mind" within it? That which "accumulates therein" refers to the reception of the preceding object in response to the dharma-objects (*dharmaviṣaya*).

(Zhangnan) Having privately examined the commentaries both within and outside [the tradition], and following the *Cishi* [commentary], I hold that "conditioned breath" is the sixth consciousness, the sovereign mind-king (*cittarāja*) capable of creating.
This means that once the false body has been formed, the sense faculties necessarily confront their objects, and there is an aspect of mental engagement (*ālambana*).

Within this, the mind gives rise to feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and formations (*saṃskāra*), whether wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate, continuing without ceasing from moment to moment; therefore, it is said that these are "accumulated therein.

Since the characteristics of the mind thus arisen are neither truly existent nor non-existent, they are said to be "semblances of objective conditions," which are the mind associated with the sovereign [consciousness].
Because it possesses only names, it is said to be a provisional designation for "mind" (Private Note). When the objects of the senses (*viṣaya*) are extinguished, the mind becomes tranquil.
Good son, if this deluded mind were without the six objects, it could not exist;

when the four great elements are analyzed and dispersed, no objects can be found, and within that state, as the conditions for objects each return to their dissolution, ultimately there is no conditioned mind to be perceived.

If one speaks of the arising of delusion from the truth and the production of phenomena through ignorance, there must first be a mind of non-awakening before there can be the world of sense organs and objects.
Now, examining this in terms of daily life, the meaning becomes clear: because the mind exists in dependence on objects, if there were no objects, there would be no mind.
As for the dissolution of the four great elements, it does not merely mean that the four elements each return to their original nature.

This passage must be explained by means of the *Sutra on the Universal Gateway of Avalokiteśvara*, which states that "the nature of earth is not solid, the nature of water has no fixed abode, the nature of wind is unobstructed, and the great element of fire is unreal," only then will its lack of substantiality be revealed (Cishì). Regarding "conditioned by objects," this refers to the four conditions and the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*).

When the mind relies upon the six sense-objects, those objects depend upon the four great elements; since the four great elements have no substantiality, the six sense-objects are themselves empty. Therefore, it is so stated.
When the conditions for dispersion and cessation have been extinguished, the substance of the mind is immediately empty;

therefore, it is definitively judged that "ultimately there is no such thing as a mind that conditions. (Guifeng) "Ultimately there is no such thing" means that when emotions are exhausted and defilements removed, [the mind] never arises again.
(Zhangnan) The phrase "among these" is not spoken in relation to external objects; it is merely a term used to point to the dharmas.
Huan’s commentary states that the phrase "that which conditions objects" refers to the mind that conditions, and not to the objects conditioned;
this is not the intended meaning of the sutra text, and one should instead rely on the *Lüshu* (Private Notes). Second, the formation of the characteristics of contemplation.
Good son, because that sentient being’s illusory body ceases, the illusory mind also ceases; because the illusory mind ceases, the illusory objects also cease;
because the illusory objects cease, the cessation of illusion itself also ceases; and because the cessation of illusion ceases, that which is not illusory does not cease.

"Those sentient beings" refers to the aforementioned person who practices contemplation. Because they have previously destroyed the body and mind as well as the objects of the six sense-fields, this concluding statement says, "the illusory body perishes," and so forth.

"Perishing" means quiescent extinction (*śānta-nirodha*), which is the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*). Because the illusory objects perish, the "perishing of the illusory" also perishes;
since birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) is already empty, nirvāṇa is likewise quiescent—this is the contemplation of the provisional (*prajñapti-vipaśyanā*). These are the latter two lines.
Regarding the Middle Way’s constant abiding: although all illusions are exhausted, one does not enter into annihilation;

yet these three wisdoms of the contemplative aspect remain as a single mind, free from delusion and indestructible, like a great round mirror where bright images appear vividly and never depart from it.
(Private Note: Part Two, illustrating by means of analogies, has two sections. First, clarifying the exhaustion of illusion and the perfection of contemplation. First, the analogy.)
For example, when a mirror is polished, its clarity appears once the grime has been exhausted.
Cultivating *vipaśyanā* (contemplation) is like polishing; the essence of wisdom is like the clarity. When body and mind are suddenly forgotten, the omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) is perfected.

(Private Note: The nature of a mirror is originally luminous; it is not obtained from without. When obscured by dust, it is hidden; when polished, it is revealed. Although there is this concealment and revelation...)
The distinct clarity of nature is not different [from the mind] (Guifeng). [The two merge.
"Good son, you should know that both body and mind are illusory defilements; when the characteristics of these defilements are eternally extinguished, the ten directions are pure."
Since body and mind are already joined with illusory defilements, then both the person's attachment to dharmas and their attachment to nature and characteristics all belong to illusory defilements.
"The ten directions" refers to the ten realms; "purity" refers to the manifestation of the intrinsically endowed enlightened nature.
This corresponds to the preceding statement that what is not illusory does not perish. (Cishi) Second, the warning against deluding the truth and clinging to the false. First, the analogy.
Good son, it is like a pure maṇi jewel that reflects five colors, each appearing according to its direction;
those who are foolish and deluded perceive that the maṇi actually possesses these five colors.
The essence of the maṇi jewel is translucent and pure, free from blemish, and devoid of any [inherent] color-form.

Because its nature is pure, when it encounters all manner of color-forms, these appear within it; the five colors—blue, yellow, red, white, and black—each manifest according to their respective directions.

The five colors are a metaphor for the five destinies, and the directions are a metaphor for following karma. The foolish do not understand the true nature of the jewel; they see only that it is entirely composed of those [colors].
Because of blue and yellow, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "Ordinary beings see all phenomena only as they revolve according to their various marks;

they do not realize that phenomena lack intrinsic nature. For this reason, they do not see the Buddha. (Guifeng) The analogy of the five colors represents the five destinies, and the analogy of the jewel represents the Dharma.

While this correspondence may seem convenient at first glance, sentient beings of the nine realms all turn their backs on their true nature and become deluded; they are all merely recognizing color and have not yet identified the pearl.

The substance (*tǐ*) is the *maṇi* jewel from Dongyang; this is translated as "free from defilement" (*li-gòu*), which is the wish-fulfilling gem. The substance of the jewel originally lacks the five colors, yet it reflects them according to those colors.
The substance of the jewel is the single nature of perfect enlightenment (*yuánjué yīxìng*). The five colors represent the body and mind, that is, the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). (Zhuan’an)
Two times two. First, this directly addresses the delusion regarding the truth.
"Good son, the pure nature of Perfect Enlightenment manifests within body and mind, responding to each according to its kind.
To those who are foolish, it is said that the pure, perfect enlightenment truly possesses such body and mind with their own specific characteristics; it is likewise so."
It is likewise so that [the manifestations] appear in accordance with the categories of deluded and defiled beings; this thus accords with the preceding analogy (the "Compassionate Chamber").
Illusion arises from awakening, and illusion is entirely awakening. To obscure one's awakening and cling to illusion—how could this not be folly?
It is like freezing water into ice; how could one see the ice and forget the water? (Private Note).

Because of this, one cannot remain far removed from illusion; therefore, I say that the body and mind are illusory defilements. In contrast to being free from illusory defilements, one is called a Bodhisattva.
When defilements are exhausted, they are said to be eliminated; thus, there is neither a "counter-object" to the defilements nor a speaker who designates them.
Originally, because sentient beings falsely cling to illusory transformations, the Buddha spoke of them as "illusory defilements.

Because sentient beings rely on the teaching to become free from these defilements, they are further called "Bodhisattvas. Since the defilements to be abandoned do not exist, what could establish the term [for the one who abandons]?
The word "one who faces" (*dui*) connects both phrases; that is, the one who faces the defilements is the Bodhisattva, while the one who speaks their name is the Buddha. Thus it is said: "Since..."

Since there is no wisdom that possesses an antidote, how could there be a person who gives rise to wisdom? Since the grasping at depth or shallowness is fundamentally non-existent, how could there be one who teaches?
Therefore, both are absent. (Guifeng) Principle transcends provisional names; based on illusion, awakening is taught.
When awakening is perfected and illusion is exhausted, subject and object are forgotten. (Private Note). The two contemplations are established through the sequential investigation of phenomena.
First, a general explanation of the realization of principle:
"Good son, because this bodhisattva and sentient beings of the final age have realized that all illusions are extinguished and their images vanish,
they then attain a boundless, pure space of non-directionality, manifested by awakening."
With the illusory body as the master, one perceives "this" and "that" externally; yet, since the mark of selfhood (*ātman*) is absent, where else could these perceptions arise?
Furthermore, space, being separate from consciousness, is not substantially real. Thus, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states:

"If there were a person who, having developed true realization, returned to the source, the empty space of the ten directions would vanish all at once. This means that what is perceived as space within the state of awakening is merely a shadow of dust, obscured by deluded sentiments.

Once emptiness has been dissolved, it is originally the manifestation of awakening; when one says that emptiness dissolves and awakening appears, this means that delusion is exhausted and the mind opens.

Examining these two states from every perspective, neither has any limit (Guifeng). One suddenly realizes that the nature and characteristics of real dharmas and provisional names are all attachments to the substance itself as being like an illusion;
therefore, it is said that one attains realization. Reaching the mind that perceives conditions as shadows, one sees the body as a reflection in a mirror—originally non-existent.
Therefore, it is called "extinction" (*nirodha*). "Without direction" means there is no spatial location; it is horizontally pervasive.
"Without limit" means there is no boundary; it is vertically profound. Because it is pure, it is like empty space; because it is like empty space, it attains purity.
This is the manifestation of the essence of awakening, precisely the sign of enlightenment—the very essence that is manifested. (Cishi) It penetrates all phenomena.
Illusory and like reflections, unreal, they are entirely the nature of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), which is quiescent in its own place.

Upon manifesting this nature, it is pure as space, pervading all places yet having no location. Since it is said that one "attains" this, one must necessarily enter the stages of perfection (*pariniṣpanna-bhūmi*);

these stages encompass the shallow and the deep, including the stages of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*), semblance, and partial realization. (Private Note: Second, a sequential demonstration of the three truths.)
Third, regarding the initial True Truth (*tattva*): one thoroughly penetrates each and every aspect of the mundane and supramundane, the self and others, and the support and the supported;

thus, when the three thousandfold world-system is perfected as the fruit, it is universally designated as "Eternity, Bliss, Self, and Purity. This section is divided into two parts. First, the specific manifestation of true purity. Within this, there are four sections concerning the various phenomena of the mundane world.
First, the sense faculties and consciousnesses.

Because awakening is perfectly luminous, the mind is revealed as pure; because the mind is pure, the objects of perception are pure; because the objects of perception are pure, the faculty of the eye is pure;

because the faculty of the eye is pure, the visual consciousness is pure; because the visual consciousness is pure, the objects of hearing are pure; because the objects of hearing are pure, the faculty of the ear is pure;
because the faculty of the ear is pure, the auditory consciousness is pure. Because the auditory consciousness is pure, [the subsequent stages follow in the same manner].
The perception of objects is pure; this applies likewise even to the nose, tongue, body, and mind.
Purity is merely another name for emptiness. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Ultimate emptiness is ultimate purity.

Because people fear emptiness, it is called purity. (Zhu Nan) Regarding the perception of objects (*viṣaya*), it is not only external forms that are termed "objects"; [the internal sense-faculties are also included].

It is not that the faculties (*indriya*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are called "objects" (*viṣaya*); for there are scriptural passages stating that these three—the object, the faculty, and the consciousness—exist independently.
Thus, this perceived object is actually the mind of self-clinging (*ātma-grāha-citta*), which, by taking on the appearance of an object, is separately designated by a name.

Since all subsequent instances merely repeat the word "seeing" (*darśana*) without mentioning "object," it is clearly demonstrated that seeing itself is the object, and not an external object. This applies equally to hearing and the other senses. As for the faculties...
Because it is the support for consciousness (*vijñāna*) and is able to give rise to consciousness, consciousness follows after objects and discriminates the six sense-fields (*ṣaḍviṣaya*).

(Guifeng) Regarding "the dust of form" (*rūpa-rajas*): this "dust" does not refer to external objects, but points to the essence of the *indriya-paramārtha* (supreme sense-faculties); because its substance is delusive and defiled, it is called "dust.

When it says "the eye-faculty," etc., it specifically refers to the *mṛdv-indriya* (physical, or "floating," sense-faculties). Since it mentions the nose, tongue, body, and mind, [it follows that...].
Having awakened to the self within, one minutely examines that consciousness is pure; thus, one awakens to the purity of the sensory objects. These two phrases seem somewhat redundant (*Cishi*).
The "nature of awakening is perfectly luminous" is manifested within the mind itself; when observing all phenomena throughout history, there are none that are not thus.

Since it has already been said that the mind is pure, the mention of the "intellect" (*manas*) follows: first, by observing a single thought-moment, one exemplifies the nature of all other minds, and the sense-faculty of the intellect is raised again for emphasis.

The [interpretation of] "many" as "two phrases" is not correct (Private Note). Regarding the six sense objects (*viṣaya*):

O son of good family, because the faculties (*indriya*) are pure, the sense object of form (*rūpa-viṣaya*) is pure; because the sense object of form is pure, the sense object of sound (*śabda-viṣaya*) is pure;
and so it is likewise for smell, taste, touch, and mental phenomena (*dharma*).
The reason all six are called "dust" (*rajas*) is that they defile and pollute the mind-consciousness (Guifeng). Regarding the four great elements:
"Good son, because the six dusts are pure, the earth element is pure; because the earth element is pure, the water element is pure;
and the fire element and wind element are likewise."
Fourth, the general principle:
"Good son, because the four great elements are pure, the twelve bases, the eighteen realms, and the twenty-five states of existence are pure.
Having previously clarified the purity of the faculties, consciousness, and the six sense objects, the reason for now again citing the twelve bases and eighteen realms is as follows:

The three categories of *skandhas*, *āyatanas*, and *dhātus* are expanded or contracted according to their respective faculties; because one desires to universally dissolve and merge them, they are again collectively exemplified.

(Private Note) The four continents, the four realms of existence (*gati*), the four dhyānas, the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), the realm of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñi-sattva*), the Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*), and the six heavens of the desire realm constitute the twenty-five states of existence (*bhava*).
However, the Brahmā King resides in the first dhyāna, while the Pure Abodes reside in the fourth dhyāna; thus, within the stages of the four dhyānas, they are distinguished separately.

The reason for citing this is that, according to Guifeng, the Brahmā King possesses views, the non-Buddhist practitioners of the Unconscious Realm (asaṃjñisattva) dwell in the Pure Abodes (śuddhāvāsa), and only the noble ones differ from other devas. Second, supramundane dharmas.
Because that is pure, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha,
and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are pure; likewise, everything up to the eighty-four thousand gates of dhāraṇī is entirely pure.
The ten powers (*daśabala*) are: first, the power of knowing what is possible and impossible; second, the power of karma; third, the power of meditative concentration;

fourth, the power of the faculties; fifth, the power of resolve; sixth, the power of disposition; seventh, the power of the path leading to all destinations; eighth, the power of recollecting past lives; ninth, the power of the divine eye;

and tenth, the power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*). The four fearlessnesses (*catvāri vaiśāradyāni*) are: first, [fearlessness] regarding all-knowledge; second, [fearlessness] regarding the exhaustion of outflows; and third, [fearlessness] regarding the proclamation of obstacles.

The four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) regarding the path that exhausts suffering are: first, the analytical knowledge of meaning; second, the analytical knowledge of phenomena; third, the analytical knowledge of language; and fourth, the analytical knowledge of eloquence.

The eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*) are: first, no failure in physical action; second, no failure in verbal expression; third, no failure in mindfulness; fourth, absence of divergent thoughts;
fifth, absence of an unconcentrated mind; sixth, absence of relinquishing without full awareness; seventh, aspiration; eighth, vigor... [and so forth].
1. Progression; 2. Mindfulness; 3. Wisdom; 4. Liberation; 5. Knowledge and Vision of Liberation—regarding these latter six, it is said that they are all without decrease;
6–8. The actions of body, speech, and mind follow wisdom; 9–11.
Through wisdom, one knows the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharmas) of the past, future, and present. These [latter] consist of seven [categories].
Section One: The Four Foundations of Mindfulness; Section Two: The Four Right Efforts; Section Three: The Four Bases of Psychic Power;

Section Four: The Five Faculties; Section Five: The Five Powers; Section Six: The Seven Factors of Enlightenment; Section Seven: The Eightfold Noble Path—these are the thirty-seven factors, consisting of four, three, two, five, single seven, and single eight, totaling thirty-seven.
A detailed explanation of these ten powers and so forth is found in the *Tiantai Fajie Cidi* (The Sequential Order of the Dharma Realm). ... [and so on].

This refers to the transcendence of many dharmas, such as the three bodies (*trikāya*), the four wisdoms (*caturjñāna*), the five eyes (*pañcacakṣus*), the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), and the eighty-four thousand *dhāraṇī* gates;
it encompasses all dharma-gates to counteract the eighty-four thousand afflictions (*kleśa*). (Private Note:
The preceding section subsumes the six ordinary realms. The first fascicle of Tiantai’s *Miaoxuan* quotes the *Bhadrapāla-kalpa-sūtra* to discuss these numerical categories in detail.
Including the four noble beings, this reveals the purity of the ten realms and the full perfection of *prajñā*.
It extensively demonstrates eighty-one categories of Dharma gates, beginning from form and mind and culminating in unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment;

because these are explained here in brief, it says "up to" (*yāvat*). Because the supreme awakening is perfectly luminous, one proceeds step by step, following the preceding conditions to manifest the world.
The purification of all supramundane dharmas is fully and exhaustively detailed across these five sections;
as for the remaining two sections, the sixth and seventh, they merely serve to connect with other bodies and other realms, and possess no further distinct meaning (Guifeng).
Third, the correct retribution of self and others.
Good son, because the nature of all true marks is pure, the single body is pure; because the single body is pure, many bodies are pure;
because many bodies are pure, it extends in this way even to the perfect enlightenment of all sentient beings throughout the ten directions.
Regarding "Purity":

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that the illumination of form and other phenomena as empty is precisely what is called the "true mark" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). This true mark is inherently pure by its own nature.
All the preceding mentions of purity are citations from the previous text; here alone, the true mark itself is specifically designated as the locus of purity.

Because one has already realized the principle of the true mark within oneself and perceives that all sentient beings share this same pure true mark, one contemplates all sentient beings as not grasping at marks, being identical with the nature of perfect enlightenment;

thus, it is not meant that while one person practices the path, many people attain Buddhahood. (Guifeng) The "one body" and "many bodies" are intended to reveal that self and others are of one essence.
Therefore, the ten directions should also be explained by means of the ten realms, so that the directions may be consistent with the aforementioned purity of ordinary beings and sages (Cishì).
Fourth, the one and many of the *niśraya-vipāka* (retributive environment).
Good son, because one world is pure, many worlds are pure;
because many worlds are pure, and so on until the very limits of space, all that encompasses the three periods of time is equally pure and immovable.

The purity or defilement of a land arises entirely from one's own mind. While sentient beings are consumed by the fires of the kalpa, my land remains peaceful and secure; how much more so when the mind is darkened by ignorance? When the nature of awakening is realized, consciousness and wisdom are non-arising; body and land rely upon the Truth, such that both defilement and purity are extinguished. Pervading throughout the Dharma-realm, it is pure and serene. "Round" means it is universally pervasive; "enveloping" means it contains and encompasses the three periods of time.
