Thus, while the inquiry into the arising of the false from the true is implicit here, it is explicitly developed later. Therefore, Master Huan’s restriction of the scope of this inquiry is incorrect.
To claim that it is permissible to combine the three into two is incorrect in meaning; for the Buddha himself concluded by stating, "Therefore, you have given rise to three delusions.
Readers should examine this carefully (Private Note). [The following] sets forth the intent of the three fetters (*saṃyojana*) and requests an answer.
I only pray that you will not abandon your unimpeded great compassion, but will reveal the secret treasury for the sake of all bodhisattvas,
and so that all sentient beings of the final age may hear such a sūtra teaching and definitive dharma gate, thereby forever severing doubt and regret.

In general discussion, doubt (*vicikitsā*) has indecision as its essential nature and functions as an obstacle to faith. Specifically, among the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*), there are three types of doubt:
first, doubt regarding oneself, thinking "I am unable to enter into the principle"; second, doubt regarding the teacher, thinking "He is unable to teach well";
and third, doubt regarding the Dharma, thinking "Does this which is studied lead to liberation, or does it not? This is like a sick person [who doubts whether they will recover].
If one doubts oneself, doubts the physician, or doubts the medicine, the illness will never be cured; among these three types of doubt, "doubting the Dharma" is precisely what is meant here.
To regret is an indeterminate state: to regret the good leads to evil, while to regret evil leads to the good. To request that [regret] be forever severed belongs to the category of evil.

However, if a person entering the Way has not yet reached a definitive resolution regarding whether birth and Buddhahood are identical or different, they may still require much effort in their practice.
At that time, he again felt doubt and regret (Guifeng). He prostrated himself with utmost sincerity three times in each of the three sections.
Having spoken these words, he cast his body to the ground in full prostration; thus he made this request three times, beginning again and again until it was finished.
The two Buddhas answered the three in three parts; first, they praised and granted permission.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, saying: "Excellent, excellent, son of good family!
You are indeed able, for the sake of all bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age, to question the Tathāgata regarding this profound secret and ultimate [truth]."
This ultimate skillful means is the supreme instruction of all Bodhisattvas and the definitive meaning of the Mahāyāna;
it enables Bodhisattvas practicing in the ten directions and all sentient beings of the final age to attain resolute faith and forever sever doubt and regret.
Listen attentively now, and I shall explain it for you.
2. Receiving the Mandate.
At that time, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva, having received the instruction with joy, along with the great assembly, listened in silence.
3. The Proper Response, Part One: The Prose Exposition. 4. Part One: First, Rebuking [the Opponent] to Arise the Root of Doubt. 3. [Subdivisions follow.]
First, a general indication of saṃsāra: "Good son, the beginning and end, arising and ceasing, before and after, existence and non-existence, gathering and dispersing, starting and stopping,
the continuous succession of every thought-moment, the revolving cycles, and all manner of grasping and rejecting throughout all worlds— all these are saṃsāra."

"All worlds" refers collectively to both the sentient beings (*sattva*) and the physical environment (*bhājana*). If one does not take into account the sentient beings, how could there be saṃsāra? Next, the following six pairs distinguish its saṃsāric nature:
namely, to abide merely in the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) is to belong to the mind of saṃsāra.

"Beginning and end" refers to the initial transformation and the ultimate realization (the *Chao* states: from the very first moment the world arises through the transformation of the mind, until one attains Buddhahood, it reaches its final exhaustion; such conceptual calculation is the view of saṃsāra). "Birth" [and so forth].

That which ceases arises anew at every moment, and every thought-moment falls away; that which precedes and follows refers to the past and future; existence and non-existence refer to abiding kalpas and empty kalpas;
gathering and dispersing refer to the kalpa of formation and the kalpa of destruction; beginning and ending refer to active conduct and subduing;

and the continuous succession of thought-moments refers to the world of sentient beings and the world of the vessel—all of which depend upon deluded thought. Since that which they rely upon is never severed, [the cycle continues].

The same applies to that which depends [upon them]: revolving in cycles, once the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*) has been emptied, it is formed again; once the realm of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*) has ceased, they are born again.
Delusions, karma, and habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) revolve as cause and effect; through kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, none can obstruct or sever this flow.

"Grasping" (*upādāna*) refers to attachment—clinging to a self and what belongs to a self; "relinquishing" (*prahāṇa*) refers to abandoning and wearying of the basis of suffering. Furthermore, regarding the body of the sense-faculties (*indriya-kāya*):
Thus, to weary of suffering, coarseness, and obstruction is to abandon them; to delight in renunciation, purity, subtlety, and liberation is to take them up.
Regarding the vessel-world (the physical universe), to weary of this Sahā world is to abandon it; to delight in that Land of Ultimate Bliss is to take it up.
Whether taking or abandoning, these various differences are all manifestations of the inverted, deluded mind—the marks of saṃsāra. (Guifeng) "Ordinary people abandon emptiness and grasp at duality."
"Riding upon the relinquishment of existence and the grasping of emptiness—the Bodhisattva who abandons extremes to seek the Middle is still within saṃsāra" (Dongyang).
"All worlds are the three kinds of worlds," which encompasses the nine realms from beginning to end. Regarding the six lines below, the first three clarify the mind of saṃsāra:
the first line clarifies the beginning and end of arising and ceasing by way of the twelve links of dependent origination in the present; the second line [clarifies] by way of... [the future].

Regarding the twelve links of existence (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) across the past and future: the past is defined by what has preceded, and the future is clarified by the presence or absence of subsequent existence; this is precisely the meaning of the aforementioned arising and ceasing.

The three phrases are defined according to formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness (*saṃbhava-sthiti-saṃvarta-śūnyatā*): the kalpa of abiding is called "gathering" (*caya*), the kalpa of destruction is called "dispersal" (*vikiraṇa*), the kalpa of formation is called "arising" (*udaya*), and the kalpa of emptiness is called "cessation" (*nirodha*). The five phrases are defined according to the afflictions (*kleśa*); thus it is said that they "continuously succeed one another from moment to moment. 1. The phrase "the past has already ceased" refers to the cessation of the causal conditions. 2. The phrase "the present exists" refers to the manifestation of the fruit. 3. The phrase "the future is yet to arise" refers to the non-existence of the fruit. 4. The phrase "the past has already perished" refers to the non-existence of the cause. 5. The phrase "the future will not arise" refers to the non-arising of the fruit. These five phrases clarify the sequence of the twelve links of existence across the three periods of time. Furthermore, the first two phrases clarify the aspect of the cessation of suffering, while the latter three clarify the aspect of the arising of suffering. This constitutes the meaning of the aforementioned arising and ceasing. Regarding the three phrases, they are defined according to formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness: the kalpa of abiding is called "gathering," the kalpa of destruction is called "dispersal," the kalpa of formation is called "arising," and the kalpa of emptiness is called "cessation. Regarding the five phrases, they are defined according to the afflictions; thus it is said that they "continuously succeed one another from moment to moment. This concludes the fifth section.
Regarding the path of suffering (*duḥkha-mārga*), it is said that one "circulates and returns" through six stages.
Regarding the path of karma (*karman-mārga*), it is said that there are "various takings and abandonments," like a centipede that takes one step and abandons another.

What was Guifeng’s intention in interpreting the Sūtra through the lens of abandoning the defiled and taking the pure? (Zhangnan) Since characteristics such as beginning and end constitute saṃsāra, there is no worldly phenomenon that does not follow this pattern.
Consider, for instance, the body of a single person: it begins with birth and ends with extinction; it may exist previously and cease later, or be absent previously and exist later.

It is a gathering and dispersing of the four great elements, the arising and ceasing of consciousness, the continuity of afflictions, and the cycling of karmic retribution through various realms—sometimes grasped, sometimes abandoned.
As it is with this one body, so it is with all phenomena; there is no need to state this further.

The text explains through pairings such as the initial transformation (*pariṇāma*), ultimate realization (*paramārtha-siddhi*), and the stages of abiding, destruction, and emptiness, as well as the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*).
Furthermore, it elucidates the characteristics of saṃsāra by correlating the two modes of liberation with the three vehicles (*triyāna*) and nine realms (*navadhātu*).

Now, although the term "transformation-death" (*pariṇāmi-jarāmaraṇa*) applies broadly, according to the subsequent Maitreya chapter which reveals the root of saṃsāra, it is here aligned with the five [aggregates].

Daowen asked: "If the Dharma-realm is solely mind and fundamentally lacks purity or defilement, yet one still harbors acceptance and rejection, thereby allowing deluded sentiments to determine that one belongs to saṃsāra—what is wrong with this?

He replied: "Upon examination, although the arousal of delight and aversion, acceptance and rejection, is said to arise from delusion regarding the Truth, it can also accord with the teachings to achieve success.
Thus, Asvaghosa established it as the foundation for initial awakening (*ādikṣānti*), and Zhiyi [the Great Master]..."
It is called the gradual path to the Pure Land; yet if one realizes that cultivation is itself the nature, then joy and aversion are fundamentally empty.
How much more so for the single gate of An-yang (Sukhāvatī), which all Buddhas jointly praise? Its coming and going throughout the *dharmadhātu* further reveals that all is but mind.

Entrusting oneself to those supreme conditions, one swiftly ascends to the precious enlightenment (*ratnabodhi*). This is truly the correct path upon which beings rely for refuge, and the wondrous skillful means (*upāya*) by which the sages lead them upward.
If one is deluded regarding the fundamental tenets of the teaching, this is not permissible. (Private Annotation: The two truths follow along with delusion. First, concerning the Dharma:
if one attempts to discern Perfect Enlightenment while still remaining within saṃsāra, that nature of perfect enlightenment would itself be identical to the cycle of transmigration;
there is no such possibility for it to escape saṃsāra.
Because the mind that is able to contemplate this cycle of saṃsāra is itself such, the Perfect Enlightenment (Pariniṣpanna) that is contemplated is likewise so;
it is like seeing precious objects in a dream, for the objects themselves are also a dream. (Guifeng). Second, the citation of analogies.

For example, it is like moving one’s eyes which causes the still water to ripple; or like fixing one’s gaze while the firebrand is whirled, creating a circle of light. It is also like this: when clouds race by, the moon appears to move;
when a boat travels, the shore seems to shift.
This occurs because the eyes are repeatedly moved, causing the still water to appear as waves; it is like a person moving their eyeballs or rubbing them with their hands.
Objects previously seen at the corners of the eyes appear inverted and moving. Furthermore, visual consciousness is sluggish;

when a whirling torch forms the appearance of a wheel, it is like a person holding a firebrand at the end of a staff and spinning it with their hand. Because visual consciousness cannot quickly keep up, one perceives the appearance of a red wheel.
The shifting of riverbanks or the movement of the moon are merely instances where the clouds move while the boat remains stationary, yet it appears as if the boat is traveling.

The four metaphors for the appearance of rushing currents (Guifeng): the first two illustrate that the true and the deluded share the same source; the latter two illustrate that one has not yet escaped saṃsāra.
The shaking of the eyes causing the clear water to ripple illustrates the true within the deluded; the fire illustrates the deluded within the true;
and the clouds, moon, boat, and shore illustrate that the nature of Perfect Enlightenment is identical to the process of transmigration (Zhangnan). Directly.
"Explanation" (*jie*) means "it is as if" or "resembles. When one stares with the eyes at a single mass of fire, one sees it revolving and resembling a circular form.
A brief commentary takes this as "due to" (*you*), but a more detailed examination [is required] (Private Note). It is the convergence of three factors.
Good son, if even when the various rotations have not yet ceased, that object which supposedly abides beforehand cannot be found,
how much less so for one whose mind is revolving in the defilements of birth and death and has never been purified, who contemplates the Buddha’s Perfect Enlightenment without returning to the cycle?
The various metaphors of the spinning wheel, the eye, the cloud, and the boat represent the defiled mind within the cycle of birth and death;

those objects—the water, fire, moon, and shore—represent Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna*). How much more so when the subsequent section provides the formal application [of these metaphors] (Guifeng). The preceding section is likewise similar;
while the meaning of this single phrase seems already to have been integrated with the previous text, this merely cites the analogies to conclude them (Private Note).
The "three fetters" (trisaṃyojana) refer to the aforementioned doubts; therefore, you have given rise to three delusions.

These three delusions are identified as the three types of doubt mentioned previously, and do not refer to the delusions of views, afflictions, dust-and-sand, or ignorance (*moha*). (Private Note: Two Similes)
Resolving Doubts Regarding Manifestation, Part Two: First, a general explanation based on the nature-qualities (*dharmatā-guṇa*) that are free from delusion, concerning the three doubts.
First, the analogy:
"Good son, it is like the illusory cataracts that falsely perceive flowers in the sky; if the illusory cataracts are removed, one cannot say that these [flowers]..."
Once the cataract has been extinguished, when would it ever arise again? For what reason? Because the two phenomena of the cataract and the flower do not exist in mutual dependence.
It is also like a flower in the sky: when the flower in the sky has ceased, one cannot say that empty space will ever give rise to a flower again.
For what reason? Because space originally had no flowers; they are neither arising nor ceasing.

One does not know that flowers exist because of the visual impairment (*taimira*); thus, one falsely clings to them as arising from emptiness. One does not know that delusion arises because of the obscuration of the truth;

thus, one falsely and arbitrarily clings to the truth as being able to give rise to delusion. Once the impairment has been cured, one no longer sees the flowers, for by removing the deluded mind, one attains purity.
Furthermore, if one still clings to the notions of "early" or "late," one is again deluded; since one would then ask when the impairment will recur, it is said that such questions cannot be made.
Regarding the question: "If the cataract is cured, it may sometimes recur; it is not necessarily gone forever. How can this serve as an analogy? The answer is:
An analogy merely takes up a single occasion at the time of discussion; it does not speak of a lifetime.

For example, when one awakens from a dream, how could one object by saying, "How can it be that one sleeps again and dreams again the next night? Furthermore, the two phenomena—the cataract and the flower—do not exist in mutual dependence.

The cataract does not wait for the flower to appear, nor does the flower arise following the cataract; it is simply that because of the cataract, one falsely sees the flower, yet the flower is not actually produced.

(Guifeng) When illusory cataracts produce flowers, the flowers vanish once the cataracts are removed. Although the cataracts and flowers arise and perish, emptiness is neither existent nor non-existent.
Thus we know that both delusion and awakening, from beginning to end, are entirely false perceptions; their wondrous, perfect, and enlightened nature is identical in both sentient beings and Buddhas.
As it is said in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*: "This delusion has no inherent nature and is ultimately empty, just as a person with cataracts sees flowers in the sky;

when the disease of the cataracts is removed, the flowers vanish from the sky. Suppose there were a foolish person who, in that space where the flowers had vanished, waited for the flowers to reappear.
Do you consider such a person to be foolish or wise? Pūrṇa replied: [He would be foolish.]

Space is fundamentally without flowers; it is through deluded vision that they arise and perish. To see the extinction of flowers and thereby perceive space itself as having been extinguished is already a perversion.
To command them to appear again is truly madness. The purport of the Sūtra is as clear as two tally-sticks meeting; how could the three delusions not be shattered? (Private Note:

The initial metaphor of cataracts and flowers refers to the deluded objects confronting the six sense organs, which are now eliminated. The subsequent metaphor of flowers in space refers to the objects confronted [by the mind].)
When the six sense objects are falsely extinguished (Zhangnan), these two dharmas merge;
birth-and-death and nirvana are identical in their arising and ceasing, and the wondrous, perfect illumination is free from the cataracts of delusion.
Deluded views perceive birth and death as the arising of flowers; awakening attains nirvana as the extinguishing of flowers.

To say that Perfect Enlightenment is free from flowers and free from cataracts is to simultaneously brush away both birth-and-death and ignorance. Since empty space is neither temporarily existent nor non-existent, what does the nature of enlightenment have to do with delusion or awakening?

Once sentient beings know that the arising of flowers is relative to something else, it becomes even more difficult [to understand] that ignorance and the birth-and-death resulting from ignorance... [are likewise relative].
Why blame emptiness for having been originally enlightened? Why would empty flowers ever arise again? How could one who has attained the fruit-stage fall back into delusion?

It is due to one's own ceaseless conceptualization that one perceives the awakened nature of others as being subject to transmigration. If you understand it thus, the three doubts are instantly dispelled.
These three doubts are like a chain of interlocking links; they are not three separate categories answered individually. The following analogy of gold ore refers solely to this.
Answer: The Buddha does not again fall into delusion because this doubt is an extremely deep error; therefore, he provides a repeated analogy (Guifeng).
Birth-and-death and nirvana are phenomena that follow conditions (*pratyaya*), while wondrous enlightenment and perfect illumination are the unchanging principle (*tattva*).

If one knows that phenomena are identical to the principle, then without moving a single dharma, one enters the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). Jingxi said: "Because it is apart from [the dualistic distinction between] cessation and illumination, cessation and illumination are entirely unified" (Private Note).
By way of the three fetters as an illustration:
"Good son, you should know that space is neither temporarily existent nor temporarily non-existent;
how much more so is the Tathāgata’s perfect enlightenment, which accords with reality, the equal and fundamental nature of space?"

This uses the emptiness of the world as a metaphor for true emptiness (Zhangnan). Since even the empty space of worldly phenomena does not accord with the arising and ceasing of flowers, how much less could the Tathāgata—who accords with perfect enlightenment and is profoundly still, eternally true, and the very essence of empty space—be like it?
That awakening is the nature of emptiness is stated in the *Buddha-śikhara-sūtra*: "Emptiness arises within Great Awakening," and again: "Quiescent illumination contains empty space."

Furthermore, regarding the term "equality": although Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-vidyā*) is the nature of empty space, it is darkly united and undivided, pervading the entire Dharma-realm without partition, limit, or distinction between the support and that which is supported; therefore, it is called "equal.

This meaning is that since emptiness resides within enlightenment, and emptiness itself is eternally quiescent, how much more so is enlightenment the nature of emptiness—how could it possibly increase or decrease?
Because the preceding analogy was still insufficient, it says, "How much more so" (Guifeng).
Second, by means of cultivating virtue to manifest the truth, he separately addresses the latter objection:
"Good son, it is like smelting gold ore; the gold does not exist prior to the smelting. Once it has become gold, it will never again become ore."
The nature of gold remains indestructible throughout infinite time; thus, one should not say that it was originally unaccomplished. The Tathāgata’s Perfect Enlightenment is likewise so.

When gold is within ore, the ore is smelted away and the gold appears; it is not as if the gold comes into being for the first time through the smelting. If its existence depended upon smelting, then one could likewise smelt a block of dull stone.
Since those [other metals] would also have to become gold, we know that although the nature of gold must undergo the furnace and smelting process, it necessarily exists inherently.

Thus, once they have become gold, those who were previously [other metals] are now [gold]. This clarifies that while the nature of gold is hidden when in the ore and manifest when extracted from the ore, though their states of concealment and manifestation differ, the nature of gold remains eternally one;
therefore, one should not say that it was not originally accomplished. This explains that the nature of gold is original.
"There is; the Tathāgata’s Perfect Enlightenment is also like this" is the conclusion.

Previously, based on the principle of perfect awakening, it was established that both sentient beings and Buddhas are fundamentally true, thereby forming the meaning of "all sentient beings attaining Buddhahood" in the section on the Universal Eye (*samantacakṣus*).
Therefore, it is stated that empty flowers originally do not arise and do not subsequently cease; this dharma corresponds to the teaching that birth-and-death and nirvāṇa are identical.

Regarding the reason why both arising and ceasing are equally subject to the three difficulties, we now speak of "smelting ore to extract gold" because we do not wish to destroy the characteristics of cause and effect.
This means that although gold was originally absent from the beginning to the end within the ore, it is only through smelting that the ore is finally exhausted.

The intent is that while the principle of the Perfect and Sudden is equal in its regard for delusion and enlightenment, it does not preclude their differences; since there remain habitual obstructions accumulated over many lifetimes, one must still [apply the remedy].
By practicing what is contrary [to delusion], the truth is revealed; once the truth is revealed, there is ultimate purity.
If one employs only the former analogy, it negates the characteristics of the causes and effects of delusion and awakening, thereby constituting a false view.

If one employs only this analogy, it implies that the sentient beings' nature of enlightenment is originally impure, which contradicts the principle of True Suchness and likewise constitutes a false view. The underlying principle is subtle and profound.
Because the analogies are difficult to equate, two matters are explained; thus, this analogy answers only the third objection (Guifeng).

Although the intent of this analogy correctly explains the third objection—that the Buddha does not fall back into delusion—it also simultaneously addresses the first two objections, as it states that gold is not non-existent after being melted, and thus the meaning of "originally not being accomplished" is also encompassed.
To explain and establish the original attainment of Buddhahood, the following verse briefly cites an analogy; this is precisely for that purpose.
Although it simultaneously explains the primary meaning of the preceding section, it nevertheless separately addresses the subsequent objection.
This is similar to how, in the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra*, when explaining Pūrṇa’s second doubt, this same analogy is cited: "Furthermore, it is like gold ore mixed with refined gold..."

Jin Yichun further raised a complex question: "If sentient beings were originally Buddhas who turned their backs on their nature to become deluded, and today, through hearing the熏 (xūn—perfuming/infusion), they turn back from delusion to return to their nature, then there would clearly be a beginning and an end to true and false. Why do the sutras and treatises say that ignorance is without beginning?

[The Master] replied: "The principle of awakening is perfectly clear and tranquil; it was never originally characterized by delusion or enlightenment. It is only when the teachings provide guidance and resolution that there appears to be a beginning and an end."
However, although the nature of birth is true, it has from the beginning been uncomprehended; because it has been uncomprehended from the beginning, ignorance is beginningless.
In the "Gate of the Non-duality of Defilement and Purity," Jingxi provides an analogy, saying: "In turbid water and clear water, the waves and moisture are no different.
Although clarity and turbidity arise through conditions, turbidity is fundamentally inherent; although turbidity is fundamentally inherent, its entire substance is [clear water]."

The *Qingzhiyaojie* states: "Turbid water is a metaphor for the defiled mind within delusion; clear water is a metaphor for the pure mind after fruition. Waves are a metaphor for the three thousand [realms] functioning together;
moisture is a metaphor for the three thousand realms sharing a common substance. The waves and moisture of the water are eternally without increase or decrease.
As for its clarity or turbidity, these must each arise from conditions: though it becomes turbid when an elephant enters and clear when a pearl is placed within it,"
The turbidity and its conditions coexist with the water, yet because one has never awakened to this from the beginning, the turbidity appears first.

It is like a mountain embracing jade, or like sand containing gold ore; fundamentally there is water, though it is originally turbid. Yet, although it is turbid, turbidity is not the nature of water; therefore, its entire substance is clear.
The wise understand through parables—please do not be further deluded. (Private Note: This chapter investigates and explains delusion.)

If one understands that nature is constant from beginning to end, why would this question and answer be in vain? Master Fu Li spoke verses on truth and falsehood to question the scholars of the world;
both Qingliang and Guifeng had verses in response. If one understands the Buddha’s answer, why would there need to be verses?
If there is a beginning and an end, it is nothing other than false seeing. Since this false seeing arises, it must be without cause.
It is said that to use a conceptualizing mind to fathom the realm of the Tathāgata’s Perfect Enlightenment is like attempting to burn Mount Sumeru with a firefly;
it can never succeed. All those who harbor such doubts possess a deluded vision characteristic of the saṃsāric mind. At the ultimate limit, there is only Perfect Enlightenment.
While the metaphor of refining gold inevitably involves the process of cultivation, one must know that the nature of gold itself does not depend on being refined.
True liberation cannot be illustrated by means of metaphors (Zhuan’an). Third, showing the nature to cause the deluded mind to cease. Part one:
The enlightened nature is originally eternal.
"Good son, the wondrous, perfect, awakened mind of all Tathāgatas is fundamentally without *bodhi* or *nirvāṇa*, nor..."
There is neither the attainment of Buddhahood nor the failure to attain it; there is neither deluded saṃsāra nor non-saṃsāra.

The wondrous, perfect, and enlightened nature is equal and eternally abiding; it is all phenomena, yet free from all marks. (Private Note: First, the awakened mind is established as the central thesis;
subsequently, the traces are swept away to clarify that it is not a state of annihilation. There are three sections for this "sweeping away," beginning with Bodhi.)
Nirvana sweeps away even the name of "transformation of the basis" (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*). Because it transforms afflictions and birth-and-death, it is called Bodhi;
yet while the essence of Nirvana is identical to the Truth, its name is derived from delusion. The following two sections both sweep away these dualistic opposites.
Within the nature of Perfect Enlightenment, none of these things exist at all; if one perceives even the slightest [duality], one is deluded regarding Perfect Enlightenment (Guifeng).
Second, the contemplation that cannot be fathomed. First, the illustration by analogy:
"Good son, the spheres of experience of all śrāvakas—in which body, mind, and speech are entirely extinguished—can never reach the nirvāṇa manifested through their own direct realization;
how much less could it be measured by a mind involving discursive thought?"

"Transcending the realm of the Tathāgata’s Perfect Enlightenment" is an instance of using the inferior to illustrate the superior. [In the case of] Nirvāṇa without remainder, both body and wisdom are stilled;

since a mind involving discursive thought can ultimately never reach it, how much less could it fathom the realm of Perfect Enlightenment? (Private Note: This passage uses the superior to manifest the inferior; the text contains two such instances.)
Regarding the initial stage of the small sage (*śrāvaka*), their principle-and-wisdom (*li-zhi*) stands in contrast to the minds of the two types of ordinary beings;

regarding true awakening (*zhen-ju*), it is said that even the true wisdom of the small sage cannot personally reach the principle of the small sage, let alone the inferior mind of an ordinary being which is further removed from that wisdom and whose true awakening is even more distant than that principle—how could it possibly create it?
It is like the hundred officials who still stand in awe of the prime minister.
"Can one's surname ever be made close to that of the Son of Heaven? (Guifeng). These two metaphors clarify this point:

just as taking a firefly to burn Mount Sumeru can never set it ablaze, so too, with a mind of saṃsāra and views of saṃsāra, one can never reach the Great Ocean of Tranquil Extinction of the Tathāgata.
Sumeru is translated as "Wondrous High" (*Miaogao*); this mountain is composed of four precious substances. "The wheeling mind" refers to discursive thought (*vitarka*) [Private Note].
The three preceding lines offer an exhortation.
Therefore, I say that all Bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age must first sever the root of beginningless saṃsāra.
If one points back to the preceding text, it refers to the Mañjuśrī chapter where ignorance (*avidyā*) was first severed; or, as Guifeng says, other sutras all speak in this same way.
As Cishih says: "Both grasping and rejecting are the mind of saṃsāra; the intent is to have [ignorance] severed first. It is raised again here to provide exhortation and admonition.
Fourth, the conclusion which rebukes doubt and delusion, not a question. Part one: Successive false conceptualizations (*vikalpa*).

Good son, there are those who engage in conceptualization arising from the mind; all such things are merely the vaporous conditions of deluded thoughts regarding the six sense-objects, not the true essence of the mind, which is like a flower in the sky.
To use such conceptualization to discern the realm of the Buddha is like using a flower in the sky to produce another fruit in the sky;
it is a succession of deluded thoughts, and no such thing can exist.
Second, failing to establish the expedient means.
Good son, a deluded and floating mind, replete with various clever views, cannot accomplish the expedient means of Perfect Enlightenment.
(Private Note: This refers to the aforementioned state of doubt as the "floating mind" and "clever views. Third, concluding that this is not a correct question.
Such a distinction does not constitute a correct question.
The previous praise of "Excellent! was intended to commend the initiation of the teaching; this critique that it is not correct reveals the ultimate reality.

This segment of doubt is the greatest obstacle to cultivation and realization; had it not been raised here, delusion would have persisted for a long time in the final age. Thus, it is Vajragarbha who raises this inquiry.
The intent lies in the Buddha’s reprimand; thus we know that this fault being rebuked is what first becomes manifest.
While the initial inquiry seems at first glance to contradict what follows, upon careful examination, it is found to be consistent from beginning to end. One should examine and savor this with care;
its subtlety lies precisely here. (Guifeng) There are two verses of praise. First, the heading.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses.
[The second section, the main verse, consists of four parts. First, acknowledging and rebuking the root of doubt:
"Vajragarbha, you should know: The nature of the Tathāgata’s quiescence Has never had beginning or end."
If one contemplates with a mind of saṃsāra, one will immediately return to it; as long as one remains within the limits of saṃsāra, one cannot enter the ocean of the Buddha.
First, the verse on deluded thought is presented; first, the true nature is presented (Guifeng).
The second verse uses a metaphor to resolve present doubts:
For example, when refining gold ore, the gold does not exist because it has been refined;
yet, although it is originally gold, it is only through refinement that it is perfected. Once it has become the substance of pure gold, it can never again become ore.
The *Guifeng* commentary states that the verse on "empty flowers" is omitted here because it appears later in the text. The three verses demonstrate the nature and the cessation of delusion:
Birth-and-death and nirvana, Ordinary beings and all Buddhas, Are equally but the appearance of empty flowers.

Since the meaning of the metaphorical text aligns with the intended sense of the analogy—that the fundamental nature of awakening is originally eternal—the significance of the "empty flower" metaphor applies throughout.
[Private Annotation: The four verses at the beginning and end conclude by refuting doubts.

To contemplate [the mind] as being like an illusion or a magical transformation—how much more so to interrogate its unreality? If one can thoroughly understand this mind, only then should one seek Perfect Enlightenment. To contemplate that it is like an illusion or a magical creation, How much more so to interrogate what is empty and false? If one can fully comprehend this mind, Then one may seek Perfect Enlightenment.
The first two lines concern "long practice," wherein one uses this contemplation to discern that the realm of the Buddha is like a flower in the sky and further produces a fruit from the void;

"discern" (*biàn*) means to investigate. The next two lines concern "arising practice based on understanding"; these are not a formal question but mutually clarify the preceding [point] regarding the formation of karmic bonds (private note).

Chapter Three: Maitreya. This chapter reveals the root of saṃsāra. As stated in the preceding chapter, "First, sever the root of beginningless saṃsāra," this section now exhaustively investigates that root as well as the nature of that which severs it.
This is divided into two parts: first, the formal inquiry; second, [the response]. [The first part] consists of three sections.
First, regarding the etiquette for approaching to inquire:
thereupon, Maitreya Bodhisattva rose from his seat amidst the great assembly, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right,
knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
Second, the formal request consists of three parts. First, celebrating what was previously heard:

"The Greatly Compassionate World-Honored One has extensively opened the secret treasury for the sake of the bodhisattvas, causing the great assembly to deeply awaken to saṃsāra and to distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox, thereby bestowing upon all sentient beings of the final age the fearless eye of the Way regarding Great Nirvāṇa."
Having given rise to resolute faith, one no longer follows the realms of saṃsāra to give rise to views of cyclic recurrence.

Regarding "saṃsāra," as previously explained, it refers to the beginning and end, arising and ceasing, and so forth; these are called false and deviant, while Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-vidyā*) is called correct.

As for "views of cyclic recurrence," they are like the three delusions mentioned before (Private Note). Second, the present inquiry: the intent of the question has four parts; first, the question concerning saṃsāra.

The first part consists of four questions: first, returning to the root; second, questioning the lineage of saṃsāra; third, questioning the depth of the gateways of practice; and fourth, questioning the skillful means for delivering sentient beings.
In general, these do not go beyond that which is to be severed and that which is capable of severing it. This is divided into two sections.
The first question concerns that which is to be severed:
saṃsāra. "World-Honored One, if bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age wish to roam within the Tathāgata’s great ocean of quiescent extinction, how should they sever the root of saṃsāra?
How many natures are there within these various cycles of existence?"

Regarding the question, "How should one sever the root of saṃsāra?"—although the intent of "severing" refers to the root, the subsequent text points specifically to affectionate attachment and craving, just as one cuts down a tree by seeking its roots or treats an ailment by cauterizing the precise acupuncture point.

Regarding the question, "How many natures are there within all forms of saṃsāra?"—previously it was stated in general that all various acts of grasping and rejecting constitute saṃsāra; now we shall investigate this in detail.

Regarding the question of how many categories of various [beings] fall within the count of saṃsāra, the answer refers precisely to the four modes of birth (*catur-yoni*) and the six destinies (*ṣad-gati*).
Master Guishan’s topical outline (*kepan*) for this chapter was somewhat inconsistent with its subsequent development;
therefore, following the *Huanshu*, I present it here first (Private Note). Second, the question concerns the capacity to sever [delusions] through practice and vows.

Regarding the cultivation of the Buddha’s Bodhi, how many levels of distinction are there? How many kinds of skillful means for teaching and transforming should be established to enter into the midst of worldly afflictions and deliver all sentient beings?
The meaning of the first two phrases is that although the Way is equal, the practice has degrees of depth; therefore, the answer below proceeds by way of...

The phrase "the two kinds of hindrances, the distinctions of the five natures, and returning to enter the defilements" refers to the request for the power of vows to employ the skillful means of great compassion to transform others (Private Note). This is the third point, which summarizes the intent of the request.

I only pray that you will not abandon your great compassion that rescues the world, so as to cause the wisdom-eye of all practicing Bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age to be cleared and purified,
illuminating the mirror of the mind and enabling them to perfectly awaken to the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed knowledge and vision.
"Wisdom-eye" refers to the wisdom of suchness; "mind-mirror" refers to the realm of suchness (Cishi).
Having uttered these words three times with utmost sincerity, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground; thus he made this request three times, beginning again from the end.
The two Buddhas answered the three questions in three parts. First, they praised and granted permission:
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva, saying: "Excellent, excellent, son of good family!
You are indeed able, for the sake of all bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age, to inquire of the Tathāgata concerning the profound, secret, subtle, and wondrous [teachings]."

This meaning shall cause all bodhisattvas to purify the eye of wisdom and cause all sentient beings of the final age to forever sever the cycle of saṃsāra, awaken their minds to the true mark of reality, and possess the patience of non-arising. Listen attentively now; I shall explain it for you.
The true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is that which is free from falsehood; because both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are equally quiescent, there is the patience regarding non-arising (*anutpattikadharmakṣānti*).
"Patience" (*kṣānti*) has the meaning of confirmation and certainty; realizing that all phenomena are eternally abiding is called the patience regarding non-arising.

Correlating this with the stages [of the *Avataṃsaka*], it corresponds to the first dwelling (*prathama-vihāra*) of the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya-yāna*) (Private Note). Second, receiving the mandate.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva, having received the instruction with joy, along with the great assembly, listened in silence.

Part Three: The Correct Answer, in two sections. Section One: The Extended Exposition, in two sections. Section One: The Detailed Answer, in three sections. Section One: The Response Concerning the Cyclic Existence to be Abandoned, in three sections.
Section One: Pointing to the Root.
Good son, all sentient beings have undergone saṃsāra since beginningless time due to various forms of affection, love, and craving.

When they give rise to a mind of craving toward the five sensory objects, they sink and revolve within the three realms of existence without ever finding cessation. As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says:
Since all sufferings have craving as their root, one must abandon attachment in order to escape saṃsāra. (Private Note: Attachment is affliction;
craving is karma. It is truly because afflictions moisten karma, and karma can moisten birth, that there is birth and death.
Thus, it is known that saṃsāra generally has affliction and karma as its root. [Cishih] Second, explaining the spiritual lineage (*gotra*).
Second, first, a general demonstration of the four modes of birth. First, the cause of life lies in desire.
In all worlds, every kind of sentient being—whether born from eggs, from a womb, from moisture, or by transformation—all correctly receive their life and nature because of sexual desire.

Since the heading states "all types of natures" (*sarva-gotra*), this clearly answers the preceding question regarding how many types of natures exist within the various cycles of rebirth (*saṃsāra*).
Various commentaries have failed to examine this, with the exception of Zhangan (Zhuangyan), who correctly identified them. Regarding the "natures and lives of the four modes of birth":

these are the fruits; sexual desire is the cause. Therefore, the conclusion below states: "Lustful desire is the cause; the life-force is the fruit. (Private Note: By means of the four modes of birth...)

Regarding the distribution across the six realms: those born by transformation (*upapāduka*) include the heavens and hell; among ghosts, both womb-birth (*jarāyu-ja*) and transformation-birth exist—referring to the "Ghosts' Sons" (*piśāca*) and terrestrial *rākṣasas*, who are womb-born, while all others are transformation-born. Humans and animals each have four types of birth.

Those who possess all four types are the mother Viśākhā, who gave birth to thirty sons from eggs; the womb-born are ordinary humans; and the moisture-born are the Nairañjanā (the daughter born from the moist place within a withered *nyagrodha* tree).

...and are born through transformation (*upapāduka*). Thus, at the beginning of the eon, among the four modes of birth, the *garuḍas* and *nāgas* are all transformation-born; the remaining beasts are all womb-born (*jarāyuja*), and the remaining birds are all egg-born (*aṇḍaja*).

Whether dwelling on land, flying in the air, in water, or on earth—including minute and crawling creatures—whether they are egg-born, womb-born, moisture-born (*saṃsvedaja*), or transformation-born, their various categories cannot be fully distinguished.
All those who establish their life and nature through sexual desire: "sexual desire" refers to—
Sensual passion, defilement, craving, and attachment are collectively termed "lust" (*maithuna*). Even for those born by transformation (*upapāduka*), this is based on karmic defilement.

Regarding the degrees of gravity within the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*), there are six types of sensual enjoyment: sexual intercourse, embracing, holding hands, laughing, and gazing. [These correspond respectively to: the inhabitants of the Earth (Jambudvīpa and others), who engage in intercourse; those of the Yāma Heaven, who embrace; those of the Tuṣita Heaven, who hold hands;

those of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, who laugh; and those of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, who gaze. The people of the four continents share the same conditions as the realm of the Four Great Kings (*cāturmahārājika*). As for other various classes of beings, [the same principles apply].
Whether born from an egg, moisture, a womb, or by transformation, the mind is stained and transmitted through the vital breath;
it is difficult to analyze fully how the nature of sensation and the endowment of life do not originate from this (Guifeng). Second, desire nourishes craving.
One should know that craving is the root of saṃsāra; because various desires assist and incite the nature of craving, they are able to cause the continuity of birth and death.
Although the lives of the four modes of birth take desire as their cause, desire arises from craving and has craving as its root. Furthermore...
Because the various desires cause the nature of craving to flourish, they ensure that the retribution of suffering continues in an uninterrupted succession (private note).
The three fetters constitute cause and effect:

desire is the cause of craving, and life is the cause of desire; sentient beings exist because of life, and the craving for life still relies upon the root of desire; thus, craving and desire serve as the cause.
Attachment to life is the fruit.
Although sentient beings' attachment to life still relies upon desire as its root— where "attachment" refers to the mind of craving and "life" refers to physical life—
and although life arises from attachment while existence arises from desire, yet it is through the nourishment and assistance of desire-karma that attachment receives inexhaustible retribution.
Therefore it is said: "Returning to rely on the root of desire" (Private Note). Second, a detailed explanation of the six destinies. Part one: specifically indicating the three [destinies].
First, the evil destinies.

Because of objects of desire, various conditions of opposition and compliance arise; through aversion toward and attachment to these objects, one gives rise to hatred and envy, thereby creating all manner of karma.
For this reason, they are reborn again in the realms of hell-beings and hungry ghosts.
Whether in opposition or accord with them, all objects are spheres for the creation of karma; the various types of karma are none other than the three poisons of greed, hatred, and delusion.

(From the *Cishisong*) Because of craving for those objects, when the objects do not accord with one's mind, one immediately gives rise to feverish affliction, resentment, and jealousy. Due to this resentment and jealousy, [hatred] arises.
Out of anger, various evil karmas—such as killing, harming, oppressing, beating, reviling, and insulting—arise from this.
Furthermore, based on objects of desire, there arise attachment, lustful theft, drinking, eating, plundering, frivolous speech, falsehoods, and various other evil karmas;
those not explicitly mentioned in the text are abbreviated here. Regarding the term "various," it refers to the ten unwholesome paths of action and so forth. [There are no animals.]
Taking the phrasing as it stands to form complete sentences, one may understand them through two examples;
furthermore, since the meaning must necessarily be complete, there are likely omissions in the transcription. Thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "The ten unwholesome karmic paths:
the superior lead to the cause of hell, the middling to the cause of animals, and the inferior to the cause of hungry ghosts" (Guifeng). Second, [the causes for] gods and humans.
Knowing that desire is to be loathed, one develops revulsion for the path of karma; abandoning evil and delighting in good, one again appears as a human or a deva.

"Knowing that desire is to be loathed" means being free from the causes of the evil realms. "Developing revulsion for the path of karma" means generating deep love and joy for the gateway of abandoning evil dharmas.
"Abandoning evil and delighting in good" means relinquishing the ten unwholesome actions and taking pleasure in the ten wholesome actions—the joy of humans and devas.

Regarding retribution, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states that the ten paths of wholesome action are the cause for rebirth among humans and devas; this is judged to be the coarse aspect of pleasant retribution.

However, if one considers the eight sufferings of the human realm and the five signs of decline (*pañca-vyasanāni*) of the heavens, as well as the cutting, hacking, harming, and banishment experienced by those dwelling on earth, how could one possibly escape suffering?
If one were to distinguish the asuras from within the realms of devas, ghosts, and animals, [the classification] would be complete.

The path for wearying of karma within the six realms (Guifeng) consists of the five precepts and the ten wholesome actions (Cishi). Regarding the three stages of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-bhūmi*):

furthermore, because one knows that all cravings are to be loathed, one abandons craving and delights in equanimity (*upekṣā*). Yet, by returning to nourish the root of craving, there presently arise the superior fruits of conditioned existence (*saṃskṛta*).

Knowing that both attachment to what is liked and attachment to what is good do not escape suffering, one abandons that heart of attachment and joyfully cultivates the dharma of equanimity (*upekṣā*).

This refers to the four *dhyānas* and eight *samāpattis*. However, because one does not realize that the mind of joyful equanimity is still identical to that attachment, it is said that "it further nourishes the root of attachment.
As for "superior wholesome fruits," these refer to the two types of retribution—both the environment and the body—which are particularly sublime within the two upper realms. This is due to...
In the desire realm, those who cultivate and attain this meditative absorption are each born in the corresponding heavens of that level (Guifeng).
Although the form and formless realms are conditioned, they are termed "superior bliss" and "equanimity" in contrast to the lower desire realm;
yet these states of bliss and equanimity fundamentally arise from craving (*tṛṣṇā*). (Cishi)
Second, the summary:
because all [these] are within saṃsāra, they do not constitute the noble path.
Third, the exhortation to abandon the three. First, the formal exhortation.
Therefore, if sentient beings wish to escape birth and death and be exempt from the cycle of saṃsāra, they must first sever greedy desire and eliminate craving-thirst.
Greedy desire and craving-thirst are the causes of karma and delusion; those who wish to emerge from saṃsāra must first remove these two causes.
If these are not severed, the retribution of suffering will be endless. Craving and thirst are so intense that they are like one who is parched and must drink (Private Note).
Second, resolving doubts:
"Good son, when a bodhisattva manifests transformations within the world, it is not rooted in unloved things;
rather, through compassion, he causes others to relinquish their attachments, and by making use of various forms of desire, he enters into birth and death."
Fearing that there might be doubt—asking how it can be that a bodhisattva undergoes birth despite having been told to abandon craving—one clarifies this by stating:
"This manifestation of taking birth does not have craving as its basis; rather, it is solely through great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and acting in common with others to benefit sentient beings.
As the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* says: "When sentient beings are ill, the bodhisattva is also ill" (Guifeng). Third, the manifestation of benefit.
If all sentient beings in the final age can renounce all desires, eliminate hatred and attachment, forever sever the cycle of saṃsāra,
and diligently seek the realm of the Tathāgata’s Perfect Enlightenment, they will attain awakening within their pure minds.
Only after one has first been able to eliminate and abandon [afflictions] can one diligently seek [the truth], just as gold extracted from ore must first be refined before it can serve as a vessel.

Previously, only "craving" (*tṛṣṇā*) was mentioned; here, it says "hatred and craving. This is because when an object of attachment runs contrary to one's feelings, hatred arises. Thus, we know that hatred also stems from craving;
therefore, although the intention includes hatred, only craving is explicitly named. (Guifeng) The previous statement said that hatred arises when the object turns its back on the mind of craving.

It is said "also" because of [the author's] resentment and jealousy (Zhangnan). Being able to sever the three obstructions is called "diligently seeking"; the mind at the point where the three obstructions are severed is pure (Cishi).
The second answer concerns the ability to sever both practice and vows. First, regarding the differentiation of the nature of practice, there are two parts;
first is the general heading.
Good son, all sentient beings, due to the manifestation of their fundamental desire, clearly exhibit five distinct natures that are unequal;
these appear as deep or shallow depending on two kinds of obscurations.

"To manifest ignorance" means to propagate, distribute, and make it clearly evident. However, fundamental ignorance merely consists of delusion regarding the Truth and originally possesses no distinctions;
it is only through the differences in craving and desire that it is perfumed and activated, causing the five distinct categories to arise (*Guifeng Xiaochao*).
All sentient beings undergo the cycle of rebirth in vain solely because of a single thought of beginningless craving.
Regarding the manifestation of craving within all realms of ignorance, the *Buddhanāmasūtra* states: "Where there is craving, there is birth; where there is no craving, there is cessation.
Thus, one knows that craving for birth and death is the root. All the Great Teachings speak in this same way. As for the distinction between the two obstacles—the shallow and the deep:

the obstacle of phenomena (*dharma-āvaraṇa*) consists of the coarse and heavy habitual tendencies (*dausthulya*), which is the shallow; the obstacle to principle (*tattva-āvaraṇa*) is subtle, which is the deep. Furthermore, there are the five natures (*pañca-gotra*) and the obstacle of objective phenomena (*vastu-āvaraṇa*). The former is shallow, while the latter is deep.

Because they are shallow, they are severed first; because they are deep, they are severed later. By means of this, the nearness and farness of obstacles to the Path are designated as "phenomena" (*dharma*) and "principle" (*tattva*).

Regarding the five natures (*pañca-gotra*): if the Dharma-character school (*lakṣaṇa-yāna*) adheres to the provisional teachings, it asserts that those of fixed nature as *śrāvakas*, those of fixed nature as *pratyekabuddhas*, and the *icchantikas*—these three—lack the Buddha-nature;
whereas Bodhisattvas and those of indeterminate nature possess it. This [latter] position adopts the perspective of goodness (*kuśala*).
The "evil nature" (*pāpa-gotra*) is as follows: now, taking the newly perfumed (*navasaṃskṛta*) [nature], there are distinctions based on hearing the teachings:
first, the *śrāvaka*; second, the *pratyekabuddha*; third, the *bodhisattva*; fourth, the indeterminate nature; and fifth, the nature of external paths.

(Zhuan’an) This section reveals the practice capable of severing [afflictions] and directly answers the previous question regarding the various distinctions among those who cultivate the Buddha-bodhi. Now, as for these practices, there are deep [levels].
Superficially, because the discussion of severance is based on the obstacles regarding both principle and phenomena, the practice reveals the five natures;

just as illnesses have degrees of severity, their treatments are not uniform. Greed and ignorance are the very substance of the two obstacles, while the distinctions among the five natures are the practices at various levels of depth.
Furthermore, practice refers to the dharmas while the five natures refer to persons; it is by means of persons that the dharmas are illustrated.
As for "manifestation," it arises from fundamental craving, which immediately gives rise to beginningless ignorance, thereby forming the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*).
This is a restatement of what was previously severed to clarify the nature of the bodhi-practice that now severs them. Master Jingxi said:

"It is solely because one forgets the intimacy or distance of wisdom that delusion becomes thick or thin; because delusion is thick or thin, the two afflictions are forcibly distinguished, though their meaning is opened up as one."

The six stages are precisely what is meant by the varying depths of wisdom; this is the intended meaning here. One should know that the five natures do not fall within the category of saṃsāra, nor are they discussed in terms of depth or shallowness based on hindrances.
The traditional interpretation appears to be erroneous; one ought to investigate the scriptural text (Private Note).
The second part consists of two distinct explanations. First, regarding the two obstacles:

what are these two obstacles? The first is the obstacle of principle, which hinders right knowledge and vision; the second is the obstacle of phenomena, which perpetuates the cycle of birth and death.

Fundamental ignorance directly obstructs the Middle Way and is termed the "obstruction of principle" (*li-zhang*); its branches and ramifications, ignorance, draw one into the three realms and are termed the "obstruction of phenomena" (*shi-zhang*).

Regarding the internal and external realms in contrast: from the perspective of the Small Vehicle, the True Principle is still subsumed under the birth-and-death of transformation (*pariṇāma-śīti-jarā-maraṇa*);

from the perspective of the Great Vehicle, the birth-and-death of transformation of the Great Vehicle, when contrasted with the Small Vehicle, is subsumed under the True Principle. This is explained below.

The two vehicles first sever the obstacle of phenomena; this refers precisely to the obstacles of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*). (Zhāngnán) Outside the realms of existence, there is no absence of birth and death;

because the suffering of transformation is light, it is merely said that [the obstacles] hinder right knowledge and vision. The obstacles of views and thought also hinder the partial truth (*ekadeśatattva*);
because the suffering of segmented existence is heavy, it is merely said that they "continue all births and deaths. (Dōngyáng) Regarding the second, fifth, and third [sections]: first, the inquiry.

What are the five natures? First, the nature of ordinary beings; second, the nature of those of the two vehicles; third, the nature of bodhisattvas; fourth, the indeterminate nature; and fifth, the nature of non-Buddhists.
Guifeng [Zongmi] then combined the two vehicles into one category to establish these five natures. First is the nature of ordinary beings, which refers to a passage from the sutra.

The commentary states: "This section generally clarifies that those who have not yet been perfumed do not belong to the category of the five natures. Now, when examining the intent of the sutra, how could it be that the four [natures] are combined to make five?

Nevertheless, one should not yet equate this with the five natures of the *lakṣaṇa* (characteristic) school. This sutra merely says they have not yet been established; it does not mean they will never possess the principle of attaining Buddhahood.
(Zhāngnán) Second, the explanation of the five [natures]. First, the nature of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
Good son, if these two obstacles have not yet been severed and extinguished, one is said not to have attained Buddhahood.

Those who take as their object of contemplation the phenomena produced by causes and conditions are the ordinary beings of the six realms. Based on this state of neither having severed nor realized, one type is revealed;

furthermore, there are four types that represent the downward progression toward severance and realization. (Zhangnan) Hearing the teaching and generating the aspiration for enlightenment through contemplation.

Because their wisdom is still weak, they have not yet subdued or severed the obstacles regarding phenomena and principles; they have not yet reached the stage of the noble ones (ārya) and remain within the category of ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana).

This distinguishes them from the fifth type, those with the error of false teachers who fall into the nature of external paths (*tīrthika*). Second is the nature of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).
If there are sentient beings who have forever abandoned craving and first eliminated the obstacle of phenomena (*dharma-āvaraṇa*), yet have not severed the obstacle to principle (*tattva-āvaraṇa*),
they are only able to awaken to and enter the stages of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, but are unable to manifest and abide in the realm of the Bodhisattvas.

They are identical in severing the views and afflictions (*kleśa*) and identical in exiting the triple world; however, regarding the teachings, the truths, conditions, and delusions, as well as the discussion of the fundamental and habitual tendencies, the Pratyekabuddhas differ slightly in their approach to eradicating the habitual tendencies (Private Note). Third, the nature of the Bodhisattvas.
"Good son, if all sentient beings in the final age wish to float upon the Great Perfectly Round Enlightenment-sea of the Tathāgata, they must first make a vow and diligently sever the two obstacles.
Once these two obstacles are subdued, they will be able to awaken to and enter the realm of the Bodhisattvas.

If the obstacles of phenomena and principle are forever severed and extinguished, they will then enter the subtle, wondrous, perfectly round enlightenment and the fulfillment of Bodhi of the Tathāgata."
The Great Nirvana.

The meaning of making vows to sever hindrances encompasses both the Four Great Vows and the two types of hindrances (*āvaraṇa*). Once these two hindrances have been suppressed, one enters the stage of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*) according to the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*);

this constitutes intellectual awakening (*jiewu*). Only when the two hindrances are eternally extinguished does it constitute realized awakening (*zhengwu*). As for the hindrance of phenomena (*shizhang*), if...

All who enter exhaustively the principle of the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) will sever their obstacles; this extends from the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) of the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya-yāna*) up to the stage of Wondrous Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
(Private Note) Fourth, those of indeterminate nature:
"Good son, all sentient beings realize Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*); when they encounter a virtuous friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), they rely upon what that person does as the cause."

When practicing the dharmas of the stages in this manner, cultivation may be either sudden or gradual; if one encounters the path of the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed bodhi and practices correctly, then regardless of whether one's faculties are great or small, all shall attain the fruit of Buddhahood.

"All sentient beings realize perfect enlightenment. Guifeng said, "To say 'by means of one's own realization, one knows that all sentient beings are none other than enlightenment' is a mistranslation of the scripture; it should rather say, 'one realizes that all sentient beings possess perfect enlightenment. Alas!
Guifeng’s preface to his commentary states, "The mind is fundamentally Buddha," so how could he dare to arbitrarily alter the scriptural text here? There is indeed [a discrepancy].
The scripture cites that "all sentient beings are, in their very nature, the mark of quiescence" to prove that this is unerring;
yet, it ultimately fails to clarify that all which the Tathāgatas cultivate and realize are the virtues of their original nature.

If these were not virtues of the original nature, they would be termed separate cultivation and separate realization, and would not be the Perfect and Sudden teaching. All [beings] realize Perfect Enlightenment, and thus they are not far removed from being originally Buddhas.

How many times did Guifeng claim that his teaching had encountered this scripture and his mind was opened beneath a single word, yet he did not realize that this particular text occasionally deviates from the intent of the sūtra (Zhuanan). I have briefly annotated this interpretation;

the former masters all rejected it, as is fully evident in the Huanshu, for it fails to clarify the inherent nature (*xingju*). Students should rely on the Dharma and not on the person. Thus it is said.
Those of indeterminate nature practice either suddenly or gradually, sometimes first and sometimes later.

Fifth is the nature of external paths.

The third section provides the correct answer in two parts: first, the prose explanation; second, the clarification of the six stages of "immediacy" (*ji*). Regarding the latter, there are two points:

first, because the principle is identical, it constitutes immediacy; second, because phenomena are distinct, they constitute the six stages. If one knows that the principle is identical, then delusion and enlightenment are equal, and one avoids despondency.

If one knows that phenomena are distinct, then cause and effect do not overlap, and one avoids the arising of arrogance. Furthermore, these six stages of immediacy encompass all ordinary beings and sages.
The nine realms and the three paths belong to the initial stage of "Li-ji" (Principle-as-such). Hearing the Perfect and Sudden Teaching belongs to "Ming-zi-ji" (Name-as-such).

The five grades of practice belong to "Kuan-hsing-ji" (Observational Practice-as-such). The ten stages of faith, the ten abidings, the ten practices, the ten transferences, the ten grounds, equal enlightenment, and the forty-one stages collectively constitute "Fen-chen-ji" (Partial Truth-as-such).
Wondrous Enlightenment is termed "Chung-chiu-ji" (Ultimate-as-such). This is the celestial [teaching].

The classification of stages (*bhūmi*) according to the Tiantai Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) accords perfectly with the sutra, for the principle is identical from the very beginning. This constitutes the first of the three [sections]: the Dharma.
First, the actual demonstration that the principle is identical:
"Good son, the self-nature of perfect enlightenment (*yuanjue*) is neither a nature nor a non-nature; it exists by following along with all natures, arising without grasping and without realization."
Within true reality (*dharmatā*), there are in fact neither bodhisattvas nor sentient beings.
The perfectly awakened nature is endowed with the three truths within its own inherent nature; it is neither empty of nature (*svabhāva-śūnya*) nor existent by nature (*svabhāva-sat*).

It is "existent" in the sense of being "inherently possessed" (*xingju*); because the ten realms are inherently possessed, through the nature of these realms, all phenomena arise through dependent origination, and each phenomenon is such.
Nature (*prakṛti*) is the fundamental reality (*dharmatā*) of both bodhisattvas and sentient beings; what, then, is there to be attained or realized within it?
This is also what is meant by the statement that within the equal and true dharma-realm (*samatā-dharmadhātu*), the Buddha does not deliver sentient beings.

Reality (*tathatā*) is simply another name for the nature of awakening (*bodhi-prakṛti*). (Private Note: "Non-nature" refers to the five preceding natures and the various distinctions of saṃsāra such as craving and so forth.)
Regarding this nature: that which possesses nature refers to the aforementioned differentiated natures, all of which follow and conform to Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*).

Perfect Enlightenment does not abide in itself but arises spontaneously, following conditions and pervading all differentiated natures. When these various natures arise, the entire nature of Enlightenment arises with them;
therefore, the Dharma-body neither increases nor decreases. As the Sūtra says: "The Dharma-body circulating through the five paths is called a sentient being."
That which is without grasping and without realization is not an object within the realm of the ordinary mind (Guifeng). Second, the reason for this is investigated and explained:
Why is it so? Because both bodhisattvas and sentient beings are all illusory transformations; since illusory transformations cease, there is no one who grasps or realizes.
Because the nature subsumes the practice, both the bodhisattva and sentient beings are like illusions;
pointing to the illusion as the very nature is called "the extinction of the illusory transformation," which, as Jingxi states, means that what is fundamentally empty is termed "extinction.

Since all are identical to the nature and share the same single perfect enlightenment (*yuanjue*), there is no longer any subject who can take it as an object of realization (Cishì). Second, the two metaphors.
For example, the eye faculty does not see itself.

The eye is but a single thing; who is the seer and what is the seen? (Cishi)
The three are unified.
The nature is inherently equal; there is no one who is not equal.
The self-nature of Perfect Enlightenment is inherently equal; the nature itself does not claim to be "not equal. (Zhuan-an) Equality.
The single nature is naturally thus; externally, there is nothing that can be equal to it.
If one further says that there is a mind that perceives phenomena outside [of itself], then among those who study the Way today, who would not speak of "nature"?

It is only because they still maintain the notion of a subject that can be equalized that they have been unable to sever discursive thought and return to the One (Cishi). Because the two matters are distinct, the six [sections] begin with a general clarification of the Great [Vehicle].
The second part concerns the mind. First is the distinction between delusion and awakening.

Sentient beings are deluded and inverted; unable yet to eliminate all illusory transformations, they manifest distinctions within the midst of their false efforts—efforts that are both extinguished and not yet extinguished.
The delusions and inversions of sentient beings are the afflictions of the five stages of dwelling; all things within the nine realms are illusory transformations of cause and effect.

Because one does not realize that the three obstacles are themselves the three virtues, it is said that they have not yet been extinguished. This distinction between "extinguished" and "not yet extinguished" is merely a matter of realization versus non-realization.

Furthermore, the five stages of realization (*pañca-yukti*) are called "realization," while the five stages of principle (*pañca-tattva*) are called "non-realization. These are again distinguished according to their sequential relationship.

Regarding the contemplation on whether delusion has been extinguished or not (Private Note): Delusion is precisely non-awakening; delusion necessarily stands in contrast to awakening. Awakening is precisely initial awakening (*ādikṣaya*). Because awakening possesses degrees of depth and shallowness, there are the stages of:
1. **The Stage of Names and Words**: Understanding through the mind is empty and pervasive. 2. **The Stage of Practice and Observation**: Coarse delusions are suppressed but not yet severed.

3. **The Stage of Similarity**: Coarse delusions fall away first. 4. **The Stage of Partial Truth**: Delusions are severed but not yet perfected. Within these four stages, one cultivates illusion with illusion; all are ultimately false.

When the application of effort reaches the ultimate fruit, the effort finally ceases; because the six stages remain distinct as before in contrast to the preceding principle of "suchness," it is said that "the differences are thereby manifested" (Dongyang). Second, the nature returns to oneness.
If one attains the Tathāgata’s quiescence that accords with reality, there is in truth neither quiescence nor one who is quiescent.
That all Buddhas equally realize the principle of quiescence and accord with it means they are in harmony with the fundamental nature without contradiction.
The latter two phrases eliminate subject and object: in reality, there is no dharma of quiescence, nor is there anyone who can effect quiescence; [all] is extinguished.

Regarding this, Jiji (Guifeng) has already entered the ground of non-action; where mind and conduct are extinguished, the path of language is cut off, and one returns to the equality of nature, which is like empty space.

Good son, since beginningless time, all sentient beings have, due to their deluded notions of "self" and those who love the self, remained unaware that these thoughts arise and perish from moment to moment;
thus they give rise to hatred and attachment, becoming addicted to the five desires.
When the whole body is in delusion, it is called "the stage of principle" (*liji*). Even if one has received the provisional teachings, the nature of awakening remains unclarified (Dongyang).
This is because, apart from the delusion of ordinary beings, there would otherwise be no stages or positions. Therefore, this is first designated to manifest conviction.

[The text explains that] my substance is fundamentally empty, yet deluded thoughts are taken as real; because one clings to them as a self, attachment arises. That which is clung to is the view of self (*ātman-dṛṣṭi*), and that which performs the clinging is the grasping subject.
(Guifeng): Those who falsely conceive of a self mistakenly identify with the four great elements, and those who cherish the self cling to the view of a self.
Having clung to this self, they preserve it as permanent; yet they are utterly unaware of its arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing.

From this point on, body and mind proceed to create various karmas: hatred and love constitute the mind that creates karma, while the five desires constitute the environment in which karma is created. (Cishi).
Second is the identity of name and reality:

if one encounters a virtuous friend who instructs and awakens one to the nature of pure, perfect enlightenment, and thereby clarifies its arising and ceasing, one immediately realizes that this very life-nature is inherently subject to toil and anxiety.
A virtuous friend is one who instructs and causes one to receive the teachings; it is that which awakens one to understanding.

To know that my own body and mind are the fundamental awakened nature—arising as perfect awakening and ceasing as perfect awakening—and to realize that what was falsely perceived as real is in fact the truth, is called "illumination.
Although one has not yet been able to forget the toil and anxiety of this life, having reached this point, one already knows that all arises entirely from the nature; therefore, it is said:

To overturn the previous state of ignorance—where one was unaware of the arising and ceasing of every thought—and to thus know them, is precisely what constitutes this mind of arising and ceasing.

When deluded, the nature of mind gives rise to and ceases with false thoughts, causing the mental faculties to toil for themselves (Guifeng). Upon awakening to the nature of Perfect Enlightenment, one realizes that it is not separate from arising and ceasing;

This citation of the fruit as proof is intended to instruct those at the initial stage of practice; hence, it is called "instruction."

This great wisdom of equality is profound and vast as the sea; this wisdom is free from conceptual thought, and all phenomena are empty (Dongyang).
The stage of the three fetters (*trisaṃyojana*).
This is called the Tathāgata’s awakening in accordance with the nature of enlightenment;
it is the stage of fruition. The *Awakening of Faith* states: "When the Bodhisattva stages are exhausted and skillful means are fully perfected, in a single thought-moment..."
