In accordance with the awakening of the mind, the mind has no initial characteristic from the outset;

because one is far removed from subtle mental conceptions, one perceives the nature of the mind, and this mind is eternally abiding—this is called ultimate awakening (Guifeng). Second, manifesting the dharma-gate for entering the stages.
First, the characteristics of perfect cultivation and practice. First, specifically indicating the method for settling the mind.
Good son, it is simply this: when Bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age dwell at all times without giving rise to deluded thoughts, yet do not seek to extinguish those deluded minds;
when they abide within the realm of delusive perceptions without applying further discernment, yet do not fail to discern the reality within that lack of discernment.
The text consists of four sections, each containing two lines. "Deluded thoughts" refers to the grasping at external phenomena through攀緣 (*pán-yuán*, clinging to conditions).
Because such thinking opposes awakening, it must not arise. If one seeks the true while abandoning the deluded, it is like discarding one's shadow while exhausting oneself;

if one attempts to extinguish the deluded while preserving the true, it is like raising one's voice to stop an echo. Objects manifest from the mind and are fundamentally one's own mind; if one adds further conceptualization to this, it is merely creating further obstruction.
That is to say, when one realizes that the capacity of present cognitive awareness is already quiescent, this is true knowledge;
true knowledge is precisely knowing who it is that knows the truth, just as the eye cannot see itself (Guifeng). This cites the most essential method within the twelve periods of the day.
As the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* says: "To be free from all marks is called the Buddhas" (Zhangnan). The practitioner should know all of this.
At that time, the time, place, body, mind, and the environment and its inhabitants are all the Dharma-realm—eternally empty, provisionally existent, and the Middle Way.

Like a pearl rolling on a tray, there is no trace left behind; the wondrous practices of inherent virtue do not transcend this (Private Note). Second, entering through awakening by relying on the Dharma.
If those sentient beings, upon hearing this Dharma-gate, believe, understand, accept, and uphold it without giving rise to alarm or fear,
this is called "conforming to the nature of awakening.
If the assembly of practitioners hears these skillful means with minds free from doubt and confusion, they will clearly comprehend and receive them with full realization.
To maintain [the practice] with composure and accord with the Way is also like what is said in the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*:
"To be neither startled, nor terrified, nor afraid is most rare," and so forth (Guifeng). Second is having planted the roots of virtue in previous lives.
"Good sons, you should know that such sentient beings have already made offerings to hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
as well as to great Bodhisattvas, thereby planting the roots of all virtues."
Verifying this now, one attains awakening and suddenly accords with the Buddha-mind; only then does one realize past causes and the prior influence of cultivation (Guifeng).
Through the three seals, one achieves Buddha-wisdom.
The Buddha said that such a person is called one who has accomplished all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*).
The knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā) is attained through this; the mutual inclusion of cause and effect is certain and beyond doubt.
Therefore, the Tathāgata’s seal of words brings it to fulfillment. (Guifeng) provides two verses in praise. First, the heading:
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:

"O Viśuddhamati, you should know: The nature of perfect enlightenment Is without grasping and without realization. (These constitute the second section, the formal verses, which comprise three parts; this is the first verse, establishing their identity through the same principle.)
There are no two distinct entities, bodhisattva and sentient being, because the six [perfections] differ in their function.
There is a gradual distinction between the time of awakening and the time prior to awakening; for sentient beings, these serve as obstacles to liberation.
The Bodhisattva, not yet free from conceptualization, enters the stages of eternal quiescence;
dwelling in no signs, his great awakening is fully perfected—this is called "universal conformity.
The first two lines of the verse provide a general heading, the next line describes the practice of contemplation, and the final two lines distinguish the stage of semblance.
The two verses on realization lack the ultimate principle; thus, even the stage of name-and-word can be understood as encompassing both the awakened and the unawakened (private note).
The three verses concern the dharma-gate of entering the stages.
If sentient beings in the final age do not give rise to delusions in their minds, the Buddha says that such people are bodhisattvas in this very life;
they have made offerings to Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and their merit is already perfected.
Although there are many skillful means, they are all called "conformable wisdom."
The final two lines provide a general summary of the stages and practices (*sthāna-caryā*); although they differ, they all accord with wisdom (Private Note). III.
The Fourfold Proof of Indeterminate Practice. A. The Chapter on Majestic Power (*prabhāva*) reveals the essence of practice in two parts.
The initial inquiry consists of three parts. First, the formal procedure for approaching the question:

thereupon, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vīryeśvara rose from his seat amidst the great assembly, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
Second, the formal presentation of the discourse in three parts. First, expressing gratitude for what preceded:
"The Greatly Compassionate World-Honored One has extensively analyzed for us such accordance with the nature of awakening, enabling all bodhisattvas to perceive the luminosity of the awakened mind;
through the Buddha’s perfect voice, they have attained excellent benefit without needing further cultivation."

Because the awakened mind shines forth brilliantly, it is called "luminosity. When the single thought is suddenly forgotten, one immediately attains the stage of Perfect Abiding (*pariniṣpanna-vihāra*), without depending on arduous effort or the gradual cultivation and realization of subtle refinements.
(Private Note). Second, the request for the latter two [verses]. First, citing a metaphor to establish the principle.
World-Honored One, it is like a great city that has four gates; those who come from any direction do not enter by only one path.
Likewise, all bodhisattvas who adorn buddha-lands and realize enlightenment do so through manifold skillful means.

The city is a metaphor for the gate of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-jñāna*), while the gates are metaphors for the gate of practice. Although the principles of contemplative practice were previously explained with clarity, I now inquire again because I have suddenly ventured into what is beyond my station;
therefore, I first establish the underlying principle and request that you further provide an instruction suited to my capacity (Guifeng).
Second is the method for making the formal request:
"We pray that the World-Honored One will extensively proclaim for us all the expedient means and gradual stages,
as well as how many types of practitioners there are in total."
First, through skillful means, he gradually asks about the types of practices cultivated— how many kinds there are in total— and asks about the person who cultivates them (Guifeng).
Third, to manifest the benefits,
so that the bodhisattvas in this assembly and those seeking the Mahāyāna in the final age may quickly attain awakening and sport [in the Dharma].
"To the Great Ocean of the Tathāgata’s Perfect Quiescence, I prostrate with utmost sincerity three times.
Having spoken these words, he cast his body to the ground in full prostration; thus he made this request three times, beginning again and again until it was finished.
The two Buddhas answered in three parts; first, they praised and granted permission.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Sovereign of Majestic Virtue, saying: "Excellent, excellent, son of good family!
You are indeed able, for the sake of all bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age, to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding such skillful means."
"Listen attentively now, and I shall explain it for you.
The two [disciples] received the instruction with reverence. Then, the Bodhisattva Vīryendriya, together with the great assembly, joyfully accepted the teaching and listened in silence.
The third part is the correct answer, which has two sections. The first section consists of the prose explanation, which has four parts. First, pointing to the essence and indicating the practice.
First, pointing to the essence and opening up the understanding:
"Good son, the unsurpassed wondrous enlightenment pervades all ten directions; it gives birth to the Tathāgatas and is identical with all dharmas."
The essence is equal across all practices; in reality, there are no two.
Now, the essence of Great Perfect Enlightenment is most supreme and most wondrous, pervading all phenomena; it is one and the same in both sentient beings and Buddhas.
Because the Tathāgatas of the ten directions have all realized this, it is called "giving birth. When principle fuses with practice, there is no difference in their conduct. (Dongyang)
The Unsurpassed Sublime Awakening is the essence of inherent virtue, upon which both the real and the false equally depend, pervading all ten directions.
That which gives birth to the Tathāgatas is its essence and magnitude, which encompasses all Buddhas and is realized by them in common.

Its equality with all phenomena means that its essential virtues are universally complete, such that there is nothing that is not Perfect Awakening (private note). Second, the enumeration of the numbers is presented.
The skillful means that accord with these [capacities] are immeasurable in number, yet they are fully subsumed within three categories according to their distinctions of nature.
These are established as various teachings according to the capacities of the faculties. "Following" (xún) refers to following along, and "nature" (xìng) refers to the nature of the faculties.
Although the capacities of sentient beings differ by ten thousand variations, all are entirely encompassed within these three gates. (Guifeng) First is the non-differentiated three.

This very differentiation is, in fact, the differentiation of non-differentiation; since there is nothing that is not the nature (*dharmatā*), it is said that "following the nature" involves three kinds of distinctions (Cishi).
As for the practices of the virtues of nature, one enters them according to one's faculties (*indriya*); since the faculties are not equal, the teachings are likewise inexhaustible.
Just as diseases have a thousand sources and medicines come in many varieties, when one examines the virtues of nature, the Three Truths (*triratna*) are revealed.

However, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) subsumes all phenomena, the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) establishes all phenomena, and the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*) wondrously encompasses all phenomena.
When these three reach unity, the one is the three, and the three are the one. In the state of ordinary beings, they constitute the three causes;

in the state of the sages, they constitute the three virtues. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* calls them the "one mind and three wisdoms," while Tiantai refers to them as "emptiness, the provisional, and the middle. This is it.

The Sūtras take the quiescence of illusory stillness as their characteristic of practice; that is to say, they establish contemplation based on the Truths, whereby the entire nature gives rise to cultivation;
they establish emptiness based on the True [Truth], thereby destroying all delusions; they establish the provisional based on the Conventional [Truth], thereby establishing all practices;
and they establish the Middle Contemplation based on the Middle Truth, whereby all natures are ultimately resolved. Although these three contemplations are entirely the nature, [the Sūtras]...

Since its manifestation is not achieved through gradual cultivation, within the single mind there are manifest three functions: simultaneously negating and simultaneously establishing, simultaneously absolute and relative.
It is not entered through successive stages, nor is it observed as distinct and separate. The Tathāgatas of the ten directions attain Buddhahood by relying upon this;
the ocean of boundless practices is perfectly encompassed therein without omission. These three aspects coexist in this sutra, which is preserved in a single Sanskrit syllable.
1. *Samatha* (translated in the vernacular as "cessation"): its characteristic is tranquility; its meaning corresponds to the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*).

2. *Samāpatti* (translated as "attainment" or "equipoise"): its characteristic is illusory transformation; its meaning corresponds to the contemplation of the provisional (*parikalpita-vipaśyanā*). 3. *Dhyāna* (translated as "meditative concentration"):
it is doubly detached from both tranquility and illusion; its characteristic is quiescent extinction; its meaning corresponds to the contemplation of the middle way (*madhyama-vipaśyanā*).
Although the explanation follows a sequential order, their function resides within a single mind; the three are complete as one, and each one necessarily possesses the three.
Thus, while the three chapters may appear as either singular or multiple, or as preceding or following, in actual realization they are perfect, though their practice is not fixed.

Therefore, all of these are designated as "Awakening to Pure Perfect Enlightenment," as the subsequent text also states: "Dwelling in the Bodhisattva vehicle and cultivating the practice of quiescent extinction, they enter together into pure reality."
Master Zhuzhi further stated: "This sutra is named the Sudden Teaching of the Mahayana;

sentient beings with sudden capacities awaken through it, and it also encompasses all classes of beings who practice gradually. One should understand this meaning so that one's discourse is not in vain.

Furthermore, as for why these three [teachings] are all named after "contemplation" (*guan*), the Chapter on Perfect Enlightenment states: "Cultivating this perfect enlightenment involves the three kinds of pure..."
This contemplation is called the primary skillful means of the three contemplations. One should study these three types of pure contemplations according to each specific matter and text;

how could one dare not rely upon them? Regarding *śamatha*, which is translated as "cessation" (*zhǐ*), the *Biàn yīn zhāng* (Chapter on Distinguishing Sounds) states that it is the "Wheel of Pure Samādhi.
One must know that it is tranquil yet capable of illumination, and that illumination does not depart from tranquility—just like still water that is free of waves.
Later, although the ability to discern is non-dual in terms of concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), it is called "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*) by way of its specific name;

furthermore, because one contemplates the concentration upon which it relies, it is termed the "wheel of concentration. As the subsequent verse states: "Unimpeded, pure wisdom all arises based on meditative concentration.

The three names in the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* do not differ from these; each follows the intent of that particular scripture. All three are termed "cessation" (*śamatha*). In the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, the meanings of the three names are slightly different.
1. Śamatha is translated as "stopping" (止); 2. Vipaśyanā is translated as "contemplation" (觀); 3.
Yuganaddha (Ubhaya) is translated as "the union of stopping and contemplation" (止觀等). Although these two names differ, their essence is not distinct.

*Dhyāna* (禪那) takes the simultaneous negation of both [extremes] as its "separation" (離), while *Yuganaddha* takes the simultaneous illumination of both as its "equality" (等). (Private Note) Regarding "expedient means" (方便): all dharmas that are practiced...
These serve as gateways, and one proceeds through them accordingly. When illness is cured by medicine, what further use is there for the medicine?

Guifeng, following the scriptures, established the names of three contemplations: first, the Contemplation of Quelling Phenomena to Clarify the Spirit; second, the Contemplation of Arising Illusions to Eliminate Defilements;

and third, the Contemplation of the Absolute, Unconditioned, and Luminous Mind. These correspond to the three contemplations of the Tiantai school—emptiness, the provisional, and the middle—though others claim they differ.

This clarifies that while the former [approach] involves the skillful means of applying the mind, the latter involves the thorough investigation of essential nature (*lakṣaṇa*) and characteristics (*dharma*). The former does not establish an objective realm, whereas the latter frequently gives rise to conceptual understanding.
Now, it is said that there is no application of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) that does not establish an objective realm, because contemplation is established in dependence upon an objective realm.

Thus, when the initial mind attains understanding, both [samatha and vipaśyanā] are understood together; when the subsequent mind engages in practice, both are practiced together. There is nothing that is not a skillful means, as has already been explained previously.

The various texts of Tiantai investigate and exhaustively analyze nature and characteristics (*xingxiang*); this is based on the gate of contemplation for dispelling and clearing away [delusions] according to Nāgārjuna, intended to shatter attachments.

If attachments have already been shattered, why necessarily investigate and exhaustively analyze? It is for the sake of seeking what accords with principle that we do not dare to divide the schools [of thought].

(Zhuan’an) If one does not exhaustively investigate the nature and characteristics of all phenomena, where would the wondrous contemplation be employed? If it does not correspond to the Three Truths, how could it be established?
To know the entire objective sphere as wisdom—alas, even within our own school this is still obscure, let alone for others (Cishi). Second, the explicit clarification of the aspects of practice;
third, the initial section on *śamatha* (calm abiding), which has three parts. First, the heading that explains it.

Good son, if bodhisattvas awaken to pure, perfect enlightenment and resolve to practice in order to attain the fruit of Buddhahood, they must first realize the nature of pure, perfect enlightenment within their own bodies as the foundation of their practice.

This "foundation" refers precisely to understanding (*jñāna*). Only by practicing in reliance upon this understanding does one engage in sublime conduct; thus, the essence of the practice and the clarity of understanding depend upon one another.

Because the eyes and feet further provide support, the subsequent headings and texts are all the same as this (Guifeng). This essence of *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* is the root-source of the myriad practices;
if one does not first attain awakening, then mere asceticism will not be the cause for *nirvāṇa* (Dongyang). This "awakening" refers to intellectual understanding (*jiewu*) (Cishi).
Second, the two explanations of practice: first, cultivating contemplation to break through obstacles.
Taking stillness as one's practice with a mind of pure awakening, by clarifying all thoughts, the agitation of consciousness and cognition is awakened;
thus, tranquil wisdom arises, and the adventitious dust of body and mind is forever extinguished.
When the mind of awakening is first established, its power is still weak and feeble; it is only through taking stillness and remaining composed that one can gradually extend the illumination.

The consciousness that discriminates through stillness, clarity, mindfulness, and vision is agitated and disturbed; because wisdom arises from stillness, it is called "still-wisdom" (*śamatha-prajñā*). "Guests" are not the fundamental nature;
when the dust of defilements does not arise within the self-substance of body and mind, it is called "extinction. (Guifeng) Regarding the "guest-dust" of body and mind:
afflictions reside in the mind, and they are spoken of in terms of grasping and conceptualization, such as the view of a self-body (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*); therefore, it is called "body."

The mind (*citta*) [is] the object of mindfulness (*smṛty-upasthāna*) and is characterized by applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*). If one correlates the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*) with the destruction of the three delusions (*trividha-kleśa*), this corresponds to the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*).
When the wisdom of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) is manifested, the essence of adventitious afflictions (*āgantuka-kleśa*) consists of the views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-saṃjñā*);

conventionally, they destroy the delusions of dust and sand (*pāṃsu-śarkara-kleśa*), and within that, they destroy ignorance (*avidyā*). If one follows the subsequent chapter on the exclusive cultivation of tranquil conduct (*śamatha-caryā*), it is said: "One eternally severs the afflictions to reach ultimate perfection."
The accomplishment of entering *nirvāṇa* without rising from one's seat—since this is called ultimate *nirvāṇa*—corresponds to the secret treasury of the three virtues (*triguṇa-guhya-kośa*).
This serves as a verification that cultivation must consist of the three contemplations within a single contemplation, and that the three delusions are shattered as a single entity.

In the first fascicle of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, Śāriputra (Cenru) provides a detailed answer regarding the two terms "guest" and "dust," which refer to the views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) and correspond to the present [context].
Slightly different (Private Note): Through the accomplishment of the two practices, manifest virtue is perfected;

one is then able to internally give rise to tranquil serenity (*praśrabdhi*). Because of this tranquility, the minds of all Tathāgatas throughout the worlds of the ten directions appear therein like reflections in a mirror.
Because one is free from sense organs and objects, the internal mind is naturally secluded, tranquil, pure, and empty;
it is light, supple, and harmonious, with the clamor of dust forever stilled and all heaviness and coarseness long dispelled. Within this, the minds of the Buddhas of the ten directions manifest.

This clarifies that the perfectly luminous nature-body of sentient beings is no different from that of the Buddhas; it is only because of deluded emotions that the ordinary and the sagely appear separated, as if by this very body.
When the characteristics of the mind are exhausted and deluded thoughts do not arise, the wondrous mind of perfect enlightenment (yuanjue miaoxin) permeates both the ordinary and the holy.
Speaking from the perspective of ultimate reality, my own body and mind are likewise able to manifest universally within the bodies of the Buddhas of the ten directions;

however, because we are currently taking the practitioner entering meditative observation as the primary subject, it is said that "the Buddhas manifest therein" (Guifeng). This tranquility is the essence of the Truth of Ultimate Reality (paramārtha-satya), which is the Bodhisattva.

Realizing that this is not the stubborn adherence of the Lesser Vehicle, it is called the "world of pliancy" as the environment (*āśraya-pratiniṣpatti*) and the Buddha-mind as the primary retribution (*adhiṣṭhāna-pratiniṣpatti*).
Once the coarse defilements of views and thoughts are exhausted, one forgets the internal and merges with the external;

spontaneously, one shares the same true emptiness (*tathatā-śūnyatā*) as the environment and primary retribution of the ordinary and sage beings across the ten realms. Therefore, one is able to see forms beyond obstructions with the eyes and hear sounds beyond obstructions with the ears.
When the *śrotra-vidyā* (hearing-vidyā) of the *Śūraṅgama* returns the flow to its source and becomes entirely one, the six functions cease their activity.

The lands of the ten directions appear brilliantly pure, like a bright moon suspended within lapis lazuli. Even all the secret, perfect, pure, and wondrous [realms] of the Tathāgatas manifest therein.

This is the sign of realization in this stage: the mirror is the metaphor for quiescence, while the images reflected are the metaphors for the environment and the inhabitants (the *dharmadhātu* and the *sattvadhātu*). (From the *Cishi*) Wondrous.
The essence and virtue of Perfect Enlightenment are all-pervasive and harmoniously fused;

the wisdom that realizes the non-differentiation of the three—mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—is the manifestation of the luminous essence, pure and clear like a reflected image. This also fully reveals the three truths, not merely the truth of emptiness alone (private note).
The name of the three fetters (*saṃyojana*). This method is called *śamatha*.

Translated here as "cessation" (*zhi*), it is a synonym for meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and carries the sense of tranquility (*śānti*); that is, regarding objects such as the defiled and the pure, the mind—
"Because it does not falsely objectify [phenomena], it is quiescent; this clarifies its characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). 'Calm abiding' (*śamatha*) is the etymological explanation (*nirukti*).

Since one cultivates calm abiding, all three are termed 'insight' (*vipaśyanā*); this is because in this school, both principle and phenomena, as well as concentration and wisdom, are entirely without obstruction.

Thus, regarding the cultivation of calm abiding, one practices insight. (Guifeng) Concentration and wisdom are non-dual; following the text, they are distinguished as before has been shown. Huanshu uses the three."
To stop and explain these three contemplations of this practice as being the "contemplation of the illusory" and to seek its faults is erroneous; it is not what is employed here.
(Private Note: 2. Samāpatti, 3. Third. First, the heading and explanation.)

Good son, if bodhisattvas awaken to pure, perfect enlightenment, there are two [sections] explaining the practice, the third being the conclusion. First is the direct demonstration of cultivation and realization:
with a mind of pure awakening, they know that the nature of the awakened mind, as well as the faculties and their objects, are all produced by illusion; thus they give rise to various illusions.

By means of the one who removes illusions transforming various illusions to open the way for the illusory assembly, because of the arising of illusion, one is able to internally give rise to great compassion and serenity (*praśrabdhi*).
The nature of the mind is consciousness; since consciousness, the sense faculties, and their objects each lack intrinsic nature, they are called illusory transformations. Thus, all illusions...

"Illusion-wisdom": "illusion" refers to fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*), which is the agent of illusion. By eliminating this agent of illusion through the power of "illusory initial enlightenment" (*ādi-bodhi*), one partially awakens from fundamental non-enlightenment.

Regarding "transforming according to [the capacity of] beings," this refers to manifesting transformations in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings who are like illusions, teaching and revealing the Dharma.
Since sense organs and objects have both vanished, self and other are non-dual; therefore, one is able to...

Internally, there arises great compassion of the same essence; this compassion arises from meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and is not due to attachment or false views, whereby pliancy and ease are fully realized (Guifeng).
That which is illusory is precisely the mind-consciousness, the faculties, and the sense objects; great compassion is the substance of conventional truth (Cishan).

To "awaken to the fact that the faculties and objects are illusory transformations and lack reality" refers to the state of meditative concentration; "thereupon giving rise to various illusions" below correctly clarifies the arising of the cultivation of contemplation.

"Using illusions to eliminate illusions, personally severing delusions, and manifesting transformations to benefit others" refers to the four teachings and four gates of the provisional [expedient means] for transforming others.

Within each gate, one knows the Four Truths; by diagnosing the illness and identifying the medicine, one employs the method of administering medicine that accords with each individual's capacity—hence it is called "transformation.

Thus, through various illusions, one opens the way for illusory multitudes. However, these illusory appearances must all be clearly perceived and known through mental contemplation (*citta-vipaśyanā*).

Thereafter, he brought forth the Tiantai *Zhiguan* (Cessation and Contemplation), stating: "In the past, the Tathāgata, through the gradual and sudden contemplations of the mind—both partial and complete—relied upon this contemplation of the mind to preach for the sake of sentient beings; this is precisely its meaning. From the passage "Because of the arising of illusions," the subsequent contemplation is established as that which is produced.
The following chapter clarifies the solitary cultivation of illusory practices; since it says, "not losing silent mindfulness," and so forth.
Because all [phenomena] are of quiescent wisdom, they cannot be definitively established by conventional truth alone (private note).
This second section further clarifies the departure from marks:
all Bodhisattvas initiate their practice from this point and gradually advance; for those who contemplate illusion are not identical to the illusion itself.
Because that which is not identical to the contemplation of illusion is entirely illusory, one is forever free from illusory marks.

All Bodhisattvas and others again reiterate what they have cultivated; in the following passage, they correctly clarify being free from marks because it is not identical to the contemplation of illusion.

This means that regarding the wisdom that forgets objects, it is not identical to the contemplation of illusion, etc.; the capacity to illuminate is also quiescent, meaning it is not identical to the contemplation of illusion.

The contemplation of objects is likewise entirely illusory; since both subject and object are discarded and both medicine and disease are forgotten, it is said that "illusory appearances are forever transcended" (Private Note). Third, the summary concludes with an analogy.
The perfected and wondrous practices of these bodhisattvas are like soil nurturing sprouts.

Soil is a metaphor for innate virtue (*prakṛti-guṇa*), while sprouts are a metaphor for contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-caryā*). The advancement of contemplative practice is like soil nurturing sprouts.

Guifeng said: "It is like planting grain and other crops; they depend on soil to grow into sprouts, yet when the harvest is gathered, both sprouts and soil are discarded. The seed is a metaphor for awakening (*bodhi*).

The mind and the soil are likened to illusory phenomena, while the sprouts are likened to illusory wisdom. Now, you ask why the meaning of "extinction" is used to interpret the sūtra’s metaphor of "growth and development"?
Moreover, the verse states: "Like the samādhi of illusion, like a sprout gradually growing" (Zhuangnan).
The name for the three fetters (*saṃyojana*) is *samāpatti*. It is also called *samāpatti*, which here means "attainment" (*tingdengzhi*);
because within this state of meditative equipoise (*samādhi*), one is able to reach the stage of the noble ones (*ārya*).
(Guifeng) states that "equal arrival" (*samāpatti*) means that illusory wisdom arrives equally and universally at the objects to be transformed.

Here, it is directly explained as the contemplation of the provisional. (Cishi) has already previously indicated the perfect understanding and cited "one is three," meaning that one is entirely provisional.
As stated in the Chapter on Perfect Enlightenment: "Sammādhi is correct mindfulness and retention" (Private Note).
The third section on *dhyāna* has three parts. First, the heading and explanation:
"Good son, if a bodhisattva awakens to pure, perfect *bodhi*.
Second, the explanation of the practice, which has two parts. First, clarifying the characteristics of cultivation.
With a mind of pure awakening, one does not grasp at illusory transformations or various states of stillness. One thoroughly understands that both body and mind are but obstructions;
when awareness and clarity do not rely upon any such obstacles, one forever transcends the realms of both obstruction and non-obstruction.

Thus, one experiences the world as well as the characteristics of body and mind within the dusty realm, like the resonance of a bell within a vessel sounding forth from without—whether it be affliction or nirvana.
There is no mutual obstruction or hindrance.
To thoroughly understand that both body and mind are entirely obstructions, it is the clarity of non-cognition that is able to transcend them;

it is not the deliberation of the mind nor the sensory awareness of the body. This clarity is the essence capable of transcending them; as for the obstructed and unobstructed objects, it is [this clarity] that is able to [transcend them].

That which is simultaneously discarded can also be obstructed; this refers to the lack of obstruction between birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and nirvāṇa. As for "enjoyment," it pertains to one's own personal requisites and conditions.

As for the "world," it refers to the shared lands and territories where beings dwell together. Regarding those who exist within the realm of sensory objects, the primary body (*adhiṣṭhāna-kāya*) and the secondary environment (*bhājana-loka*) rely upon and support one another as they abide.

From the fifth stage (*pañcama-bhūmi*) onward, those born with physical bodies who have attained forbearance (*kṣānti*) all remain within the realm of segmented existence (*paricchinna-bhava*), even if they enter the state of transformation (*nirmāṇa*).

Furthermore, as long as one has not yet departed from the aggregates (*skandhas*), these all belong to the realm of obstruction; it is precisely because they are obstructive that they are non-obstructive, like the gong-rings within a bronze vessel.

However, this meaning of "precisely because it is obstructive that it is non-obstructive" is not seen in the original Dharma-texts; it must be revealed through a metaphor, which demonstrates the skill of the translator.

Regarding the metaphor of the vessel, the afflictions (*kleśas*) are placed below to correspond to it. Guifeng remarked that the character *huáng* (gong-ring) is not fixed, fearing that the translator may have erred, and thus he [proposed]...
Regarding the three explanations for the single character *huáng* (鍠): 1. Based on its phonetic value, it is interpreted as "harmony" (*hé*) and "joy" (*lè*).

This does not refer to the sound within a musical instrument, but rather to the resonance of striking a *qìng* (gong) and similar instruments, where the sound vibrates with a *huáng-huáng* resonance. The translator was somewhat unskillful here. 2. It is read with the same pronunciation as *kuàng* (鑛), which refers to a large bell.

Alternatively, the character *huáng* may have been written incorrectly as *huáng* (鐄). 3. It is read with the same pronunciation as *huáng* (簧), referring to the reeds of a *shēng* (sheng) mouth organ.
Because there are various types of instruments that possess reeds, it is not restricted solely to the *sheng* (mouth organ); rather, it refers to the reeds within the instrument in general.
This is because the translators were not proficient in the phonology and orthography of this region, resulting in both the characters and the pronunciation being erroneous.
The commentaries of others all rely on this interpretation. I, however, maintain that Guifeng’s commentary frequently censures the translators, as he was deeply pained by their errors.

He was profoundly erudite; furthermore, among all the translations produced during a single generation, none matched the balance of literary elegance and substantive meaning found in this scripture translated by Juejiu (Kumārajīva).
How could there be a single erroneous character? Thus, he was unjustly held responsible for the faults of unskillful dialects and phonology.

The *Guangyun* commentary on the character "Huang" states that according to the *Shuowen*, its pronunciation is "huang"; how can one exclusively hold him at fault for using the "heng" (horizontal) tone? The people of the world [have thus] falsely accused him.
The two iron clamps hidden within the drum are used to extend the resonance of its sound;

now, this sutra specifically takes the subtle sound of the vessel being great as a metaphor for penetrating the state of non-obstruction precisely where there is obstruction (Zhuangnan). It does not take illusory stillness as the ultimate, but rather attains transcendence of both obstructed and unobstructed realms.
This reveals the simultaneous negation of the two extremes and the true entry into the Middle Way. "Receiving and using" below clarifies the Middle.
The essence of the contemplation of the Way is all-pervasive and boundless; the "aspect of being present" (xiāngzài) should be pronounced with a falling tone (*xiàng*).

It is simply that the various aspects of body and mind, one by one, are identical with the Center; though localized, they are omnipresent (private note). Second, showing the completion of the contemplation.
One is then able to inwardly give rise to tranquil extinction and subtle pliancy, wherein the wondrous awakening accords with the realm of extinction;
this is beyond the reach of the body and mind of oneself or others, and the life-span of sentient beings is seen as nothing but floating thoughts.
Quiescence (*śānti*) is the essence of the Middle Truth; because the Bodhisattva dwells herein without attachment, it is called "light ease" (*praśrabdhi*).

Since the three truths are all the Middle, it is termed "quiescent wondrous enlightenment. To accord with the realm of quiescence is for the wondrous, perfect, and complete enlightened wisdom to be in conformity with the Middle Way.
Regarding "self and others" and so forth: although this realm of quiescence pervades all phenomena...
Furthermore, to be free from all conceptualizations regarding the five aggregates— such as the attachment that designates them as "sentient beings" or the grasping at long duration as "life span"—
and to understand these three fetters as names, this skillful means is called *dhyāna*.
This "dhyāna" (静虑) is precisely the essence that doubly negates; this too is directly explained as Madhyamaka (慈室).
Third, the summary reveals the perfection.
Good son, these three dharma-gates are all the causes for approaching and conforming to the Tathāgatas of the ten directions within Perfect Enlightenment.
All the various skillful means of the Bodhisattvas of the ten directions who attain Buddhahood, whether identical or different, depend entirely upon these three kinds of practice;
if one attains perfect realization of them, one immediately achieves Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*).

These three gates all arise based on the realization of the pure, perfect *bodhi* (*vimala-vibuddha-bodhi*); their contemplative practices (*vipaśyanā-caryā*) likewise all enter into *bodhi*, never departing from it from beginning to end.
Thus, it is said that they "draw near to" and "accord with" the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, realizing and practicing together.

While their modes of practice vary according to individual capacities and circumstances—whether many people collectively practice a single gate or a single person does so—the essential principle remains the same.

One cultivates various practices extensively, yet all must rely upon these three types of karma—whether practicing all three together, singly, or in combination, as clarified in the "Twenty-five Wheels" (Guifeng).
Since all three are Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*), and it is said that they are "perfectly realized," this proves they are not merely simple or shallow sequential practices;
rather, while their application varies according to the capacities of beings, the essence of the practice remains only these three. (Private Note)
4. Comparing and Revealing Superiority:
Good son, suppose there were someone who practiced the teachings of the Noble Ones and brought to fruition the fruits of a hundred thousand million *arhats* and *pratyekabuddhas*;
this would not equal someone who hears this unimpeded Dharma-practice of Perfect Enlightenment for even a single moment.
At that time, one practices in accordance [with the teachings].
The partial and small [vehicles] belong to the provisional, while the Perfect Vehicle accords with the nature of reality; how could the sun, the moon, or a torch ever be equal to it? (Private Note).
The two verses praise two things: first, the formal presentation.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses.
[Part Two: The Proper Verses; Part Three: The Commentary. First, the verse that indicates the explanation:
"Vīradeva, you should know: The mind of the unsurpassed Great Awakened One Is, from the primordial limit, devoid of dual characteristics."
The various skillful means that accord with [the needs of beings] are immeasurable in number; the Tathāgata has summarized and revealed them as having three types of modes of activity (ākāra).
These two verses describe their characteristics.
Quiescent śamatha is like a mirror reflecting all images; The illusory-like samādhi is like a sprout gradually growing;
Dhyāna is solely cessation, like the decorative rings within a vessel.
These three verses provide a summary.
These three kinds of sublime Dharma gates are all in accordance with awakening;

by means of them, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions and the great Bodhisattvas attain the realization of the Way. Because these three matters are perfectly realized, it is called ultimate *nirvāṇa*.

II. Chapter on Distinguishing Sounds: Clarifying the Indeterminate Characteristics. The three preceding dharma-gates concern the sequential, gradual cultivation according to the specific inclinations of practitioners;

however, there may also be instantaneous, perfect cultivation—whether practiced singly or in combination, alternating between them or in succession. Therefore, they are called "indeterminate practices.

Although the practices are indeterminate, the understanding must necessarily rely upon the Perfect [Teaching]. (Private Note) This section is divided into two parts; first, the inquiry, which is further divided into three. First, the formal etiquette of the request.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Viśvabhāṣin rose from his seat amidst the great assembly, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet,
circumambulated him three times to the right, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
Second, the formal presentation of the words in three parts. First, celebrating what was previously heard:
"The Greatly Compassionate World-Honored One, such a Dharma-gate is truly rare.
Second, asking how many times it should be practiced.
World-Honored One, regarding all these skillful means, how many ways of cultivation are there for Bodhisattvas within the gateway of Perfect Enlightenment?

Although the three contemplations previously explained have their distinct characteristics clearly defined, I do not yet know whether the cultivation practiced by a Bodhisattva involves one person possessing all three, or three persons each having one;
whether they are practiced sequentially or simultaneously; and whether they follow a fixed order or allow for skipping stages (Guifeng).
Third, the intent of the request:
I pray that you will provide skillful instruction for the sake of the great assembly and sentient beings of the末法 (mofa) age, enabling them to awaken to the true nature (*dharmatā*).
Third, third, I prostrate with utmost sincerity.
Having spoken these words, they prostrated themselves with their five limbs touching the ground; thus they made this request three times, beginning again and again.
The two Buddhas answered them thrice, first praising and granting their request.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Viśvāmitra, saying: "Excellent, excellent, son of good family! You all..."
"You are able to ask the Tathāgata on behalf of the great assembly and the sentient beings of the末法 (mòfǎ) age regarding such cultivation;
listen attentively now, and I shall explain it for you.
The two [disciples] received the command.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Viśvāghoṣa, having received the instruction with joy, along with the great assembly, listened in silence.
Regarding the threefold correct answer, there are two parts: first, the prose section, which has three sub-divisions. First, the statement of intent and the enumeration of the numbers.
"Good son, the perfect enlightenment of all Tathāgatas is fundamentally pure and originally devoid of both cultivation and a cultivator.
It is only because all Bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age rely upon the power of illusion due to their lack of awakening that they engage in cultivation;
at that time, there arise twenty-five kinds of wheels of pure concentration."

Perfect Enlightenment is without cultivation; it is the luminous basis upon which all things depend. It clarifies the meaning of the various wheels, such as the wheel of the fundamental and derivative consciousnesses.

"Wheel" (*cakra*) has the sense of crushing and grinding; it can crush the obstacles of delusion so that right wisdom may turn. (Guifeng) Fundamentally, there is no cultivation, nor is there any dharma to be cultivated, nor any cultivator who practices.
The nature of humanity is non-active (*anabhisaṃskāra*). This is based on the illusory power of unawakened mind.

Regarding the practitioner: based on non-enlightenment (*abodha*), there is the practice of cultivating the virtue of initial enlightenment (*ādi-bodhi*). Regarding the wheel of concentration (*samādhi-cakra*):
the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states that "the ability to contemplate the mind in concentration is called the supreme concentration" (Zhu Nan). Second, the presentation of the three types of cultivation:
first, the single cultivation of the three primary wheels; second, the mutual cultivation of the twenty-one wheels; third, the perfect cultivation of the one wheel. (From the *Jiao Shu*).
Regarding these twenty-five wheels, each is established with a name based on a metaphor;

Guifeng used them all [in his commentary], but here we shall follow the Sūtra by categorizing and explaining them as "quiescence," "illusion," "tranquility," and "characteristic" (private note). In the first three wheels, one practices the three initial quiescent conducts in isolation.
If a bodhisattva grasps only extreme tranquility and, by the power of that tranquility,
permanently severs the afflictions and ultimately achieves accomplishment such that they enter nirvana without rising from their seat, this bodhisattva is said to practice śamatha alone.
Each of the twenty-five wheels has its specific enumeration and *mudrā*; these should also be individually identified as "Awakening to Pure Perfect Enlightenment.
Due to the prolixity of the text, they are abbreviated here. Without arising from the seat of the emptiness of dharmas, one enters directly into the nirvana of quiescent extinction (Guifeng).

Although the contemplative practices of the initial gate are gradual, the teachings are entirely perfect and flow through to the end. The final chapter speaks of sentient beings with sudden faculties.
From this point on, awakening also encompasses all classes of beings who practice through gradual cultivation;

this is precisely because the Perfect Dharma is sovereign, allowing entry according to individual capacities without hindering the practice of either the single or the manifold, thus entering the sudden from the gradual.
(Zhuan’an) Although the practice may be single, since the Nirvana entered is both perfect and sudden, how could it not be that the one inherently possesses the three? Below.

The two contemplations follow this principle. (Cishì) Question: May one cultivate only one [of the three immeasurables] while abandoning the other two? Answer: One does not abandon them; it is not a case of "single abandonment.
If that were so, how could the practice of illusion (*māyā-caryā*) not lose its silent mindfulness and various tranquil wisdoms?
Answer: To maintain the three while employing one is not to abandon the two wheels (*cakra*). Second, the practice of illusion.

If bodhisattvas contemplate all things as being like illusions, yet by the power of the Buddha manifest various functions within transformed worlds and fully practice the pure and wondrous conduct of a bodhisattva—
maintaining the samādhi of dhāraṇī without losing their tranquil mindfulness and various still wisdoms—
such bodhisattvas are said to practice *samāpatti* alone.

Because one must rely upon the Buddha’s empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) to exhaustively transform and deliver [sentient beings], it says "by the power of the Buddha" and so forth. "Tranquil mindfulness" (*jìngniàn*) refers to stillness;

"wisdom" (*huì*) refers to emptiness (*śūnyatā*). (Compassionate Chamber) Although various transformations and functions are manifested, since the conclusion states that these are cultivated through unification, they are the wondrous provisional (*prajñapti*) illuminated by the contemplation of the mind.
Furthermore, one's own power of awakening may also be called the "power of the Buddha. As for *dhāraṇī*:
The Middle Way, the Total Retention (*dhāraṇī*), and Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*) are merely different names for the same thing. As the preceding text states:
"There is a great *dhāraṇī* gate named Perfect Enlightenment" (Private Note). This refers to the three practices of stillness.
If bodhisattvas merely extinguish all illusions without engaging in their functions, and solely sever afflictions until those afflictions are completely exhausted,
thereby realizing the true mark of reality— such bodhisattvas are said to practice *dhyāna* alone.
"Extinction" (*nirodha*) means the severance of thought; "solitude" (*ekāgra*) means not relying on conditioned phenomena—this is the meaning of transcending all dependencies (Guifeng).

To extinguish illusions is to negate the provisional; does this not also negate the empty? Since both are negated, one enters the Middle Way; furthermore, by realizing the true aspect (*dharmatā*), the one embodies the three—how could this not be worthy of trust?
(Private Note) Second: the twenty-one wheels are cultivated mutually. Third: the first seven wheels consist of tranquil contemplation (*śamatha*).

In the first seven wheels, one primarily cultivates the contemplation of illusion while concurrently cultivating tranquility; in the middle seven wheels, one primarily cultivates the contemplation of tranquility while concurrently cultivating illusion;

and in the final seven wheels, one primarily cultivates the contemplation of tranquility while concurrently cultivating illusion. Within each of these three groups of seven, there are three distinct intentions:

the first two wheels are practiced in alternation, the next two are practiced in combination, and the final three wheels are practiced simultaneously. Furthermore, the first seven wheels are categorized according to the scriptural text.
Seventh: first stillness, then illusion.

If a bodhisattva first attains ultimate stillness and, with a mind of still wisdom, illuminates all illusions, thereby giving rise to the bodhisattva practice therein, this bodhisattva is said to have first cultivated śamatha and subsequently cultivated samāpatti.
Second, first tranquility and subsequently stillness.
If bodhisattvas, by means of tranquil wisdom, realize the nature of ultimate tranquility and thereby sever the afflictions, forever emerging from birth and death,
such bodhisattvas are said to have first cultivated *śamatha* and subsequently cultivated *dhyāna*.
Because of stillness-wisdom (*śamatha-prajñā*), there is "stillness" (*jing*); because one realizes the nature of ultimate stillness, there is "tranquility" (*ji*).
The causes of affliction perish and the fruits of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) are lost (Guifeng). First comes stillness, next illusion, and finally tranquility.
If bodhisattvas, by means of tranquil wisdom, further manifest various transformations through the power of illusion to deliver sentient beings,
and subsequently sever their afflictions to enter into quiescent extinction— such bodhisattvas are said to have first cultivated *śamatha*,
then cultivated *samāpatti*, and finally cultivated *dhyāna*.
The fourth is: first tranquility (*śamatha*), then stillness (*vipaśyanā*), and finally the illusory-like.

If a bodhisattva, having severed the afflictions through the power of supreme tranquility, subsequently gives rise to the pure and wondrous conduct of a bodhisattva to deliver all sentient beings, this bodhisattva is said to have first cultivated *śamatha*, then cultivated *dhyāna* (meditative concentration), and finally cultivated [the illusory-like].
Regarding samāpatti: fifth, first stilling and aligning the illusory and quiescent.
If bodhisattvas, by the power of ultimate stillness, sever afflictions with the mind and further deliver sentient beings while establishing worlds.

This Bodhisattva is one who first cultivates śamatha and then cultivates samāpatti and dhyāna in equal measure. Having first stilled the illusions through these six equal practices, they subsequently attain quiescence.
If a Bodhisattva utilizes the power of ultimate stillness to inspire and manifest transformations, and thereafter cuts off afflictions, this Bodhisattva is [one of such a kind].
This is called practicing *śamatha* and *samāpatti* simultaneously, followed by practicing *dhyāna*.
Seventh is practicing stillness and silence simultaneously, followed by the illusory.
If Bodhisattvas employ the power of ultimate stillness to support their quiescent extinction, they subsequently initiate activity to transform the world.
This Bodhisattva is named Qi (Equal Cultivation), who first cultivates śamatha and dhyāna, and subsequently cultivates samāpatti.
He takes the illusory contemplation of the two seven-day cycles as his primary practice, combining both stillness and tranquility; first the illusory, then the tranquil.
If a bodhisattva, through the power of transformation, employs various forms of adaptation to attain ultimate stillness,
this bodhisattva is said to have first cultivated *samāpatti* and subsequently cultivated *śamatha*.
Second is "illusion first, then stillness.
If bodhisattvas attain cessation through various realms by means of the power of transformation,
these bodhisattvas are said to have first cultivated samāpatti and subsequently cultivated dhyāna.
Third: first illusion, next stillness, and finally tranquility.

If a bodhisattva performs buddha-work through the power of transformation, abides in tranquility, and cuts off afflictions, this bodhisattva is said to have first practiced *samāpatti*, then practiced *śamatha*, and finally practiced *dhyāna*.
The fourth is: first illusion, next tranquility, and finally stillness.

If a bodhisattva, by means of the power of transformation and unimpeded activity, severs the afflictions and abides in ultimate stillness, this bodhisattva is said to have first practiced *samāpatti*, then cultivated *dhyāna*, and finally cultivated *śamatha*.
Fifth, first through illusion one attains stillness and tranquility.
If Bodhisattvas, by means of the power of transformation and skillful application, reach the ultimate stillness and extinction, and both [samādhi and prajñā] accord with this,
such Bodhisattvas are said to have first cultivated samāpatti while concurrently cultivating śamatha-vipaśyanā.
Sixth is "equally cultivating *samāpatti* first and *śamatha* later.
If bodhisattvas, by means of the power of transformation, employ various functions to support ultimate stillness and subsequently sever afflictions,
these bodhisattvas are said to be "equally cultivating *samāpatti* first and practicing *dhyāna* later."
Seventh is the practice of stillness after the completion of illusion and tranquility.
If bodhisattvas, by means of the power of transformation, support their tranquility and subsequently abide in pure, effortless meditative concentration (*dhyāna*),
such bodhisattvas are said to be practicing *samāpatti* (meditative attainment) and *dhyāna* (contemplation) together, followed by the cultivation of *śamatha* (calm abiding).
The thirty-seventh is the contemplation of stillness as the foremost, wherein one concurrently cultivates both tranquility and illusion.

First comes stillness, followed by tranquility. If a bodhisattva, through the power of cessation, gives rise to supreme stillness and abides in purity, this bodhisattva is said to first cultivate dhyāna and subsequently cultivate śamatha.
Second is "first tranquility, then illusion.
If bodhisattvas, by the power of cessation (*śamatha*), initiate activity within all objects such that their tranquil activity accords with this,
these bodhisattvas are said to "first cultivate *dhyāna* and subsequently cultivate *samāpatti*."
The three stages are first tranquility (*śama*),

then stillness (*samatha*), and finally illusion (*vikalpa*). If bodhisattvas, by the power of cessation, abide in meditative concentration through various intrinsic natures and give rise to transformations,
such bodhisattvas are said to have first cultivated *dhyāna*, then cultivated *śamatha*, and finally cultivated *samāpatti*.
Fourth: first quiescence (*śama*), then illusion (*māyā*), and finally stillness (*śānti*).

If a bodhisattva, through the power of cessation (*nirodha*) and the unconditioned nature (*anabhisaṃskāra-svabhāva*), gives rise to activity within the pure realm and returns to meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), this bodhisattva is said to have first cultivated *dhyāna* and subsequently cultivated *samāpatti*.
One cultivates śamatha.
First, one pacifies and brings stillness to the illusion.
If bodhisattvas, through the power of cessation and various forms of purity, abide in meditative concentration and give rise to transformations.
This bodhisattva is one who first cultivates dhyāna, practicing śamatha and samāpatti in equal measure.
After the six stages of simultaneous stillness, there is the illusory manifestation.
If a bodhisattva, by means of the power of cessation, supports ultimate stillness and gives rise to transformations, this is that bodhisattva.
This is called practicing *dhyāna* and *śamatha* simultaneously, followed by practicing *samāpatti*.
It is the stillness that follows the simultaneous quiescence of illusions.
If bodhisattvas, through the power of cessation (*nirodha*), augment their transformative manifestations (*nirmāṇa*) and give rise to the wisdom of the most profound stillness and luminous clarity.
This Bodhisattva is named Simultaneous Cultivation of Samāpatti followed by Śamatha.
This is the cultivation of the three in a single perfect wheel.
If all Bodhisattvas, with the wisdom of Perfect Enlightenment, perfectly unify all things such that no natures or characteristics depart from the nature of enlightenment, [they attain this].
This Bodhisattva is said to have "perfectly cultivated the three kinds of self-nature purity in accordance with reality.

Because the perfect and sudden sublime contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) realizes that the objects created are immediately the Middle Way, it is called "perfectly harmonizing with all things. This phrase "all" encompasses the ten realms of existence, including both the environment and its inhabitants, as well as cause and effect.
Furthermore, the nature and characteristics of every phenomenon within the ten realms are all truly real; there is nothing that is not the Three Truths.
It is said that regarding all natures and characteristics, one contemplates the three truths through the nature of awakening that is free from [dualistic] cognition and transcends thought;
thus it is called the "perfect cultivation" that accords with the three kinds of intrinsically pure self-nature (Private Note). Third, this concludes the exhortation to practice.
"Good son, these are called the twenty-five wheels of the Bodhisattva. All Bodhisattvas practice in this manner.

If any Bodhisattvas or sentient beings of the final age rely upon these wheels, they should maintain pure conduct (*brahmacarya*), contemplate with tranquility, and seek compassion through repentance for a period of twenty-one days.
They should place identifying marks at each of the twenty-five wheels and seek [the goal] with a sincere mind."
"Compassionately following the hand to grasp and untie the knots reveals them; thus one immediately knows the sudden and gradual [paths]. A single thought of doubt or regret means non-attainment.

This demonstrates the ritual method for cultivation: pure conduct (*brahmacarya*) is the precepts (*śīla*), tranquility is concentration (*samādhi*), and reflection is wisdom (*prajñā*). It is complete."

With the mind of precept, concentration, and wisdom focused on the gate of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), practicing in this manner will surely lead to the attainment of Buddhahood. Regarding practices such as repentance:
fearing that the karmic burdens accumulated over many lifetimes might obstruct the pure mind, one should repent, seek compassion, and disclose prior transgressions.
Even if the number of days is few, one must ensure sincerity; within twenty-one days, one’s earnest supplications will become manifest. Thus, the names of the twenty-five wheels are written down.
Place the characters and phrases within the *bodhimaṇḍa* and perform prostrations with sincere devotion and earnest prayer.

If you personally prefer one particular gate, practice it accordingly. If you cannot distinguish between superior and inferior and are unable to decide for yourself, rely on the power of the Sage to divine what you should believe;
simply let your hand take [the scroll] without deliberation. Once selected, untie the knot and examine it.
If you suddenly realize for yourself that you have no greed [for further practice], yet harbor doubts and obstructions regarding other contemplations of the mind, you will lose all prior merit.

Even if you were to cultivate it again, success would be somewhat difficult to achieve. Judging by your faculties and verifying the principle, this must be the case; do not treat these matters with indifference or take the ritual forms lightly.
(Guifeng) There are three methods for performing repentance: taking signs as the object, taking non-arising as the primary focus, and the method where both words and tears are employed.

Because it is a preliminary stage, it is called "seeking compassion" (Dongyang). The twenty-one-day period is not yet formal cultivation; rather, it is for the purpose of making a definitive selection regarding what is to be cultivated.
As for the markers, these are slips of paper or similar items; as for the records, they are the twenty-five names. One must gather them together in sequence, then pray with grief:
"In which contemplation do I have the seed? Which contemplation is appropriate for me? Then, reaching into the collection at random, one ties one slip of paper with a string.
Thereafter, upon examination, one may find twenty-four wheels representing the gradual [approach], while the final wheel represents the sudden.

How could one then doubt that this contemplation is not accomplished, or regret that the other contemplation was not attained? (Compassionate Chamber) The subsequent *Chapter on Perfect Enlightenment* states:

"If this contemplation is not attained, one should again practice that contemplation," thereby verifying that the various wheels are indeterminate as to whether they are gradual or sudden. (Private Commentary) Two verses in praise of these two.
First, the brief thematic statement.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse.
Second, the actual verses. First, the verses expressing the intent.
"O Prabhanetra, you should know that the unimpeded and pure wisdom of all bodhisattvas arises entirely from meditative concentration.
Thus [it is said] in two verses concerning cultivation.
What are called śamatha, samādhi, and dhyāna— these three dharmas are cultivated through both sudden and gradual methods in twenty-five ways.
Among all the Tathāgatas of the ten directions and all practitioners of the three periods of time,
there are none who have not attained bodhi by means of this dharma, with the sole exception of those who achieve sudden enlightenment.

Furthermore, regarding those whose dharmas do not accord with the Tathāgata, the prose commentary does not mention them; it was based thereon on their causal practice (*hetu-caryā*). Now, however, both cause and effect are fully set forth.

With the exception of those of sudden enlightenment and those whose dharmas do not accord [with the Tathāgata], these two categories are likewise not mentioned in the prose commentary; this is because we now clarify that they do not [accord].
Because they involve the realization through the practice of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), twenty-five types [of practitioners] are clarified according to their gradual and sudden approaches.

However, for those who follow the perfectly sudden (*yuantun*) practice and realization, as well as those who do not believe in or accord with this teaching, it cannot be said that there is no one who will attain *bodhi* by means of this;

therefore, it says, "excepting... (as in the phrase "only excluding..."). Regarding the two interpretations of Mount Gui (Guishan), I shall now employ the latter meaning; those in need should consult the original text themselves (private note).
The three verses conclude with an exhortation:
All bodhisattvas And sentient beings of the final age Should always uphold this wheel, practicing it diligently in accordance with it;
Relying on the power of the Buddha’s great compassion, They shall before long realize nirvana.
III. The Two Chapters on Purifying Karma and Universal Awakening: Showing the Dharma and Illnesses. Part One:
The Chapter on Purifying Karma, showing the four illnesses such as "I" and so forth. Sub-part One: The Initial Inquiry. 1.
The Manner of Approaching and Questioning.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Purifying All Karmic Obstructions rose from his seat amidst the great assembly, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet,
circumambulated him three times to the right, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
Part Two: The Formal Presentation of the Text, in Three Sections. First, expressing gratitude for what preceded:

"The Greatly Compassionate World-Honored One has extensively expounded for us such inconceivable matters—the modes of conduct of all Tathāgatas during their stages of practice—causing the great assembly to attain what they had never before experienced, beholding the Tamer [the Buddha] throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges."
All the efforts and activities within the realms of diligent practice are like a single thought; we Bodhisattvas deeply rejoice and comfort ourselves.

Extensively expounding the three types of Dharma-gates, their various wheels interlace so that, within the non-differentiated nature of awakening, their characteristics are distinguished—this is called the inconceivable matter.
Among the ten titles of the Tamer (Śāstṛ), this is one; a Buddha is endowed with ten thousand virtues.
The names are likewise immeasurable, as described in the "Chapter on Names and Epithets" of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* (Dongyang). This is the realization of causal practice.

Now, while the fruit-deity accords with reality and can be illuminated through principle, causal practice involves the treatment of defilements, and its essential understanding is difficult to attain.

Yet, in a single thought-moment, one fully knows them all, manifesting clearly and simultaneously, like many mustard seeds contained within a crystal vase; therefore, it is profoundly consoling (Guifeng).
Second, the present inquiry:
"World-Honored One, if the fundamental nature of this awakened mind is inherently pure, for what reason is it defiled such that the great assembly is bewildered and distressed,
unable to enter [into realization]?"

Because he heard in the preceding chapter that Perfect Enlightenment is pure and fundamentally free from cultivation, he is now able to seek instruction [from the Compassionate Chamber]. [The Master replies:

"As for those who speak of defilement, this must be discussed in terms of cultivated virtue; it is shown that because one is unaware of the fundamental enlightenment of the nature-qualities, how could there be any defilement?
(Zhangnan). This was the third request and the response.

We only pray that the Tathāgata will extensively awaken us to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), so that this great assembly and the sentient beings of the final age may serve as eyes for the future.
(Three times, with utmost sincerity.)
Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground, making this request three times, beginning again and again.
The two Buddhas answered him three times.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Purifying All Karmic Obstructions, saying: "Excellent, excellent, son of good family! You..."
"Only those such as you are able to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding such skillful means for the sake of the great assembly and sentient beings of the末法 (mofa/declining age).
Listen attentively now, and I shall explain them for you.
The two [disciples] received the command.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Purifying All Karmic Obstructions, having received the instruction with joy, along with the great assembly, listened in silence.
Part Three: The Correct Answer, in two sections. Section One: The Extended Exposition, in three parts. Part One: A Brief Demonstration, in two parts. Part One: Citing Faults and Correctly Responding.
Initially, delusion arises from delusion.
Good son, all sentient beings, since beginningless time, have falsely imagined and clung to the notions of self, person, sentient being, and life-span;
they take these four inversions to be their real self-substance. From this, there arise the two objects of aversion and attachment.
The body of false delusion and the grasping at false delusion—these two delusions depend on one another to give rise to the path of false karma.
Because there is false karma, false views circulate; those who weary of this circulation falsely perceive nirvana.

"Beginningless" refers to that which has never been awakened to; hence, there follows the analogy of one born blind. "Delusive conceptualization" (*vikalpa*) refers to the arbitrary imputation of a self, persons, and so forth within what is non-existent.

Taken collectively, these constitute the mark of selfhood (*ātman-lakṣaṇa*). Because the meanings are applied in successive stages, there are four names, and these four names further comprise two types of marks:

first, delusion regarding the objects of consciousness (*vijñāna-viṣaya*); second, delusion regarding the objects of wisdom (*jñāna-viṣaya*). Of these, the former is that which is imputed by the emotional consciousness (*kleśa-vijñāna*).
This refers to grasping at one's own body as a self and conceiving of it as a self; conceiving of it as a "person" as it transmigrates through various realms of existence;
conceiving of it as a "sentient being" as it undergoes various transformations such as prosperity and decline, suffering and pleasure, in continuous succession;

and conceiving of it as a "life-principle" as it persists with its karmic retribution and vital faculty remaining uninterrupted. As described in the two treatises (*Madhyāntavibhāga* and *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*) by Vasubandhu and Asaṅga, these are the delusions regarding the object of wisdom.
Upon realizing the awakened nature (*bodhicitta*), one should successively dispel the subject-object duality from the coarse to the subtle;
this should be understood from the actual text of this sutra. Regarding "inversion": the true self is primordially present, yet through delusion it is said to be non-existent;

the false self is primordially empty, yet through clinging it is said to exist. From here, of the ten subsequent lines, the first four concern the arising of afflictions from delusion, followed by the next two...

The first two phrases concern the creation of karma through afflictions; the next two concern the retribution summoned by that karma; and the final two concern turning away from the three paths and falling into the two vehicles.
Furthermore, within the context of the Two Vehicles' doctrine of the four truths of arising and ceasing: the first six phrases correspond to the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*);

the next two to the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*); the next one to the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*); and the final one to the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*). From this, it follows that...
The arising of both hatred and love toward objects occurs because one clings to the four marks as being the substantial essence of a self;
thus, one gives rise to love for oneself and hatred for others. One loves those who accord with the self and hates those who oppose it.

This is due to the repeated clinging to what is false—the four elements and five aggregates—which, though delusively produced from the nature and falsely combined through various conditions, are already empty and illusory.

Furthermore, because one again clings to the two false conceptions of self and person upon that [foundation], producing karma that leads to the fruits of suffering and pleasure, it is called the "path" (*mārga*).
Once the karma is completed, one undergoes the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*). Those who loathe this cycle cease their conditions and sever their delusions;
those who perceive *nirvāṇa* proceed toward quiescence and sink into emptiness. (Guifeng) This flow of the three paths is the false vision of the six classes of ordinary beings regarding *nirvāṇa*.
Thus, one must understand that within the realm of the two vehicles, the nine realms turn their backs on the true nature and become deluded, resulting entirely in defilement (Cishi).

Regarding the four pairs of opposites in this sutra, as contrasted with the *Vajracchedikā*, it is said that delusion concerns the sphere of wisdom; yet, when viewed from the perspective of the Middle Way, even the subject that grasps is ultimately nothing but the functioning of consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Because sentient beings have not been free from discursive thought since beginningless time, it is said that they "delusively grasp at existence" and so forth.

Furthermore, although these four similes are distinguished here according to the stages of realization and awakening—progressing from the coarse to the subtle and from the shallow to the profound—a close examination of the intent of the sutra suggests that each of these similes possesses its own levels of coarseness and subtlety, as well as both shallowness and depth.
Zhuan-an (Zhao Daoyi) stated: "In this chapter, the four inversions are eliminated; I am the root of them all. This self-clinging has both coarse and subtle aspects. Now...

This refers to the manifestation of coarse grasping at a self. As for those on the stages (*bhūmi*), they possess subtle grasping at a self of which they are not even aware and which they have not yet been able to eliminate.
If this is so for those still in the stage of faith and understanding (*adhimukti*), where their sense of self is vast, how much more so for those who have not yet attained true realization?
Their coarse grasping at a self is entirely identical to that of ordinary worldlings; the growth of such *māna* (conceit) is indeed the great malady of those who study the Buddha-dharma.
It is fitting to read this chapter thoroughly: "The current grasping at self is like a thief who has destroyed one's house" (Hand-mirror Text).

Regarding the two objects of aversion and attraction: although aversion and attraction belong to the mind, it is said that the mind follows after objects because the subject is manifested by the object.
As for the body of false delusion, those who stubbornly cling to what is false take the four inversions to be the essence of the self. From [this point]...
Because my own substance gives rise to hatred and attachment, it is called "heavy clinging" (private note).
When the awakening to the two obstacles becomes delusion, one cannot thereby enter pure awakening. It is not that awakening rejects those who would enter;
rather, there are those who would enter who do not enter by means of awakening. Therefore, both the movement of thought and the cessation of thought both return to delusive confusion.
Because delusive thoughts obstruct pure awakening, yet original awakening is fundamentally such that it is merely separated by one's own state of confusion;

it is not that awakening rejects or refuses to allow entry. Those who can enter do so by leaving behind discursive thought, which is itself awakening; nor is it a matter of using the nature of awakening to pull oneself in.
To stir the mind is to cling to existence, while to suppress thought is to sink into emptiness; therefore, both stirring and suppressing lead back to delusion and distress.

The preceding section clarified how delusion arises from delusion as a direct answer to the question of why there is defilement; this present section concludes by responding to the inquiry regarding why one fails to enter [the state of awakening] due to confusion (Private Note).
This consists of three parts: first, a double examination of the root of delusion; second, the initial interrogation and restatement of the premise.
Why is this? Because beginningless fundamental ignorance (*avidyā*) has taken possession as its sovereign.
When thoughts stir, one turns away from awakening; when thoughts cease, one accords with the truth. Why, then, are all these states called "delusion and confusion"?
