It is because beginningless fundamental ignorance acts as my master: when there is movement, it is its movement; when there is stillness, it is its stillness.
Since the mark of selfhood is present, both movement and stillness are equally deluded (Guifeng). The second part provides an explanatory interpretation:
"All sentient beings are born without the eye of wisdom; the nature of their body and mind is entirely ignorance, just as a person cannot cut off their own life."
Since turning one's back on awakening, one has not yet encountered the instruction of a teacher; thus, one’s movements deviate from the Buddha-wisdom like those born blind.
Although all phenomena of body and mind are none other than Perfect Awakening (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*), because they are not understood, they are entirely ignorance (*avidyā*).
Ignorance and self-clinging are like a person who loves their own life and cannot bring themselves to cut it off. (Private Note). This concludes the third section: the refutation of errors.
Therefore, you should know that for one who has attachment, I accord with them; yet toward those who do not accord, resentment and enmity arise.
Because the mind of attachment and aversion nourishes ignorance, their continuous pursuit of the Way fails to achieve fulfillment.
If people love me, I am pleased; if they oppose me, I am resentful. By means of this calculation, ignorance (*avidyā*) is nourished;
from the beginning until now, there has been no way to sever it. As for the continuity [of consciousness], it fundamentally arises from ignorance;
through resentment and attachment, the seeds of ignorance are perfumed again, and their active manifestation continues without interruption. One should seek the Way by means of this.
Ultimately not established (Guifeng). II. Extensive Explanation of the Two [Points]. First, listing and explaining the four characteristics. The *Lüshù* (Brief Commentary) states:

"Now, regarding these 'self' and so forth, their modes of activity (*ākāra*) differ from those of permanence. 'Permanence' refers merely to deluded attachment; the first fruit [of the path] has already removed this.

This [section], however, proceeds directly from cultivation and realization. An Arhat has not yet fully understood: first, the 'self' as verified by phenomena; second, the 'self' that constitutes a person; third, the full comprehension..."

In every instance, four [aspects] arise and continue secretly like a life-force. Furthermore, it is said that although four distinct characteristics are explained based on the varying depths of conceptual attachment, they are in fact nothing other than the view of self (*ātman*).

Thus, apart from the specific enumeration of the four names in the sutra text, the word "self" appears in every section; if this attachment is removed, it is precisely the Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*). To examine this in detail according to the *Lüshù* (Brief Commentary): [The text continues with the analysis of the four aspects of the view of self. ...therefore, the four types of views are established. Although these four views are distinguished by their respective characteristics, they are all merely the view of self. Consequently, the sutra text, beyond the separate listing of the four names, contains the character for "self" at every juncture. If one eliminates this attachment, it is indeed the Perfect Enlightenment. To consider this in detail according to the *Lüshù* commentary: [the following analysis follows].
The four marks have already ceased to be the coarse attachments manifested by the initial mind; [the text] cites the "dust-like ignorance" beyond the realms as its reference.

Now, according to the preceding passage, it is due to the attachment to a self and the false views that one undergoes the cycle of birth and death; according to the subsequent passage, failing to understand the four marks, one may practice the path for kalpas, yet this is merely called "conditioned" and does not constitute the attainment of the holy fruit.

The intended meaning of the scripture precisely concerns the coarse defilements of *darśana-heya* (delusions abandoned through vision) and *bhāvanā-heya* (delusions abandoned through cultivation). Thus:
I understand that Guishan’s interpretation of the meaning was excessive, and his explanation of the four marks (*catur-lakṣaṇa*) based on the gradations of depth and shallowness;
yet even regarding the first mark, there is an internal distinction between coarse and subtle, shallow and deep, so I fear it may not be as he says.

I venture to suggest that beginners, following a biased vehicle and relying on obscure realization, claim to have attained what they have not yet attained, leading them into successive erroneous calculations that do not exceed these four attachments. This, then, is the realization [of their error].

If awakening is not achieved by severing thoughts, it is still a realization that turns its back on one's true nature; since this is the case for realization, it is likewise so for cognitive awareness (*buddhi*), for both involve the persistence of the self-ego and are equally false imaginings (*vikalpa*).
Therefore, it is said: "To take the four inversions as a real self-substance, even down to every movement and stillness, all returns to delusion and confusion.

Zhuan-an points this out as the coarse grasping of active manifestation (*samudācāra*), which seems to have some semblance of form and features, as if within the stages of spiritual attainment (*bhūmi*).

Because the wisdom of all modes has not yet been perfected and the grasping at a self remains subtle, everything prior to the vajra-like samādhi belongs to the realm of ordinary beings; therefore it is said:
"If his mind, even up to the point of realizing the ultimate, pure nirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, still conceives of it as 'I,' this is the mark of selfhood.

Furthermore, it says: "If his mind, even up to the point of perfectly awakening to nirvāṇa, still conceives of 'self' and 'person,' then the other two [marks] are likewise to be understood by analogy," as stated in the Sūtra.

The reader should know that while the texts preserve only the essentials, both [the former and this] are shallow and profound respectively; I do not dare to misrepresent them. (Private Note) The text consists of four parts:
first, the mark of the self (*ātman*); second, the initial presentation and clarification of coarse attachments; within this, the first is the presentation by way of dharmas.
"Good son, what is the mark of self (*ātman*)? It refers to that which is realized by the minds of sentient beings.

To abandon the false and realize the true is called the mark of self; this is because one clings to that which is realized. (Zhuan-an) The character "one" (*yi*) specifically points to the essence of the self.
(Ci-shi) Regarding "that which is realized by the mind," Guifeng said: "Mind" refers to the seventh consciousness, and that which is realized is the eighth [consciousness].
The seeing-division (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eight consciousnesses is spontaneously grasped by all sentient beings as an internal self;

this refers here to the seventh consciousness, which is termed the "mind of the Two Vehicles sinking into emptiness," for its stage is already profound. This passage is provisionally based on the active *dṛṣṭi-heya* and *bhāvanā-heya* selves of ordinary beings;
the subsequent text, which establishes [the nature of] the Tathāgata and so forth, will then discuss the seventh and eighth consciousnesses in their vertical progression.
Regarding the term "realization" (*zhèng*), its meaning is that of grasping and attachment; therefore, it is said below: "For this reason, one realizes and grasps" (*zhàngnán*).
Second, it is clarified by means of a simile:
"Good son, it is as if there were a person whose hundred joints are in harmony and comfort, yet who suddenly forgets his own body, and whose limbs become slack and limp."

When nourishment is contrary to the proper method, even a slight application of acupuncture or moxibustion causes one to perceive the existence of a self; thus, the realization of this self-body manifests immediately.
(Guifeng) When the strings are taut, they are slackened; when the limbs are unbalanced, the hands and feet lose their proper measure. When at ease, one forgets the body;

yet when the pain of acupuncture or moxibustion occurs, one recognizes the self. This is like a practitioner who has no realization while [in a state of ease], but upon having realization, [the self is perceived].

Because of this attachment, it is said that one must realize and grasp [the truth] for the essence of the self to manifest; yet, although gold dust is precious, when it falls into the eye it becomes a cataract.
As stated in the following passage: "How should one know that those sentient beings of the final age who practice Bodhi do not understand liberation?
Because they take their own slight realization to be pure, they are unable to exhaust the root of the mark of self."
Based on this, it is not a realm for the vulgar or base; it is that which those of noble lineage who study the Buddha should regard with profound sincerity (Private Note).
Second, the binding of the fingers refers to the subtle marks.
Good son, their minds continue until they realize the Tathāgata’s ultimate, thoroughly understood, and pure nirvāṇa.
This is the mark of self (*ātman*).

That which realizes [it] in the mind is the subject; that which is realized below [in the text] is the object. Furthermore, within the realization of the object, that which understands is the subject, and *nirvāṇa* is the object.
Not forgetting this relationship between subject and object is precisely the mark of self. (Guifeng) Regarding the phrase "and so forth" (*naivamādi*), it does not refer merely to ordinary people...

At the time of attaining realization, which belongs to our own school, even on the day of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) following awakening, this "self" still exists (Zhuangnan).
There are two types of mutual characteristics; the first is the coarse characteristic.
"Good son, what is meant by the 'mark of a person' (*pudgala-nimitta*)? It refers to those sentient beings whose minds have attained realization.

Good son, one who realizes there is a self no longer identifies with 'what belongs to the self. The realization that there is no self is likewise so. Having realized this, one transcends all who claim to have attained realization;
all such cases are the mark of a person."
Regarding the phrase "one who realizes through mental awakening perceives their former errors": the word "person" (*pudgala*) precisely refers to the mark of a person (*pudgalalakṣaṇa*).

No longer identifying with a self, one thus does not produce a mind that seeks realization; mental awakening is likewise like the former error. (Guifeng) To cling to the capacity for awakening as a person is the mark of a person.
(Zhuan’an) These are two subtle attachments.

Good son, if the mind—even up to the point of perfectly awakening to nirvana—regards both as "self," and if the mind retains even a slight trace of awakening while claiming to have fully exhausted the realization of principle, this is all termed the mark of person (*pudgala-nimitta*).

Perfect awakening is the subject (*neng*), and nirvana is the object (*suo*); that which is to be exhausted. Once one has entered the stages (*bhūmi*), although the realization is entirely eliminated, [the mark of person persists].
Because the attachment to principles still persists slightly while the awakening that exhausts them is yet incomplete, this forms the mark of a person (private note).
Third, the mark of a sentient being, in three parts. First, the heading:
"Good son, what is the mark of a sentient being? It refers to those things regarding which the self-realization and awakening of all sentient beings do not reach."

If one considers that the "awakening" preceding it is the subject capable of awakening, while that which is awakened is the object; once that has become the object of awakening, it is further named the subject capable of unfolding [the next stage].
Thus, they revolve infinitely, all becoming subject and object. Wherever this occurs, it is entirely a matter of mutual dependence.

Because one realizes there is no fixed essence, one abandons the previous [notion] and does not conceive of what is beyond the reach of calculation; yet, failing to realize this, such calculation itself constitutes the multitude of sentient beings.
"Sentient beings" (*sattva*) refers to the lack of fixed attachment to any single [identity]; it also carries the sense of many births arising in an uninterrupted succession (Guifeng).

In contrast to the aforementioned "self" (*ātman*) and "person" (*pudgala*), this single name "sentient being" is established. While the grasping at self-characteristics (*ātma-grāha*) and the grasping at person-characteristics (*pudgala-grāha*) each calculate one side and do not constitute the meaning of "sentient beings," the characteristic of sentient beings here is neither self nor person; it is called "many" (*saṃgha*) because it possesses the dual meaning.
(To the south of the barrier). Second, the illustration:
"Good son, it is like a person who says, 'I am a sentient being. One should know that when such a person speaks of a 'sentient being,' it is neither the self nor another.
Why is it not the self? Because if 'I' am a sentient being, then that which is 'I' is not the [true] self."
Why is it that "neither he nor I" refers to sentient beings? Because they are neither "he" nor "I.
Borrowing the common parlance of worldly people to establish the force of the meaning, the characteristic of sentient beings is revealed as being neither "I" nor "he.
Since they are sentient beings, they are not "I"; and since it is said "I am," they are further not "he. Thus, because they are neither "he" nor "I," [it is said "neither he nor I"].
It is not the "self" of that person (Guifeng). [The Master] then pointed his three fingers and said:

"Good son, all sentient beings who have attained realization or awakening do so only in terms of 'self' and 'person. That which is beyond the reach of the characteristics of self and person, yet wherein there remains something realized, is called the characteristic of a sentient being."
If one realizes that what is realized is empty, then "I" do not reach it; if one realizes that the one who realizes is empty, then "person" does not reach it.

To maintain a sense of having something realized is called the mark of a sentient being (*sattva-nimitta*), for the mind has not yet forgotten it. This refers to the character "superior" (the *Guifeng* commentary).
The fourth is the characteristic of the life-span, which has two parts; first, the direct explanation:

"Good son, what is the characteristic of the life-span? It refers to that which is perceived by the pure illumination of the mind and understood by awakening, yet which all karmic wisdom cannot see for itself, being like the life-root (*jīvitendriya*)."
Because it is the illumination of the very mind, it is called "pure awakening. The three preceding phases are termed "awakening" because they are what is to be understood by this awakening.

Furthermore, one intends to cultivate all untainted (*anāsrava*) karma through this wisdom; since karma refers to karmic activity, the wisdom of all functional operations is called "karma-wisdom" (*karma-jñāna*).
Although it can eliminate delusion, it does not eliminate itself; therefore, it does not see itself, nor does it [see] itself.
Because it is seen to be like the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*). Regarding "like the life-faculty," according to Guifeng, this also incorporates the meaning of continuity:
clinging to the uninterrupted succession of the activity of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) is called the mark of a "life-span" (*āyuṣka-dharma*), not the worldly life-span.

This refers to the three things—warmth, breath, and consciousness—which are obtained as a result of maturation (*vipākaja*) over the course of a single lifetime; they maintain the life-faculty so that it does not cease.

The metaphor of clinging to a self is called the "life-principle" (jīva). [Zhuan’an] forgets what was previously understood and merely says it is "pure," yet persists in maintaining a capacity for illuminating awareness as if it were a life-force.
The term specifically refers to this capacity for awakening-awareness, which is not seen by any karmic wisdom.
It is feared that this refers to the fact that the karmic wisdom cultivated by ordinary beings and sages does not see this capacity for awakening itself.
[Private Commentary]: Second, revealing delusion.
Good son, if the mind perceives that all states of awakening are but defilements, for that which is awakened to does not depart from defilement;
it is like hot water melting ice—there is no separate ice apart from the water. To know that the ice has melted and yet to maintain a self-awareness of "I" is likewise [delusion].
It is likewise so.
If the mind perceives the aforementioned delusions as being identical to universal enlightenment, this enlightenment is still not free from delusion and is termed a defilement;
for it persists in the subject that perceives and the object that is perceived. Thus it is said that one who perceives an object of perception does not transcend the realm of dust.
"Dust and grime" merely signify the sense of defilement; the intent of the sutra is precisely to reveal that the "capable cognizer" (*neng jue*) is itself delusory.

A brief commentary states: "All that is a cognizer refers to the three preceding characteristics. Let the reader examine this carefully. The metaphor of "water" represents the capable cognizer, while "ice" represents the object cognized (*suo jue*).
Since the object cognized has been exhausted, how could the capable cognizer remain? Therefore, it is said that there is no separate ice that knows the ice has melted.
If one holds that ice can know the melting of ice, it would be the same as [claiming] that the existing [self] can perceive the awakening of the previous self-phase;

therefore, it is said that "the existing self perceiving itself" is likewise so. The *Lüshū* (Brief Commentary) states that this uses a metaphor to reveal by contrast (*pratibhāsa*) and applies the principle to conform through synthesis (*anuloma*).
Question: The first chapter states that the mark of perfect illumination (*paripūrṇa-prakāśa*) eternally severs ignorance (*avidyā*); how is it that here there is "illumination"?

Juejuda said: "To manifest the principle, one must illuminate; to eliminate attachments, one must let them go. This is the same principle as the four views—single or combined—in the *Tiantai Zhiguan*, where even the pursuit of the ineffable is exhausted.
Furthermore, regarding "perfect illumination": without moving a single dharma, one traverses with thoughts cut off;
affairs and principles are suddenly forgotten, and the holy and the ordinary are equal. This is not easy to speak of; only the practitioner truly knows it. (Private Note)
Second, delusion constitutes an obstruction to the Dharma; third, initially having a self constitutes losing the Way. First, the heading:

"Good son, if sentient beings in the final age do not understand the four marks, even though they undergo diligent and painful cultivation of the Path for many kalpas, it will be merely called 'conditioned' and will ultimately fail to achieve any of the fruits of sainthood. Therefore, this is called the 'final age of the True Dharma.'"

In the first three periods of teaching, the duration of practice is long and distant; since perfect understanding has not yet arisen, one can never achieve the holy fruit of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).

By inferring from the deep to the shallow, this is evident even for ordinary beings on the vast ground [of the mundane world]. (Zhangnan) "The end of the True Dharma" refers to the final age of the orthodox Buddha-dharma.

Indeed, during the period of the True Dharma, all who practice attain realization; however, in the final age— *Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment. The translation reflects the available portion.*
At that time, people mostly grasped at external signs; now that they grasp at the signs of realization, the True Dharma likewise becomes like the degenerate age.

If one encounters this teaching and thoroughly understands the source of the affliction, then even in the degenerate age, it will be as if it were the True Dharma. (Guifeng) In Śākyamuni’s Dharma, the *Saddharma* (True Dharma), *Saddharmapratirūpaka* (Semblance Dharma), and *Kṣaya-dharma* (Age of Decline) each last for one thousand years.
When the four dharmas—principle, teaching, practice, and fruit—are all fully present, it is called the True Dharma. Although...

When there are few who possess the teaching, practice, and realization of the fruit, it is called the Semblance Dharma (Saddharma-pratirūpaka); when only the principle remains while teaching, practice, and realization are all absent, it is called the Final Dharma (Paścima-dharma).
The "ten thousand years" of the Final Dharma does not mean they are entirely non-existent; rather, it is said according to the majority of cases (Dongyang).
Second, the interrogation and explanation of the six points. First, the interrogation as to how it is that one who has practiced for a long time does not attain realization:
"For what reason?
Since the number of kalpas is already vast and the practices have been diligent and arduous, by what principle does one fail to realize the fruit of sainthood? (Guifeng).
The second [position] is the interpretation that the realization of the grasping of a self is not true:
because one takes all forms of "self" to be *nirvāṇa*, there is realization and awakening, which is called "attainment.
This is like a person who mistakes a thief for their son; they will never achieve mastery over the family's wealth and treasures.
What delusory phenomena are there that do not arise from the self? Therefore, it is said that all [are thieves]. (Cishi) If a thief were outside, one might still be able to guard against him;
but how can one protect a child whom one has raised? Furthermore, knowing a thief to be a thief, the thief can do no harm;
yet if one recognizes him as a child, how can one avoid ruin? (Guifeng) Third, regarding the realization of the fruit, how does it obstruct the Path? This is the inquiry.
Why is this? Even if one were to recognize me and attain realization, how would that hinder the Path?
(Guifeng) To love stillness and loathe clamor is not liberation.
Those who love me also love *nirvāṇa*, for they have subdued the root of my craving as the characteristic of *nirvāṇa*.
Those who hate me also hate *saṃsāra*, yet they do not realize that craving itself is true *saṃsāra*; thus, to separately hate *saṃsāra* is called non-liberation.
The cycle of birth and death fundamentally arises from hatred and attachment; if one seeks liberation, these two sources must be exhausted.

Now, to love *nirvāṇa* is still the same as original attachment, and to hate *saṃsāra* is likewise the same as original hatred. Although rejecting suffering and delighting in bliss differ in form, they are essentially rooted in the habitual tendencies of hatred and attachment.
If one carries these along while practicing the Way, how could the fruit of Buddhahood ever be achieved? One must subdue this root of craving.
Those who seek *nirvāṇa* do so by suppressing [the afflictions] so that they do not arise, mistaking this semblance for true *nirvāṇa*;

hence it is said thus. Fundamentally, they cherish *nirvāṇa* intending to eliminate birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*). Since the craving for *nirvāṇa* still exists, the root of true birth-and-death remains;

with the root of craving as the soil and the sprouts of aversion, how can this be called liberation? (Guifeng) Because one clings to a self, aversion and craving arise; therefore, it is spoken of as "self-love" and so forth.

If one hates me because one considers *nirvāṇa* to be that which is realized by the two vehicles, then this "love" is a "love for the Dharma"—that is, a distinct affliction beyond the [three] realms (*dhātu*), which is the very root of true transformation-death (*pariṇāmi-jarāmaraṇa*). Both Huàn’s and Yún’s commentaries employ this interpretation;
however, it seems to conflict with the meaning of the subsequent praise for joy and censure of anger, because those who realize emptiness are without both anger and joy.
(Private Commentary). Fifth: How is it known that the realized Dharma is not liberation?
How should one know that the Dharma is not liberated?
Regarding "Dharma," it refers to *nirvāṇa*; as explained previously, one who craves *nirvāṇa* is called "unliberated. This is the inquiry.

It is said: "If one loves birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), it is acknowledged as bondage; now, having awakened to *nirvāṇa* as the dharma of quiescence, by what sign is it known that one is not yet liberated?
(Guifeng) Sixth, praising joy and reviling anger serves as proof of my [lack of] self. This means that one who has realized the truth necessarily possesses no self;
because there is no self, there is likewise no anger or joy. If one now feels anger or joy toward the Dharma, it is known that one has not yet realized the Dharma.
This is not the true self because it has not been exhausted; the text is divided into two parts. First, the indication that the self has not been exhausted:
"Good son, those beings of the final age who practice for Bodhi take their own realizations as proof of their own purity, yet they are still unable to exhaust the root of the mark of self."
The evidence for this purity is precisely my own essence (the "Loving Abode"). Second, it is known through the examination of objects:
if someone else praises that Dharma, one immediately feels joy and desires to deliver them; yet if someone else slanders what has been attained, one immediately gives rise to resentment.
From this, one knows that the mark of selfhood is firmly grasped and lies latent within the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).
The play of the various faculties never ceases.
While the coarse and heavy states of worldly objects—whether adverse or favorable—are easy to perceive, it is most difficult to discern them within the gateway of the Dharma.

To merely claim "I am practicing for the sake of the Dharma" while harboring anger toward others, without realizing that this mind is fundamentally the mark of selfhood (*ātman*) lurking within the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), is the seed [of further bondage].
The "son" refers to the manifestation of the various sense-faculties (*indriya*) through their active engagement.

Because one observes external objects, it is verified that the internal mind’s grasping at a self (*ātman-grāha*) remains firm and continues to lie latent in a continuous stream (Guifeng). The "containing seeds" specifically refers to the eighth consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*);

however, according to the phrase "playing with the various sense-faculties," this should refer to the six consciousnesses. Here, following the *Yuan* [school], it is spoken of generally as the *liye* (ālaya). (Cishi)
Third, the summary:
"Good son, that practitioner of the path does not eliminate the mark of self; therefore, he cannot enter pure awakening.
Second, explaining illness as the Dharma, in two parts: first, the teaching on the existence of a self.

Good son, if one knows that the self is empty, there is no one who can destroy the self; yet because the notion of a self persists, I continue to teach the Dharma, for the self has not yet been severed.
It is the same for sentient beings and their life-span.

Because of hearing [the teachings], one may feel anger or joy, but this is a false conceptualization that "this is the self. Since the emptiness of the self eliminates those instances of praise and disparagement, it is said that "there is no one who can destroy the self."
One should also say, "There is no one who praises me," though the text is merely abbreviated.

Furthermore, the fact that the three remaining characteristics have not been exhausted while my own view of self-existence (*ātman*) in preaching the Dharma has not yet been severed is likewise the case; however, the word "person" (*pudgala*) does not appear in the text for the sake of completing the sentence (Private Note).
The second explanation is likewise a sickness.
Good son, sentient beings in the final age explain sickness as the Dharma; therefore, they are called those who are to be pitied.
Though they exert themselves with diligence, they only increase their various ailments, and for this reason they cannot enter pure awakening.
If the four characteristics [of conditioned phenomena] persist, they are collectively termed "sickness. To take sickness as the Dharma is truly pitiable;

because one practices while carrying this sickness, all manner of ailments increase (Guifeng). Third, using the ordinary to confound the sagely has two parts. First, suppressing the sagely to make them conform to oneself.

Good son, the sentient beings of the final age do not understand the four marks; taking the understanding and the sphere of practice of the Tathāgata as their own cultivation, they will ultimately fail to achieve success.

The understanding and practice of the Tathāgata transcend all phrases and are utterly free from dwelling in marks; how could such [a practice] ever lead to success? It is like grasping at clarified butter...
Ghee is like poison (private note). Second, the arising of overweening pride (*adhimāna*):

there may be sentient beings who, having not attained, claim to have attained; having not realized, claim to have realized. Upon seeing those who have achieved superior progress, they give rise to jealousy in their hearts.
Because these sentient beings have not severed self-love (*ātmasneha*), they are unable to enter pure awakening.
Those who have not attained the principle nor realized the wisdom, yet claim to have attained and realized it, are people of overweening pride (*adhimāna*).

If one knows for oneself that one has not realized [the truth] yet says one has realized it, this constitutes a fundamental offense of great falsehood (*mṛṣāvāda*) within the primary precepts. This is not the view of this text;

rather, it arises from the jealousy of those seeking excellence and the testing of ordinary sentiments. However, the physical forms of the various sages are not fixed, and their attainments and... [are likewise indeterminate].
One cannot internally realize this within the mind; how then can one discern whether others have not yet attained or realized it?
Therefore, one examines the mental activities of others to verify their truth or falsehood. When a sage applies his mind, there is no duality between self and others.

Seeing another’s superior progress or the circulation of the Dharma teachings, he rejoices in every thought and is surely able to accord with them. By thus verifying his own inner mind, he may immediately attain realization.
Awakening is not in vain. If you perceive yourself as declining while others flourish, you harbor jealousy; if you perceive yourself flourishing while others decline, you feel joy.
Even if you have a profound understanding of the wondrous realm, it is merely an object of the mind; do not mistakenly recognize this as attainment or realization.
Both arise from self-love and thus become obstacles to awakening (Guifeng). To claim that one has attained the third fruit or realized the fourth fruit when one has not is [delusion].
One may give rise to overweening pride upon attaining realization, as in the case of the bhikṣus of the four dhyānas (Dongyang). The three admonitions and exhortations:
First, the admonition not to seek awakening.
"Good son, in this degenerate age, sentient beings who hope to achieve the Way must not seek awakening; it will only increase their erudition."
This prolongs one's views.
This admonition means that one should wait for awakening with the mind. Generally speaking, as for what is called "awakening," there is originally no substantial dharma;

it is merely a provisional name for the point where the pathways of the mind are cut off. If one seeks awakening by means of the mind, one will only become more deeply mired in delusion; therefore, the admonition says: "Do not let..."
Furthermore, because one seeks awakening by relying on the mind, one instead interprets and reconciles the words and phrases of the sutras and treatises;
thus it is said that this only increases one's learning (*bahuśruta*). One fails to realize that such clear interpretation is precisely one's own human intellect and consciousness;

hence it is said that it increases the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*). (The intent of the various commentaries is that one must first seek awakening. Now, having re-examined the sutra, I have humbly adopted [the insight of] Cishi.
If one's dwelling is not appropriate, one should follow the established precedent and not issue prohibitions against others (private note).
Second, I urge you to apply yourself further:
simply be diligent and exert effort to subdue the afflictions, giving rise to great valor so that what has not yet been attained may be attained and what has not yet been severed may be severed.
When greed, anger, craving, pride, flattery, and jealousy do not arise toward objects, and all notions of self and other, as well as affectionate attachment, are completely extinguished—
the Buddha says that such a person gradually achieves accomplishment, seeks out virtuous friends, and does not fall into wrong views.
One should simply say that what is stated above corresponds to "attaining what has not yet been attained" and "decisively penetrating the Great Dharma.
To sever what has not yet been severed is to directly and decisively realize insight; for those with greed, anger, and so forth, it means forgetting emotional attachments when facing objects.
If one practices in this manner, how could it be considered the Way itself? It is only because the Tathāgata allows for further progress that it is called "gradual accomplishment."
(Cishih) states that those to be severed are precisely the greed, anger, and so forth listed below;

one who seeks a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) is like a merchant entering the sea who must rely on a guide, for a student practicing the path must certainly depend upon a virtuous friend. (Guifeng) says:

"In the world there are those who study the Mahāyāna in a superficial manner, claiming only 'this very mind is Buddha. Since it is said that the mind is Buddha, one's conduct ought to be identical to that of the Buddha."
If one’s practice is merely superficial or consists of empty talk, greed and anger will only increase and jealousy will flourish even more.

If one does not move even an inch from where one formerly practiced, it is feared that one will not even be able to escape the hells. To hope for Buddhahood under such conditions is like trying to catch fish by climbing a tree;
if one relies solely on innate nature without observing the necessary effort, how could it ever be attained? I address this to those of future virtue: reflect upon your own hearts.
In discussing the mind, do not fail the Tathāgata’s compassionate and bitter-mouthed instruction (Dongyang). Third, the heavy demonstration of the faults:
if one generates further attachment or aversion toward that which is sought, one will be unable to enter the ocean of pure awakening.
This conversely reveals that by not giving rise to hatred or attachment, one enters awakening (Guifeng). The two verses praise these two points. First, the heading:
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
The second part consists of three verses. The first verse provides a brief demonstration:
"Pure karma, you should know: All sentient beings Are caused by clinging to a self and craving to flow through beginningless delusion."
The two verses provide a detailed explanation:
Without having eliminated the four characteristics, One cannot achieve awakening.
When love and hatred arise in the mind, And crookedness persists in one's thoughts, For this reason, there is much delusion and distress, And one cannot enter the city of enlightenment.

The analogy of the city and the analogies for the dharmas each have three meanings: first, realizing that the nature of the mind is empty so that no delusions can enter, like defending against external enemies;
second, seeing the virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and the myriad practices as fully perfected, like nurturing a population;
third, the path being unobstructed in all respects, like opening gates to welcome and guide others (Guifeng). Third, the verses of exhortation and admonition.
If one can turn toward awakening, first eliminate greed, anger, and delusion; when attachment to dharmas no longer dwells in the mind, one may gradually achieve success.
Since my own body is fundamentally non-existent, from what cause could hatred or love arise?
Such a person seeks virtuous friends and will never fall into false views; as for the objects sought, they do not give rise to a separate mind.
Ultimately, that which is not accomplished is the realm;
just as this world enters the land of Tang such that all territory belongs to the Tang domain, so it is here.

If one reaches the state of awakening, then every phenomenon belongs to awakening; the state of delusion is likewise. If there is delusion, ignorance persists; as the verse says, if there is pride, [delusion] persists.
There is a verse but no prose; this is an abridged version. "Dharma-love" refers to craving for *nirvāṇa*. "My body" refers to that which is the basis for both hatred and love.
Since the basis is empty, how can that which depends upon it exist? To realize that the lands and my own body are all vast and eternal—this is the verse (Guifeng).
II. The Chapter on Universal Enlightenment: Showing the Four Illnesses of Practice, etc., Part Two. A. The Initial Inquiry. 1.
The Manner of Approaching the Question.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Universal Enlightenment rose from his seat amidst the great assembly, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and circumambulated him to the right.
He circumambulated [the Buddha] three times, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Second, the formal presentation of his words has two parts. First, expressing joy for what preceded:

'O Greatly Compassionate World-Honored One, you have skillfully explained the maladies of dhyāna, causing the great assembly to attain an unprecedented state of mind, their hearts becoming vast and serene.'"
One attains great peace and stability.
Regarding the "four signs" as illnesses of meditation (Guifeng): how could there be any illness in Chan? It is merely that the practitioner’s application of mind is erroneous (Cishi).
Second, after the request:
"World-Honored One, in the final age, sentient beings will gradually distance themselves from the Buddha; the worthy and holy ones will remain hidden, and false teachings will blaze forth.

What kind of person should these sentient beings seek to rely upon? To what Dharma should they rely? What practices should they perform? What ailments should they eliminate? And how [should they do so]?"
He resolved to ensure that those blind masses would not fall into false views.

Just as a person is especially anxious for a child who is ill, the Bodhisattva’s great compassion first takes pity on the sages and worthies of the final age who remain hidden while the True Dharma is about to sink;
wishing to bring extensive benefit to those of the future, he therefore raises this question in advance. Furthermore, because...
The previous passage spoke of seeking a *kalyāṇamitra* (virtuous friend) so as not to fall into false views; now it asks what constitutes a *kalyāṇamitra*.
The remaining text clarifies this for those individuals, making their purpose clear. (Guifeng) Regarding the sequence of the five questions: in the study of the Way, one must rely on a teacher;
a teacher must possess the Dharma; the Dharma prizes cultivation and progress; cultivation requires freedom from afflictions; and when afflictions are removed, practice flourishes.
To achieve the benefit of others, there must first be an examination of how one initially resolves to attain enlightenment (*bodhicitta*). As Tiantai stated:
"If the resolve for enlightenment is deviant, the myriad practices will be applied in vain. Therefore, the inquiry into the initial resolve concludes [this section].

However, the intent of these five questions is that the teacher is primary, while the remaining four arise from the first question; were it otherwise, this would have already been clarified repeatedly previously.

The *Dharmaparyāya of Perfect Enlightenment* and its three types of practice describe the characteristics of various wheels of cultivation; furthermore, it urges the diligent severing of afflictions such as greed and anger.

However, the meaning of merely arousing the aspiration (*cittotpāda*) has not yet been extensively clarified. Why, then, must one raise these questions again at this point? To understand the intent of the subsequent answers:
first, [the text] extensively elaborates on seeking virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) in order to prevent the errors and delusions of false teachers in the final age. Next...

Answer: This is simply the wondrous Dharma of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*). By means of this Dharma, one manifests the departure from the four types of illness—such as the illness of activity—and practices by relying on the teacher to settle the mind in the principle of enlightenment.

The intent of the cultivation of the Dharma returns to the characteristics and illnesses of the various contemplations mentioned previously; these illnesses also correspond to the aforementioned self and other, and hatred and love.
Now, however, we merely add the methods for treating them, as well as the arousal of the bodhicitta, all of which can be seen in the text through Your Holiness’s compassionate grace.

In pitying sentient beings, he has exhausted every means to this end; furthermore, these various mental states—*ābhoga*, *anābhoga*, *praśrabdhi*, and *nirodha*—are of the utmost importance, yet they have never before been fully elucidated.
If one grasps the great outline, all the subordinate details will naturally be correct;
therefore, this chapter is summarized as "Showing the Four Illnesses of *Ābhoga* and the Others" (Private Note). Third, [the author] unfolds his sincere devotion threefold.
Having spoken these words, they prostrated themselves with their five limbs touching the ground; thus they made this request three times, beginning again and again.
The two Buddhas answered them thrice, first praising and granting their request.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Universal Enlightenment, saying: "Excellent, excellent, son of good family! You all..."

"You have been able to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding such practice, which can bestow upon all sentient beings in the final age the fearless eye of the Way, enabling those beings to attain the holy path. Listen attentively now, and I shall explain it for you."
II. Receiving the Mandate.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Pujue (Universal Awakening) received the instruction with joy, and together with the great assembly, they listened in silence.
II. The Direct Response. Part One: The Extended Discourse. Section Five: The First Response to the Inquiry for a Teacher. Subsection One: Instruction on Selecting a Teacher.

Good son, when sentient beings in the final age are about to resolve upon the Great Mind and seek a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) in order to practice, they should seek one who possesses all correct knowledge and vision;
whose mind does not dwell on signs (*nimitta*) and does not cling to the realms of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas;

who, though manifesting amidst the afflictions of the world, remains ever pure at heart; who displays various faults while praising the holy life (*brahmacarya*), yet never causes sentient beings to enter [into those faults].
One who seeks non-restraint will immediately achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. "Those of great mind" distinguishes them from those of other vehicles.
"Knowledge of reality" means being well able to distinguish true consciousness from deluded consciousness; knowing the illness, one knows the medicine.
For those who wish to practice, it is for the sake of seeking right knowledge and vision. As the *Dharmapada* says: "Deep understanding..."

The Dharma is empty, signless, wishless, unarisen, and unceasing; having thoroughly realized that all dharmas have been ultimately equal from the very beginning, they abide in suchness within the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
To establish the Buddha-dharma within this ultimate emptiness is called a true spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).
As for "the mind does not abide in signs," it means being free from the afflictions (*kleśa*) of ordinary beings and...
The two vehicles stagnate in quiescence; those who manifest worldly toil (kleśa) do so through greed and the like. Those whose minds are pure manifest defilement yet remain undefiled.
To demonstrate various faults, they employ the means of "harmony" (samānārthatā) to gather beings, as stated in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*:

"Entering brothels," which is also consistent with the examples in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* regarding Puṣpamitra and others praising the holy life (brahmacarya). This is done either for the sake of benefiting others or...

There are those who, due to other conditions, momentarily deviate from proper decorum and the true teachings; they may only reproach themselves for their errors and must not gloss over their faults or mislead the common people by expounding on principles.

This is fundamentally different from those heterodox persons who create various transgressions themselves and then claim that non-celibate conduct is the truth, causing immeasurable people to fall into great perilous realms.

This is done merely for... [the sake of... (Note: The final phrase "但為" suggests an incomplete thought or a specific motive, such as "merely for the sake of gain," which is often implied in such contexts.)
Because of the inclusion through common practice (*samānārthatā-saṃgraha*), although one may manifest various faults, one must always praise true *brahmacarya*. Thus, the treatise says:
"A person who has destroyed their views, even if their conduct is not destroyed, is unfit to serve as the 'Eye of the Path' for sentient beings;
whereas one whose conduct is destroyed but whose views are not broken is a truly superior field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*) among humans, and shall achieve accomplishment."

This brings about great benefit (Guifeng). Today, there are those who attach themselves to sacred sites and act according to their own whims, consuming what is not the Dharma while claiming to have attained the path of non-obstruction;
yet inwardly they are actually mediocre and foolish. These are people of corrupted views and corrupted conduct, devoid of shame—how lamentable!
Nevertheless, in this degenerate age, the Four Reliances are rarely encountered; one can only ensure that the mind does not dwell upon signs.
One who does not destroy right view and is well-versed in the contemplation of objects is also worthy of reliance (Dongyang).
One with right knowledge and vision deeply penetrates the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*) and does not cling to the two extremes. *Anuttara* is translated as "unexcelled" (*an-ūrdhva*);

*samyak* is translated as "right" or "equal"; it is also called "right and universal. *Samyak-saṃbodhi* is translated as "right awakening. Combined, they are called "Unexcelled Right Universal Awakening" (*Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
"Perfectly Awakened One" (Sambuddha) is also called "Unsurpassed Perfectly All-Knowing One" (private note). Second, the exhortation to serve:
sentient beings in the final age who see such a person should make offerings without sparing even their own bodies or lives;
within the four modes of deportment of that spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), they should always perceive purity, and even when various faults are displayed, their minds should remain free from pride.
How much more so, if a good son does not give rise to evil thoughts toward his spiritual friends regarding wealth, wife, children, or kinsmen;
he will then be able to ultimately accomplish perfect enlightenment, and the flower of his mind will emit radiance that illuminates the lands of the ten directions.

Those who do not begrudge their own bodies or lives include such as the youth who sacrificed his body in the Snowy Mountains (*Nirvāṇa-sūtra*) and Sadāprarudita who broke his bones in Gandhavatī (*Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*).
Even in the Confucian classics, it is said that one should serve one’s father with all one’s strength and dedicate oneself to serving one’s sovereign; how much more so for the sake of the Dharma!

Those who constantly manifest purity and practice various forms of "conformity" amidst suffering and affliction, yet remain free from pride even when practicing "non-conformity," are indeed Bodhisattvas who transform beings.
The manifestation of the provisional path is difficult to fathom; one should rely solely on the Dharma-gate and not doubt its traces.

One should not assume that because a practice does not yield immediate results, it lacks sincerity, nor should one give rise to arrogance upon seeing what appears to be a contrary course of action. Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Regarding all teachers and venerables, one should conceive of them as the World-Honored One.
If there is anyone capable of elucidating profound meanings and unraveling the knots of doubt, they will be of benefit to me. Thus...
One should serve them with all one's heart and respect them without dwelling on their faults. It is like a worn-out bag containing jewels;
one must not refuse to take the jewels because of the bag’s poor condition. Or, it is like traveling at night along a perilous path where a person holding a torch guides the way;
one must not refuse the light because of the person’s flaws. A bodhisattva is likewise: they receive the light of wisdom from the teacher without regard for their shortcomings.
Consider that being a teacher is difficult and being a disciple is no less so; do not, because of this warning, mistakenly treat a coarse person with reverence.
To verify whether one is genuine or false, apply the same discernment as before. Once you have mastered the Way, follow it accordingly.

Furthermore, this medicine is for both disciples and teachers; do not take it incorrectly, for if taken wrongly, it will increase the illness until no medicine can cure it—whereby that which binds is used to unbind.

"It is impossible" refers to those who scramble for wealth and the like; whereas previously the difficulty of sacrificing one's body and life was cited, this illustrates the ease of [giving] that which is external to the body.
"Scrambling" (*daun*) means eating; "wealth" (*cai*) refers to money and silks. The ancient translation is erroneous and abbreviated; it should properly be called "lump food" (*kavadīkāra-āhāra*).
"Not giving rise to evil thoughts" is due to the absence of pride mentioned previously. If arrogance (*māna*) arises, evil thoughts will immediately produce obstruction and concealment.
Regarding the phrase "How can the dharmas of one's own mind enter the flowers of the mind? it means that once the awakening of the mind is clear, the light of wisdom is manifested;
because whatever it encounters is untainted, they are called "mind-flowers. These correspond to the essence and are boundless, illuminating the lands of the ten directions (Guifeng).
Regarding "gathering wealth," the *Guifeng Chao* states: "According to the intent of the sutra, this refers to wealth and food. There are four kinds of food; this corresponds to..."

Regarding "edible food" (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*), it is categorized generally as "edible" and specifically as "portioned. To distinguish it from other types of food, ancient translations of the sūtras and śāstras erroneously rendered it as "lump-food" (*tuánshí*).

Now, this Tripiṭaka Master follows the ancient usage by using "lump" (*tuán*), yet he does not differentiate between the general and the specific; thus, he maintains that "lump" (*tuán*) itself is the "food," omitting the character for "food" (*shí*).
Therefore, it is called "lump-property" (*tuán-cái*). The Master Xian says: "In India, spoons and chopsticks are not used; one merely immerses fragrant water [in the mouth]."
"One bowl of rice, one bowl of a hundred flavors, and one bowl of fragrant water to moisten the hands for kneading the rice to eat"—this is not a mistranslation (*zhāngnán*);

"knead" (*tuó*) means to gather. It refers merely to gathering wealth and treasures, raising wives, children, and kinsmen. This uses ordinary worldly standards to illustrate the extreme inferiority of the former [state].
As for what was previously called "calamities," it includes everything from greed, anger, lust, and falsehood; such a state is already unacceptable.

How could one harbor malicious thoughts by showing that pride is identical to the eternal Way? (Cishi’s commentary) Now, fearing that "bol" merely refers to food, I have not yet dared to decide whether to accept or reject Cishi’s interpretation;
furthermore, Master Xian’s meaning still requires further investigation. (Private Note) Regarding those who constantly manifest purity within the four modes of deportment:
they remain unmoving amidst the daily activities of the three karmas and four deportments, remaining unstained by any phenomena.
However, all things are eternally manifest as pure. (Zhuan-an) Second, regarding the response based on the Dharma, there are three parts. First, the heading:
"The Dharma is free from illness. Good son, the wondrous Dharma realized by that spiritual friend should be free from the four illnesses.
This is titled "The Sublime Dharma" to explain reliance upon Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*), for Perfect Enlightenment is the dharma upon which one relies.

This dharma can only be relied upon once it is free from the four maladies; therefore, the questions regarding the removal of these maladies are answered within the text itself. The maladies of the Dharma are boundless, yet they are essentially limited to these four;
if even one of them is present, one is unfit to be a teacher (Guifeng). Although they are called "knowledgeable ones," this refers only to what has been realized by them.
Because it is truly that upon which disciples rely, the conclusion below states: "One who practices this contemplation is said to practice right contemplation.

Furthermore, regarding this wondrous Dharma, one must clearly understand its freedom from the afflictions; the World-Transcending King of Physicians’ compassion is so profound that he does not allow the poisonous dregs to mingle with the *tīrāmaṇḍa* (clarified butter).
[Private Note: Second, the explanation of the characteristics of the four illnesses. First, the inquiry.
What are the four types of illness? There are two explanations for these four.
First, the illness of fabrication: if there is a person who speaks thus, "I shall perform various practices within my original mind," this is the illness of fabrication.
To seek *pariniṣpanna-bodhi* (perfect enlightenment), because that nature of perfect enlightenment cannot be attained through effort, is called an "affliction" (*vyādhi*).

The first phrase indicates the name; "if again," and so forth, defines its characteristics; "those who speak" refers to the intention behind the words; "that perfect," and so forth, points to the essence in order to refute [the notion of effort];
the subsequent phrases conclude the name. The three sections below are identical. (Guifeng) "Engaging in various practices" means to arouse the mind and set it in motion.

Regarding the eighty-four thousand gates of the *pāramitās* where body and speech assist one another, since one cannot sublate cultivation with nature, they all belong to biased and heterodox asceticism;
they merely serve to suppress and extinguish the mind, lacking any further path [to liberation]. (Zhuangnan)
Second, the illness of non-exertion.
Second, as for the illness of non-exertion: if there are people who speak thus, saying, "We now do not sever birth-and-death nor seek nirvāṇa;
since neither nirvāṇa nor birth-and-death arises or ceases, we shall leave all things as they are, following the nature of all phenomena."
To seek perfect enlightenment while that nature of perfect enlightenment is not something that can be arbitrarily attained is called a "sickness.

To allow everything to follow its own dharma-nature—just as fire is hot and water is wet, each possessing its own distinct nature—and to say that the false follows from the other's falsity and the true follows from the other's truth, each according to its own mind: why should one necessarily [strive against this]?
If one alters the aforementioned practice, one will instead gallop about in search of the Buddha; this is merely to let the body and mind run wild.
Even if one allows neither good nor evil to be restricted, this is termed the nature of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). (Guifeng). This is the third illness of cessation.

Third is the illness of cessation. If there is another person who says, "I shall now cause all thoughts in my own mind to cease forever, so that I may attain the quiescent equality of all natures and seek perfect enlightenment," then that nature of perfect enlightenment is not attained through cessation;
therefore, it is called an illness.

Regarding the statement, "To attain the nature of the lack of nature in all phenomena is neither to identify with the nature of awakening nor merely to conjoin with it" (Guifeng), this refers to the previously mentioned point that one does not even extinguish or suppress the various deluded minds. This constitutes the fourth elimination of afflictions.
Fourth is the sickness of extinction. If there is someone who speaks thus: "I have now forever severed all afflictions;
body and mind are ultimately empty and non-existent—how much more so the false realms of the sense organs and their objects? All are eternally stilled.
Yet they wish to seek perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*), that nature of perfect enlightenment is not a state of stillness; therefore, this is called a sickness.
The essence of awakening is numinous and luminous; it is not merely quiescent extinction. If one now extinguishes delusions to abide in quiescence, how could that be in accord [with the true nature]?

(Guifeng) If one acts, there are the three studies and six perfections, known as various practices. If one follows [the natural course], then birth and death, nirvana, arising and ceasing do not exist.

If one stops, it is the cessation of discursive thought and the realization of the nature. If one extinguishes, it is the severing of delusions and returning to stillness. How could these be considered faults? It is only when one clings to them that they become so.
Because these thoughts seek to attain Perfect Enlightenment, they are all termed "illnesses.
The two phrases, "desiring to seek Perfect Enlightenment," constitute the very essence of the illness (Cishi). Third, the conclusion indicates the correct and the erroneous.
One who is free from the four illnesses knows purity. To contemplate in this manner is called right contemplation; to contemplate otherwise is called wrong contemplation.
By using the preceding four practices to examine one's own mind, if it falls into any one of these gates, one knows that it is an illness; therefore, it is said "to be free."

One then knows that [the mind] is pure; however, these four preceding gates are all exhortations and praises found in various sutras, let alone the fact that the first three contemplations already contain such texts.
Now, there are two reasons why these are considered "illnesses": first, among those four, none possess the wisdom of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*);
second, they merely follow one's own impulses and dwell exclusively in a single practice. If one can achieve thorough penetration in all four, [these faults will be eliminated].

Not being obstructed by a single gate means that within these four [approaches], one enters the Way through all of them simultaneously. Thus, the Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra says: "One merely eliminates the illness, but does not eliminate the dharma.
To eliminate the dharma is precisely right contemplation (*samyag-darśana*). Although one does not grasp at the four illnesses, one's wisdom and understanding remain clear;
yet one must not fear falling into these four and consequently fail to establish one's resolve and maintain one's integrity. Furthermore, there are those who hear this...
These four errors depart from the four [correct principles], yet they further give rise to mental states that act according to one’s own whims and form distinct views;
therefore, they are called "perverse contemplations. Furthermore, those who practice such contemplation depart from the four [principles], while those with other views grasp at the four.

(Guifeng) If one realizes the principle of the inherent nature, then all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are non-active; how could there be any of the four ailments? Therefore, these are attachments of the mind.
Thus, all things are demons when they contradict one's nature, yet all four are medicines when they accord with it. It depends on the method one employs and the person who applies it.
If a thief becomes a general, that general must be protected; if he remains a thief, how could he maintain his integrity?

Examine each point with care so that attachment does not arise. Cultivate contemplation based on this: if you act in accordance with it, it is correct; if you act contrary to it, it is erroneous. (Private Note) *Note: The term "作" (zuò) at the end of the passage indicates that the preceding text is a personal commentary or private note.*

Cessation and naturalness, extinction and non-existence—none are not wondrous medicines; it is only when one clings to them that they become illnesses. Thus we know that as for gain and loss, who is to blame?
Regarding right contemplation and false contemplation, the *Zhao lun* states: "Because one sees the reality of dharmas and knows them, it is called right contemplation;

if it differs from this, it becomes false contemplation. The *Sutra of the Sixteen Contemplations* distinguishes and clarifies this in such a manner, using the explanatory terminology to elucidate it.
It is called "contemplation" (*guan*) because it involves contemplating phenomena (*dharma*). In this sutra, as in the *Zhao lun*, it refers specifically to the seeing of phenomena (*jianfa*);
by distinguishing and revealing the heterodox from the orthodox, it is collectively termed "contemplation" (Zhu'an). Third, the response concerning the practice of cultivation.
Good son, those living beings in the final age who wish to practice should, for the remainder of their lives, make offerings to virtuous friends and serve spiritual benefactors (*kalyāṇamitra*).
When those spiritual benefactors come to approach them, they should sever arrogance; if they depart, they should sever resentment.
Even when confronted with conditions of opposition or compliance, they should regard them as being like empty space, understanding that body and mind are ultimately equal.
All sentient beings are of one essence and without difference; practicing in this way, one enters Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*).

If the mind is obscured by arrogance, one will not enter the Path. Furthermore, a single thought of anger gives rise to a million obstacles; not only does one lose the Path, but one also falls into the three miserable realms (*apāya*).
Therefore, causing all such [afflictions] to be severed and kept at a distance is called "contrary," while approaching them [with mindfulness] is called "conforming. Moreover, to oppose...
When emotions follow [the mind], it is called "rebellious"; when emotions follow [the nature], it is called "compliant. That which is like empty space is a mind that undergoes no change (Guifeng).

The heading says, "For those who wish to practice," and the conclusion says, "Only then does one enter Perfect Enlightenment. This indicates that what is manifested is the capacity; this is the practice of Perfect Enlightenment.

If one discusses the characteristics of contemplation, their meaning is fully detailed in the preceding chapter. Thus we know that seeking a teacher and requesting the Dharma—this Dharma is Perfect Enlightenment—and arising in accordance with the Dharma.
How could there be any divergent paths in practice? The first section concludes with a renewed exhortation to serve the teacher; the subsequent section demonstrates the method for settling the mind.

The teacher is mentioned again because one who delights in the Way must revere the teacher, and because a beginner in cultivation must seek reliance upon another, as there is ground for inquiry and doubt.
Regarding "the equality of body and mind," both are the Dharma-realm; regarding "sentient beings being of the same substance," self and other are one.
"Thus, through this, the practice of wondrous, perfect enlightenment advances" (Private Note). Fourth, the answer regarding the removal of afflictions has two parts;
first, pointing out the source of the illness:
"Good son, that sentient beings in the末法 (mofa) age cannot achieve the Way is due to the existence of beginningless self and other, and hatred and love."
Because they possess all seeds, they have not yet attained liberation.

Although the mutual feelings of hatred and love between self and others have been clarified repeatedly previously, they are restated here because they are the seeds [of affliction] and are subtle ailments that enter the Path.
Due to these seeds, it is difficult to accord with perfect clarity (Guifeng). As soon as hatred and love arise, the Holy Path [is obstructed].
Because it is difficult to accomplish and requires deep investigation of its source, it is called the "seed" (Zhangnan). Second, the method for eliminating [afflictions] is shown:
if there is a person who regards an enemy as their own parent, with a mind free of duality, they will immediately eliminate all illnesses;
regarding all phenomena, the same applies to hatred and love toward self and others.

Because one contemplates enemies and kin with equality, the mind is without duality; because the mind is without duality, one eliminates hatred and love, as well as the distinctions between self and other, the supported and the supporting, the true and the false.
If one can contemplate all things with perfect equanimity, then hatred and love regarding all phenomena will also be exhausted;
thus it is said, "it is also like this. All commentaries cite the practice of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) as the explanation for the "empty and troublesome phenomena" (*śūnyāḥ kleśadharmāḥ*).
[Commentary]: Fifth, the response on generating the aspiration for enlightenment.
"Good son, sentient beings in the final age who wish to seek Perfect Enlightenment should generate the aspiration by speaking these words:
'Throughout the entirety of space, I shall cause all sentient beings to enter ultimate Perfect Enlightenment; within that Perfect Enlightenment, there is no [duality]...'"
The one who attains awakening eliminates all marks of self, other, person, and so forth; thus, by generating the mind of enlightenment in this way, one does not fall into false views.
This corresponds to the possession of the four minds described in the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāpāramitā Sūtra*. Maitreya’s verse states: "Vast, foremost, constant, and its mind non-erroneous.
Regarding "exhausting the entirety of space": the vast mind refers to all sentient beings. As it says: [the vast mind is directed toward] all sentient beings throughout the reaches of empty space.
"I cause all beings of the four modes of birth and nine categories to enter the ultimate, perfect *bodhi*, which is the foremost mind.
This refers to the constant mind that, within perfect *bodhi*, has no grasping for enlightenment.
"There are truly no sentient beings who attain extinction"—this refers to the non-inverted mind that eliminates all marks of self, other, person, and phenomena.
It is said: "If there are signs of a self, persons, and so forth, one is not a bodhisattva.

All Buddhas, throughout the stages of the causal ground, give rise to this mind and cultivate according to this vow before finally attaining perfect enlightenment (Guifeng). There are two verses in praise of these two [points]. First, the heading.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
[The second section, the main verses, is incomplete; the fourth section, excluding the text on curing illness, begins here. First, the verse on seeking a teacher:
Pujue, you should know: In the final age, all sentient beings Who wish to seek a virtuous friend...
One should seek right view, with a mind far removed from the two vehicles.
(These two verses rely on the Dharma.
Within the Dharma, one eliminates the four maladies, namely: effort, cessation, indifference, and extinction.
The three verses on practice:
Draw near to others without pride; Remain far removed from malice and resentment.
Upon encountering various circumstances, one should give rise to a sense of wonder, As if the Buddha had appeared in the world; One must not transgress the non-disciplinary rules.

The root of the precepts is eternally pure, as in the verse on the long-term absence [of transgression] following the appearance of a Buddha; there is no violation, for this is not a matter of non-discipline.

The root of the precepts is eternally pure, which is a subsequent verse summarizing the passage from the *Guru-paryeṣaṇā* (Seeking the Teacher) that does not allow sentient beings to enter into non-discipline. Furthermore, regarding the present matter:
The Master’s verses within the practice section mutually clarify the intent of the sutra, as teacher and disciple achieve one another (Private Note).
The four verses on generating the mind of enlightenment:
To deliver all sentient beings, ultimately entering Perfect Enlightenment, free from the marks of self, other, and person.
By relying on right wisdom, one shall transcend false views and realize awakening and *parinirvāṇa*.
(The final phrase is longer; in Sanskrit it is *parinirvāṇa*, which is translated as "extinction" [mièdù]. Master Sengzhao said:
"Great affliction is forever extinguished, and one transcends the four currents. It is also called "perfect stillness" [yuánjì]. Xianshou said: "There is no virtue that is not complete.")
It is called "Perfectly Obstructing" because there is nothing that is not exhausted; it is also called "Quiescence" because birth and death are eternally ended (Private Note).

○ Fourth, the Chapter on Perfect Enlightenment, which reveals the method and procedure, has two parts: first, the formal inquiry, [which has three sub-sections]. First, the ritual posture for advancing with the question.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Perfect Enlightenment rose from his seat amidst the great assembly, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet,
circumambulated him three times to the right, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
Second, the formal presentation of the discourse has two parts. First, expressing gratitude for what preceded:
"The Greatly Compassionate World-Honored One has extensively expounded various skillful means for pure awakening for our sakes, so that sentient beings in the final age may achieve great benefit."
Second, the request following [the teaching]:

"World-Honored One, we have now attained awakening. However, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, for those sentient beings of the final age who have not yet attained awakening, how should they dwell in retreat to cultivate this pure realm of Perfect Enlightenment? Within this Perfect Enlightenment, there are three kinds..."
"Pure contemplation—what is its primary basis? I only pray that, out of great compassion, you will bestow great benefit upon this great assembly and sentient beings of the末法 (mofa, final dharma) age.

Although the question concerns the period after [the Buddha's] parinirvāṇa, it also includes the time when the Buddha is still in the world; therefore, the answer below states: "If the Buddha is currently present, one should contemplate correctly."
Only those who dwell in the summer retreat (an-gyō) establish themselves in the Pure Abodes (jōju), which is the site of enlightenment (dōjō).

Regarding the question "What constitutes the beginning?"—this asks for the skillful means (hōben) of observing the beginning [of practice] (shikan-shu) [Private Note]. With threefold prostrations, they manifest their profound sincerity.
Having spoken these words, they prostrated themselves with their five limbs touching the ground; thus they made this request three times, beginning again and again.
The two Buddhas answered them thrice, first praising and granting their request.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Perfect Enlightenment, saying: "Excellent, excellent, son of good family! You all..."
"You have been able to ask the Tathāgata about such skillful means that bring great benefit to all sentient beings;
listen attentively now, and I shall explain it for you.
The two of them accepted the instruction.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Perfect Enlightenment, having received the instruction with joy, along with the great assembly, listened in silence.
Part Three: The Direct Answer, in two sections. First, the prose section, in two parts. First, the duration of the summer retreat (*varṣā*), in two parts. First, referring back to what preceded.
"Good son, whether the Buddha remains in the world, after his parinirvāṇa, or during the final age of the Dharma,
if there are sentient beings who possess the nature of the Mahāyāna, who have faith in the Buddha’s secret, great, perfectly enlightened mind, and wish to practice it—

whether they are in a monastery dwelling with a community of followers or due to some circumstantial necessity— they should contemplate and examine things according to their capacity, as I have already explained."

"Extinction" (nirvāṇa) refers to both the True Dharma and the Semblance Dharma; "nature" (gotra) refers to the causal factor for awakening (the *jñāna-hetu*). "Gārama" is translated here as "monastic garden" (*saṅghārāma*).
As previously stated in the "Chapter on the Universal Eye": "He settled his disciples in quiet chambers for meditative seclusion. (Private Annotation).
Second, the formal exposition has four parts. First, one must establish a period of three types of retreats.
Furthermore, if there are no other circumstances or causes for interruption, one should establish a ritual site (*maṇḍala*) and set a time limit:
a long-term retreat of one hundred and twenty days, a medium-term retreat of one hundred days, or a short-term retreat of eighty days, in which one establishes a pure dwelling.

When a Bodhisattva encounters beneficial circumstances, they should simply respond to those conditions; however, if there is no such benefit, one must establish a *maṇḍala* (place of practice), apply oneself with diligence and resolve to seek the sacred fruit.
Thus, all three periods [of retreat] constitute self-cultivation (*sva-caryā*). To distinguish this from benefiting others, it is termed "the affairs of others" (*para-kārya*).
Furthermore, matters such as threats from kings or bandits and life-threatening dangers may also be termed "the affairs of others. If one exceeds the fixed three periods [of retreat], then...
If weariness arises due to a short duration, one's practice will not reach completion; therefore, it is appropriate to extend the period to three kalpas, which carries no further hidden meaning.

Nevertheless, when applied to the three faculties, there are two interpretations: first, regarding the ease or difficulty of exhausting the hindrances, the long period is assigned to those of dull faculties, the middle period to those of middling faculties, and the short period to those of superior faculties. Second, regarding diligence and indolence, it is as follows:
Is this not what is meant by the statement that these faculties have degrees of sharpness or dullness and their timing has periods of nearness or distance?

To prescribe medicine according to the illness, one establishes the Pure Abodes (śuddhāvāsa), desiring to make both the internal and external pure, the body and mind immaculate, and the phenomena and principles harmonious.
The Great Sage [Guifeng Zongmi] established these three periods so that practitioners may measure their own strength, whether they are capable of long-term or short-term practice.
Why must one necessarily face the three directions? Furthermore, this merely restricts the time limit and does not regulate physical posture;

among the four types of samādhi, it belongs to the category of various methods for walking meditation (caṅkrama). (Zhuāngnán) Regarding the method for establishing the *dharmadhātu* (site of practice): first, one should smear the ground with fragrant mud and so forth;
hence it is called the "Pure Abode" (*śuddhāvāsa*) or "Compassionate Chamber. Second, the method for practicing within the *dharmadhātu*.
Whether the Buddha is present or has entered parinirvāṇa, one should practice correct contemplation;
by fashioning an image and maintaining it in mind and visualizing it with the eyes, one gives rise to right mindfulness, which is equivalent to the day the Tathāgata remains in the world.

By suspending banners and flowers for twenty-one days, prostrating before the names of the Buddhas of the ten directions, and seeking compassion through repentance, one will encounter auspicious signs and attain lightness and ease of mind.
For the seven days following the passing, one should single-mindedly focus the mind on mindfulness.
If the Buddha were still in the world, there would be no need to laboriously fashion images; since the Buddha has already passed away, one must rely upon his physical form and appearance.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* quotes a sūtra as saying: "If one does not conceive difficult thoughts regarding clay or wood, how could one not know that the nature of the image is equal to empty space? (3)
The body appears as if perfectly complete, with the four virtues undiminished; to cultivate such mental visualization is no different from the time when the Tathāgata was still in the world.

These twenty-one days constitute the preliminary practice of skillful means prior to formal cultivation (Dongyang). As for the creation of an image—whether by painting or carving—it serves as a support for maintaining the visualization that the Buddha does not pass away.
