Furthermore, the characteristics of Sudatta are neither characteristics nor non-characteristics; they are mind and are [the manifestation of] mind.
Only then can one be said to have generated the adornment of right mindfulness. The essentials of making offerings require the utmost sincerity;
for brevity’s sake, it is simply said that one should suspend banners and flowers. Regarding the periods of twenty-one days and so forth, these are the preliminary expedients for focusing the mind.

One should perform prostrations, repentance, and worship of the Buddha, entreating his empowerment and protection, while confessing transgressions and seeking the removal of long-standing obstacles, following the ritual procedures as set forth in various sutras.

There are ten categories of such experiences: seeing light, beholding flowers, hearing sounds, having dreams of inspiration, or seeing jewel characters or seals upon one's arms, or being touched on the crown by a golden hand.
Encountering these sublime states, the body and mind advance further; hence they are called "light and ease. Yet even encountering such states still belongs to the realm of skillful means (*upāya*).
As stated in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*: "To temporarily attain such [states] is not a holy realization; do not mistake them for holiness."
"The mind is called the realm of goodness; if one takes this to be the realization of the holy, one will instead receive manifold evils. This refers to those who exclusively focus their mindfulness.

In the correct cultivation of *Avalokiteśvara-bodhi* (Perfect Enlightenment), one should maintain right mindfulness and remain far removed from all illusions; such is the practice throughout the three periods [of the retreat].
(Compassionate Chamber) As for "repentance" (*chànhuì*), its full name is *chànmó*, which translates as "regretting one's transgressions. To explain it separately: "Chàn" (Repentance) refers to...
To speak of "exposing past transgressions" means to repent; to speak of "rectifying the past and cultivating the future" refers to the methods of confession (*chān*).
These do not exceed the inclusion within the three obstacles: afflictions (*kleśa*), karma, and retribution. Regarding the practitioner who arouses faith, the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* states:

"If one practices *śamatha*, one should dwell in a quiet place, sit upright with a correct mind, and even when the mind wanders and scatters, one should immediately withdraw it and abide in right mindfulness."
One who contemplates should know that there is only mind and no external objects (Guifeng). If we correlate this with the text according to the three types of repentance:
maintaining the visualization in the mind while focusing on the forms is the Repentance of Grasping Signs; bowing the head and seeking compassion is the Ritual Repentance;

and exclusively gathering the mind in mindfulness of non-arising is the Repentance of Non-Birth. However, one who cultivates Perfect Enlightenment must first develop wondrous understanding and only then initiate practice.

Therefore, the first two [periods] are not deficient in the "unborn" (anutpāda). Furthermore, Guifeng categorizes these three periods of seven days as "cultivation within the limit," while all commentaries state they are "expedient means outside the fixed period.
Now, examining the intent of the sutra, the exclusive focus on mindfulness is simply the cultivation of the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*) through the various wheels;
thus, the "Chapter on Bhadrapāla" at the end again mentions the expedient means of the three periods of seven days merely as an addition.
The arrangement of forms, images, and so forth is more extensive than what was previously described; here, however, twenty-five wheels are omitted.

To summarize this, the preceding and succeeding sections mutually clarify one another, and the practitioner should take the various commentaries as their standard. "Prostrating with the head" means touching the head to the ground;
according to the *Rites of Zhou* (Zhouli), the Grand Master of Sacrifices distinguishes nine types of prostration, and this corresponds to the first. "Single-mindedly gathering the mind" means...

Within the three periods [of the year], one practices the single meditation seat (ekāsana) alone, whether in single or double retreat, such that everything is nothing other than the gathering of mindfulness. (Private Note:

This occurs when meeting the summer retreat (*varṣā*) three times, or even if meeting the summer retreat within the period; although one practices Mahāyāna, one does not entirely abandon the Hīnayāna.

Thus, on the days of the retreat, one presents a formal declaration before the Buddha. However, since one is not bound by a retinue of disciples, it ultimately constitutes reliance upon the Great Text.)
Regarding the first of these two initial instructions on relying on the Mahāyāna,

this is the introductory statement: "If, at the commencement of the summer retreat during the three-month *varṣā*, one should dwell as a pure bodhisattva with a mind detached from the Śrāvaka vehicle and without depending on a retinue."

However, when one establishes a *dharmapūjā* site—whether in a monastery or elsewhere—if the fixed period has not yet expired but the beginning of the summer retreat (*varṣā*) has already arrived, entering the assembly for the *anagga* (rainy-season retreat) would violate one’s vow.

If one then forms the intention to enter the summer retreat, those within the *dharmapūjā* site who practice contemplation of the mind will consequently harbor doubts, thinking that the Tathāgata is far removed from their mindfulness. Therefore, in order to clarify this and because the secular [practice] deviates from the Vinaya, [it is said]:

"It is not that the Great [Vehicle] abandons the Small [Vehicle] without cause, nor is there any loss of the assembly; this is the sixfold harmony (ṣaḍ-sāmagrī). If one were to perform the *poṣadha* together, it would hinder the cultivation of mindfulness;
yet if one does not enter the assembly, one might fear violating the disciplinary rules (*vinaya*). Therefore, this decision states that it does not depend upon the assembly" (Guǎngnán).
Second, regarding the legal procedures for establishing the summer retreat (*varṣā*), the method for the face-to-face ritual between two persons says: "Venerable One... (Guìfēng).
I, the bhikṣu [Name], now, within the great boundary of the saṃghārāma at [Place Name], shall observe the three-month summer retreat (varṣā) for the purpose of repairing dilapidated dwellings;
I now rely upon the Great One, the Buddha. (The wording differs from that used for the Small Boundary.)
On the day of the *varṣā* retreat, one should speak thus before the Buddha:

"I, the bhikṣu [or bhikṣuṇī, upāsaka, or upāsikā] named so-and-so, who has mounted the Bodhisattva vehicle and cultivates the practice of quiescence, together enter the pure reality-mark (*dharmatā*) and abide therein.
Taking Great Perfect Enlightenment as my monastery, I dwell in peace within body and mind, the wisdom of the equality of all phenomena, which is *nirvāṇa*."
Because my own nature is without attachment, I now respectfully request that you do not rely on the śrāvakas,

but rather enter the three-month summer retreat together with the Tathāgatas of the ten directions and the great bodhisattvas; for the sake of cultivating the great causal conditions for the supreme, wondrous enlightenment of a bodhisattva,
I shall not bind myself to a retinue of disciples.
"Bhikṣu" is a Sanskrit term that contains three meanings: first, "frightener of Māras"; second, "mendicant" (lit. "one who begs");

and third, "one of pure precepts. "Bhikṣuṇī" refers to a female bhikṣu. "Upāsaka" means "male lay follower" (lit. "one who attends closely"), and "upāsikā" means "female lay follower" (lit. "one who attends closely").
This refers to those who attend closely upon bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs to receive their services; that is, those who have taken the three refuges and the five precepts.

These are the men and women of the [Buddhist] community; while the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) is restricted to the two assemblies [of monks and nuns], the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna) benefits both the ordained and the laity.

As for "So-and-so," each person’s name should be called out. Regarding the differences between the Small and Great Vehicles concerning the summer retreat (*varṣā*), there are briefly eight distinctions:

first, the difference in basis, namely the distinct boundaries (*sīmā*) and the perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna*); second, the difference between the provisional and the real, namely the actualized and the manifested; third, the difference in maintenance, namely conventional phenomena (*saṃvṛti-dharma*) and ultimate reality (*dharmatā*). Fourth...

When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, all the bodhisattvas, devas, nāgas, ghosts, spirits, and the eight classes of followers, as well as the various heavenly kings, the Brahma kings, and the entire great assembly, having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly rejoiced; they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
Since the concluding assembly mentions that the eight classes of beings were "verified" as having heard the teaching together with the others, it is clear that not only bodhisattvas were present;

furthermore, deities such as devas and nāgas must have internally realized the *dharmatā* while externally manifesting these forms. These individuals—whose precepts may have been lax but whose aspiration for the vehicle was urgent—were all included in the Dharma assembly and experienced great joy.

This concludes the benefits of hearing the sutra, which do not exceed the *siddhānta*. Furthermore, by means of the four teachings (*catur-yāna*), this [present teaching] is now specifically identified and demonstrated.

Narrated by the Śramaṇa Zongmi of Caotang Monastery on Mount Zhongnan:

"Yuan, heng, li, and zhen" are the virtues of Qian (Heaven). They originate from the single qi (vital energy). "Nitya, sukha, ātman, and śubha" (eternal, blissful, self, and pure) are the virtues of the Buddha.
It is rooted in the single mind. By concentrating the vital energy (*qi*), one attains pliancy; by cultivating the single mind, one accomplishes the Way.

As for this mind: it is profound, empty, wondrous, and pure; it is brilliant, radiant, numinous, and luminous. It neither departs nor arrives, darkly penetrating the three periods of time. It is neither middle nor outside, transparently pervading the ten directions.
It is neither extinguished nor born; how could it be harmed by the four mountains? It is detached from nature and detached from form; what need is there for the five colors?

It can render one blind. Dwelling within the stream of birth and death, the black pearl shines alone amidst the vast blue sea; perched upon the shore of nirvana, the crescent moon is solitary and bright against the azure sky.
How great it is that the myriad dharmas derive their origin from this! The myriad dharmas are empty and false, arising through the convergence of conditions.
The nature of arising dharmas is fundamentally non-existent; all is but consciousness. Consciousness is like an illusion or a dream, yet it is simply the One Mind. When the mind is quiescent...

Know that this is called the Perfect Enlightenment (Cakravajra). It is all-pervading and pure, with no room for anything else within it. Therefore, its virtuous functions are boundless, yet all share a single nature.
When this nature arises as phenomena, the object and wisdom are distinct; when these phenomena attain the nature, body and mind become vast and open.
Compared to the Sea-Seal Samādhi, it surpasses even the great void. Vast and expansive, brilliant and radiant, it utterly transcends the realm of thought and speculation. I—

The Buddha realized this and, pitying those beings who were deluded by it, twice sighed in wonder at its marvel. He contemplated the Great Matter three times; having perfected the Ten Powers, he was able to crush the demonic armies beneath the tree.
Thereupon, he gave rise to the Four Minds, desiring to reveal the treasure-store within the house. Yet, they were like those who lose their heads and abandon their fathers.

Awakening may be either easy or difficult; thus, in the Garden of Immortals and the Field of Enlightenment, the teachings were established as sudden and gradual. The gradual approach sets forth the distinctions of the five periods, wherein emptiness and existence manifest alternately.
The sudden approach lacks even the differentiation of the two truths, for its profound spirit is beyond all dependence.

Is this present sutra not of the sudden type? Therefore, when the Tathāgata enters the Land of Quiescent Light, ordinary beings and sages share a single source; he manifests the Body of Enjoyment, where the principal and the retinue assemble together.
The Great Being Mañjuśrī first inquired about the cause of its original arising; the Bhagavat, the Most Honored One, first set forth the ultimate fruit.
Illuminating this true essence, one extinguishes those dream-like forms. Knowing that there is no self or person, who is it that undergoes saṃsāra? All these are but various illusory transformations.

Born from the awakened mind, when illusion is exhausted, awakening becomes perfect; the mind penetrates all and phenomena pervade everywhere. The mind is fundamentally the Buddha, yet due to the arising of thoughts, it drifts and sinks.
The shore does not actually move, yet because the boat travels, it appears to rush by. Suddenly eliminate the false ruler, and the void will no longer produce flowers.

Gradually exhausting the source of craving, there is no ore from which gold can be further refined; in principle, there is nothing to be cultivated or realized, yet wisdom appears to have gradations. One recognizes the errors of each preceding stage as one ascends to the subsequent levels.

How much more so regarding the arising and ceasing of delusions—how could they compare to those whose virtues are equal to perfect luminosity? Nevertheless, it is like a fine steed emerging from its stall.

The shadow of the whip has already been brandished; the Great Jewel buried in dust requires the application of a method of governance. Therefore, the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*) are clarified and made lucid, such that both the provisional and the real are entered together.

The various wheels interlace and alternate, cultivated either singly or in combination to achieve perfection. The four signs (*catur-lakṣaṇa*) remain latent within the spirit, not rejected by awakening; the four ailments (*catuḥ-roga*) reveal their essence, and the flower of the mind shines forth with brilliance.

Furthermore, one is instructed to apply the preparatory practices (*prayoga*) through long-term, medium-term, and short-term periods of focused mindfulness and mental containment, whether specifically or universally.

Through mutual cultivation, the obstacles of karma and the obstacles of delusion are extinguished. One achieves the body of wisdom; when stillness reaches its ultimate limit, awakening pervades hundreds of thousands of worlds, and the realm of the Buddha manifests before one.
For this reason, hearing these five names surpasses the merit of bestowing jewels upon lands, and explaining the meaning of even half a verse [surpasses the merit of giving away one’s own body].
He surpasses the sands of the Ganges of those of the Lesser Vehicle; this is truly because there is no dharma he does not uphold and no capacity that he does not reach. Alas!

When the songs of Ba are harmonized with the crowd, the semblance-measure (pramāṇa) leaps from the monkey-like minds of men. When the "Snowy Melody" (the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*) is rarely responded to, the definitive meaning (nītārtha) remains hidden within the Dragon Treasury.

Zongmi devoted himself to the Classics of Lu since childhood and investigated the ancient texts of Zhuguo after donning his cap. Yet both were submerged in the traps of the teaching-tools (the *upāya*), tasting only the dregs. Fortunately, [he found clarity] upon the banks of the Fu River.
The needle and the mustard seed meet; Zen encounters the Southern School, and the Teaching meets this scripture. Under a single word, the ground of the mind is opened;
within a single scroll, the sky of meaning shines brightly. Recently, I realized that the Way is not a fixed way and that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent;

now I know that my own mind is the Buddha-mind, and I shall certainly become a Buddha. Yet, since the Buddha is called the One of All-Knowledge (*sarvajñā*), and cultivation relies upon extensive learning, I must therefore continue to practice.
I traveled to a hundred cities, sitting and exploring the various scriptures. Although my lectures were perhaps overly expansive, my learning was modeled after that of Dao’an.

Having been unworthily bathed by the grace of the Tathāgata’s acceptance, I have mistakenly received the seal of a true disciple. Meeting my kinsmen and friends once more, I am moved even deeper by the Buddha’s benevolence. Long have I lamented my own solitude and poverty;
now, intending to present this Dharma-gift, I have gathered the Prajñāpāramitā, threaded together the Avataṃsaka, extracted the essentials of the Vinaya, and elucidated the Vijñaptimātratā. However—

Among the myriad varieties of medical prescriptions, one should select those that provide an appropriate remedy; among the thousand kinds of treasures of the ocean, one first seeks the wish-fulfilling gem.

Observing that its literary richness and breadth of meaning truly rival the *Saṃpuṭa* (Flower Garland) Sūtra, and that its pointing to the essence and its application to the occasion have no peer in the *Awakening of Faith*, I have therefore examined various treatises and repeatedly studied the works of a hundred schools to sharpen my faculties before composing this commentary.
With my mind merged in the Sage’s intent, I have applied my thoughts with utmost refinement and precision to elucidate its meaning.

I have prepared this work, encompassing both the characteristics and nature [of reality], and integrating both sudden and gradual approaches to meditation, into three fascicles for the transmission of those with diligent learning.

However, as the faculties, desires, and natures of superior, middling, and inferior types differ, I shall now model myself after that [principle of] "bending to complete" [the individual], following what is easy and simple.

Having further extracted the essential points, I provide a direct commentary on the root scripture, so that practitioners may realize phenomena as mind and achieve daily increase in virtue and daily diminution of afflictions.
